title: Apolipoprotein E4 (ApoE4) causes disruption of glypican-1 recycling and processing in ApoE4/4 fibroblasts and induced neurons.
abstract: The apolipoprotein E4 (ApoE4) isoform confers increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. ApoE2 and ApoE3 can be S-nitrosylated (Cys-SNO), but not ApoE4. The recycling heparan sulfate (HS) proteoglycan glypican-1 (GPC1) can also carry SNO and release HS by a Cu/NO dependent cleavage. ApoE3/3 and ApoE4/4 fibroblasts and the respective induced neurons (-iN) were exposed to inhibitors of NO-synthases (NOS), to NO donor or ascorbate and examined by immunofluorescence microscopy. Exposure to NO donor increased co-localization between ApoE3-SNO and GPC1 in ApoE3/3 fibroblasts. Co-localization between ApoE3 and GPC1 diminished when cNOS/NOS3 was inhibited in ApoE3/3 fibroblasts. Exposure to NO donor or ascorbate indicated almost fully utilized capacity to release HS from GPC1. When nNOS/NOS1 and iNOS/NOS2 were inhibited in ApoE3/3-iN, release of HS decreased, and exposure to ascorbate again showed that the capacity to release HS was almost fully utilized. In ApoE4/4 fibroblasts endosome transport was retarded and HS and GPC1-SNO accumulated in late endosomes. Inhibition of cNOS/NOS3 in ApoE4/4 fibroblasts had no effect on HS release but inhibition of iNOS/NOS2 had a substantial effect. Exposure to NO donor or ascorbate revealed unutilized capacity to release HS from GPC1. In ApoE4/4-iN, nNOS/NOS1 and iNOS/NOS2 were major producers of NO. Inhibition of nNOS/NOS1 and iNOS/NOS2 in ApoE4/4-iN again showed unutilized capacity to release HS. We propose that expression of ApoE4, which retards endosome trafficking, but also activates iNOS/NOS2, results in accumulation of GPC1-SNO and slow exit of HS from endosomes which can be restored by ascorbate.
authors: Cheng F, Fransson LÅ, Mani K
overview: The apolipoprotein E4 (ApoE4) isoform confers increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease.
main: Exposure to NO donor increased co-localization between ApoE3-SNO and GPC1 in ApoE3/3 fibroblasts.

title: Intraoperative technology in skull base and vascular neurosurgery: a two-stage cross-sectional national survey.
abstract: Skull base and vascular neurosurgery rely on diverse intraoperative technologies, but contemporary data describing how frequently they are used at the level of individual operations are limited. On behalf of the Society of British Neurological Surgeons (SBNS) MedTech Committee, we aimed to establish a dated descriptive baseline of reported technology use across three operative paradigms. We conducted a two-stage cross-sectional survey of neurosurgeons in the UK and Ireland via the Society of British Neurological Surgeons (SBNS). Six MedTech Committee members compiled a pragmatic technology list. Respondents reported frequency of use for three exemplar procedures: transsphenoidal pituitary adenoma, retrosigmoid vestibular schwannoma, and pterional aneurysm surgery. Use was recorded on a four-point ordinal scale and analysed descriptively, with Kendall's tau-b used to explore the relationship between experience and reported use. Twenty-four responses from 20 of the 32 adult or mixed adult-paediatric UK units were analysed (11 units per index procedure). Reported use was strongly procedure specific. Neuronavigation was used always or almost always by 8/12 transsphenoidal respondents but infrequently elsewhere. Endoscopy had displaced microscopy in transsphenoidal surgery, whereas microscopy was used always or almost always by all retrosigmoid and pterional respondents. Indocyanine green and micro-Doppler were routine for aneurysms. Neurophysiological monitoring was universal for vestibular schwannoma but evenly divided for aneurysms. Exoscopes, intraoperative MRI and robotics were used infrequently or not at all; augmented reality was reported by 5/13 pterional respondents. No association was found between experience and reported use, though this was underpowered. Reported intraoperative technology use is strongly shaped by operative paradigm, with established technologies clustering around recurring procedural needs. Newer technologies were used infrequently. Because availability was not recorded, non-use cannot be distinguished from lack of access. These data provide a dated baseline against which future change can be assessed.
authors: Ali AMS, Hanrahan J, Turner C, Alalade A, Boukas A, Paraskevopoulos D, Plaha P, Marcus HJ
overview: Skull base and vascular neurosurgery rely on diverse intraoperative technologies, but contemporary data describing how frequently they are used at the level of individual operations are limited.
main: Reported use was strongly procedure specific.

title: Guam disease features chronic traumatic encephalopathy-like tau seeds in brain and spinal cord.
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis/parkinsonism-dementia complex (ALS/PDC) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder that was once hyperendemic in the island of Guam (Mariana Islands, US) and a few other Pacific locales. Despite extensive investigations into its origins, the etiology of ALS/PDC remains unclear. ALS/PDC is, at the neuropathology level, characterized by tau-dominant multiple proteinopathy in brain and spinal cord. It was recently reported that Guam ALS/PDC brain extracts exhibit tau seeding activity in fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET)-based biosensor cells. To build upon those findings and explore the nature of tau seeds in ALS/PDC in more detail, we used an alanine mutational scanning (Ala scan) approach to determine the seeding profile of tau in nervous tissues of Guam ALS/PDC cases. First, we confirmed the detection of tau seeding activity in ALS/PDC brain samples in tau biosensor cells. Notably, we could also detect potent tau seeding activity in spinal cord. Subsequent Ala scan assays demonstrated that ALS/PDC tau displays an aggregate incorporation pattern that resembles that of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE)-type tau. This result is consistent with recent electron cryo-microscopy studies of tau, which revealed that ALS/PDC tau filaments are predominantly of the CTE-type. The structural characteristics and seeding behaviour of ALS/PDC tau, as well as the regional distribution of tau pathology at post-mortem, suggest that ALS/PDC is a CTE-like tauopathy.
authors: Saez-Calveras N, Verheijen BM, Morgan N, Hill E, Chabria P, Taylor S, Tak Y, Oyanagi K, Kakita A, Song Y
overview: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis/parkinsonism-dementia complex (ALS/PDC) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder that was once hyperendemic in the island of Guam (Mariana Islands, US) and a few other Pacific locales.
main: Subsequent Ala scan assays demonstrated that ALS/PDC tau displays an aggregate incorporation pattern that resembles that of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE)-type tau.

title: Enhancer-targeted CRISPR-A rescues haploinsufficiency and mutant phenotypes in organoid models of autism.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable condition with diverse clinical presentations. Approximately 15% of the genetic susceptibility of ASD is imparted by de novo haploinsufficient mutations of major effect. We mapped enhancers of two high-confidence autism genes, CHD8 and SCN2A, and used CRISPR-based gene activation targeting enhancers (eCRISPR-A) in human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived excitatory neurons and cerebral forebrain organoids to correct the effects of haploinsufficiency, taking advantage of the presence of a wild-type allele of each gene and endogenous gene regulation. Here we show that eCRISPR-A induced a sustained increase in CHD8 and SCN2A expression specifically in mutant neurons and cortical organoids, with rescue of gene expression levels and mutation-associated phenotypes, including gene expression and physiology. These data support gene activation via targeting enhancers of haploinsufficient genes as a therapeutic intervention in ASD and other neurodevelopmental disorders.
authors: Chen GT, Nair G, Osorio AJ, Holley SM, Ghassemzadeh K, Zhou Y, Gonzalez J, Martin JM, Lu C, Sanjana NE
overview: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable condition with diverse clinical presentations.
main: Here we show that eCRISPR-A induced a sustained increase in CHD8 and SCN2A expression specifically in mutant neurons and cortical organoids, with rescue of gene expression levels and mutation-associated phenotypes, including gene expression and physiology.

title: Echinacoside Attenuates α-synuclein Pathology and Lysosomal Dysfunction in PFF-Induced Models Relevant to Parkinson's Disease.
abstract: Abnormal aggregation of α-synuclein (α-syn) and impaired lysosomal degradation are core pathological features of Parkinson's disease (PD). Echinacoside (ECH), the major active component of Cistanche, has been shown to protect dopaminergic neurons in MPTP-induced PD models, but its effects on α-syn clearance and lysosomal function remain unclear. Here, we established a PD-relevant α-syn pathology mouse model by stereotaxic injection of α-syn pre-formed fibrils (PFFs) into the left striatum of C57BL/6 J mice. Mice were divided into four groups: Control, PFFs, PFFs + ECH20 (low-dose), and PFFs + ECH40 (high-dose). The Control group received intrastriatal injection of 0.9% saline, whereas the other groups received α-syn PFFs. ECH was administered orally at 20 or 40 mg/kg for 1 month after modeling, while the Control and PFFs groups received equal volumes of 0.9% saline by oral gavage. Motor function was assessed by rotarod and pole tests at 1, 3, and 6 months, while tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), phosphorylated α-syn (p-α-syn), and lysosome-related proteins were detected in the substantia nigra. In vitro, SH-SY5Y cells were pretreated with ECH before PFFs exposure to evaluate lysosomal morphology, acidification, and proteolytic activity. BafA1, an inhibitor of vacuolar H+-ATPase, was further used to interfere with lysosomal acidification and lysosomal degradation. Six months after PFF injection, mice exhibited significant motor deficits, decreased TH expression, and increased p-α-syn accumulation, accompanied by abnormal lysosomal aggregation, reduced expression of lysosomal proteins (GBA1, CTSD, CTSB, LAMP2, TMEM175). Oral ECH treatment, particularly at 40 mg/kg, improved motor performance, increased TH expression, reduced p-α-syn accumulation, and partially attenuated lysosome abnormalities. In SH-SY5Y cells, ECH also reduced lysosomal abnormalities and improved acidification and proteolytic readouts after PFF exposure. In addition, BafA1 treatment weakened the improvement in lysosomal functional readouts and partially reversed the reduction in p-α-syn accumulation observed after ECH treatment. These findings suggest that ECH attenuates PFF-induced PD-relevant α-syn pathology and is possibly associated with improved lysosomal function, supporting further investigation of ECH as a candidate intervention targeting α-syn pathology and lysosomal dysfunction in PD.

overview: Abnormal aggregation of α-synuclein (α-syn) and impaired lysosomal degradation are core pathological features of Parkinson's disease (PD).

title: HDAC6 Inhibition Promotes Peripheral Nerve Development and Regeneration via Neurofilament Acetylation.
abstract: Peripheral nerve injury remains challenging due to limited neuronal regeneration. Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6) regulates microtubule dynamics, but its role in peripheral nervous system (PNS) development and repair is incompletely understood. This study investigates the expression, function, and mechanism of HDAC6 in PNS maturation and regeneration. HDAC6 was abundantly expressed in dorsal root ganglia and sciatic nerves. During postnatal development (P1-P28), HDAC6 expression progressively declined, inversely correlating with increased α-tubulin K40 and global acetylation. Pharmacological HDAC6 inhibition with Tubastatin A (Tub A) or suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid (SAHA) accelerated nerve maturation, evidenced by enhanced conduction velocity, myelination, and cytoskeletal integrity. In a sciatic nerve crush model, HDAC6 inhibition promoted functional recovery, axonal regeneration, and remyelination. In vitro, HDAC6 inhibition or siRNA knockdown enhanced neurite outgrowth and growth cone expansion in both motor and sensory neurons. Mechanistically, acetylome identified neurofilament light chain (NEFL) as a novel HDAC6 substrate. Among several hypoacetylated lysine residues post-injury, K316 showed the greatest decrease. Direct HDAC6-NEFL interaction was confirmed by molecular docking and co-immunoprecipitation. Expression of an acetylation-mimetic NEFL (K316Q) mutant promoted neurite outgrowth and growth cone maturation compared with wild-type or acetylation-deficient (K316R) mutants. Collectively, HDAC6 acts as a key negative regulator of PNS development and regeneration, and NEFL K316 acetylation serves as a critical molecular switch for axonal growth. Targeting HDAC6 represents a promising strategy for peripheral nerve repair.
authors: Chen Y, Zhang X, Wu Y, Luo K, Shen M, Ji Y, Ding F, Zhang Q
overview: Peripheral nerve injury remains challenging due to limited neuronal regeneration.
main: Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6) regulates microtubule dynamics, but its role in peripheral nervous system (PNS) development and repair is incompletely understood.

title: iPSC-based Approaches to Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: from Drug Screening to Regenerative Medicine in Early Clinical Translation.
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterised by progressive loss of upper and lower motor neurons (MNs), with limited therapeutic options and modest benefit from currently approved drugs. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have emerged as a versatile platform for ALS research, enabling both regenerative medicine and phenotypic drug screening. iPSC-based transplantation strategies aim to replace lost cells or deliver neuroprotective support, while iPSC-derived MNs support drug discovery and repositioning. In the two decades since their discovery, iPSC technologies have progressed from concept to clinical translation, with both cell therapy products such as AstroRx and XS-228 entering trials and three screened drug candidates, Ropinirole, Bosutinib, and Ezogabine, advancing into clinical trials, underscoring their translational potential. In this review, we summarise iPSC-based approaches to ALS, focusing on cell therapies and drug discovery, highlight factors influencing transplantation success, and discuss ongoing clinical trials. We further discuss constraints that impede clinical trial progress, including limited understanding of ALS pathogenesis, absence of robust biomarkers to guide patient stratification and evaluate treatment response, and technical challenges related to the maturation of iPSC-derived neural cells. Finally, we advocate that advancing iPSC approaches requires both deeper understanding of ALS biology and technical innovation. Key priorities are refining iPSC differentiation protocols to improve neuronal maturity and implementing trial designs with adequate duration and rigorous patient stratification.
authors: Lu JJ, Cheung M
overview: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterised by progressive loss of upper and lower motor neurons (MNs), with limited therapeutic options and modest benefit from currently approved drugs.

title: G-quadruplex profiling using single-cell CUT&Tag offers insight into the epigenetic landscape of the developing mouse brain.
abstract: BACKGROUND: G-quadruplexes (G4s) are non-canonical DNA structures that have gained increasing attention for their potential roles in gene regulation and role in neurodegenerative diseases and cancer. Despite their biological significance, G4 structures have not been studied systematically across tissues and cell types. RESULTS: In this study, we employ G4 single-cell CUT&Tag (G4 scCUT&Tag) to characterize G4 landscapes in postnatal mouse brain cells, leveraging single-cell analytical approaches commonly used in scRNA-Seq and scATAC-Seq datasets. Using conventional single-cell omics workflows to process and explore our data, we distinguish distinct cell lineages based on G4 heterogeneity and establish that a subset of lineage-specific genes show unique promoter G4s. Multi-omics integration with scRNA-Seq gene expression profiles, using both a covariance-based technique (canonical correlation analysis) and a transfer learning-based approach, enables more accurate cell-type annotation. These integrations not only reveal correlations between G4 signal and gene expression, but demonstrate that G4 scCUT&Tag enables detailed examination of G4 heterogeneity in complex tissues and supports integrative analysis of G4 profiles with other omics layers, offering new insights into the epigenomic landscapes of the developing brain. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings establish G4 scCUT&Tag as a framework for investigating the cellular heterogeneity of G4 landscapes in complex tissues and provide a basis for exploring their relationships with gene regulation and other layers of chromatin organization.

title: Single-nucleus multiomic profiling uncovers epigenetic dysregulation driving hippocampal vulnerability in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits region- and cell-type-specific vulnerability, yet the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain poorly defined. We performed integrated single-nucleus RNA-seq and ATAC-seq of human hippocampus to resolve gene regulatory architecture in AD. By linking chromatin accessibility to transcription, we identified more than 1000 disease-associated cis-regulatory interactions, highlighting coordinated epigenomic-transcriptomic remodeling. Excitatory cornu ammonis (EX.CA) neurons exhibited disproportionate regulatory disruption, characterized by increased chromatin accessibility coupled to activation of apoptosis-related gene programs, whereas dentate gyrus (EX.DG) neurons remained comparatively resistant. In glial cells, regulatory network inference revealed activation of transcription factor modules centered on SPI1/KLF4 in microglia and STAT3 in astrocytes, defining epigenetic programs that are highly associated with inflammatory and metabolic state transitions. Comparative evaluation with the prefrontal cortex uncovered conserved inflammatory activation alongside region-specific immune regulatory divergence, indicating spatially distinct microglial responses. Furthermore, cross-species integration demonstrated that a substantial fraction of AD-associated regulatory elements are human-specific, with AD-risk variants enriched in microglial cis-regulatory elements at loci including BIN1 and APOE. Together, these results provide a mechanistic framework linking chromatin remodeling to cell-type-specific dysfunction and reveal human-specific regulatory architecture as a crucial factor to AD vulnerability and translational limitation.
authors: Tao Q, Luo T, Wang P, Jiang M, Lai Z, Jin B, Liu Y, He Y, Wei Y, Gao Y
overview: Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits region- and cell-type-specific vulnerability, yet the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain poorly defined.

title: Microglial Metabolic Reprogramming Regulated by HIF-1α/HK2 Positive Feedback Inhibits Adult Hippocampal Neurogenesis in Diabetes-Associated Cognitive Dysfunction.
abstract: Diabetes-associated cognitive dysfunction (DACD) is a significant complication with few effective treatments and unclear underlying mechanism. The aim of this study was to investigate how hyperglycemia disrupts adult hippocampal neurogenesis (AHN) through metabolic-immune interactions, seeking to identify potential treatment targets for DACD. DACD models were developed using db/db mice or streptozotocin-induced mice, and their cognitive function was assessed through behavioral tests. Next, we integrated multi-omics analyses (transcriptomic, single-cell, and lactylome profiling) with metabolic studies in BV2 cells exposed to diabetic conditions. Pharmacological modulators (3-BP, C646, TSA) were used to clarify the underlying mechanisms. The mice with DACD demonstrated cognitive deficits, impaired AHN, and activation of hippocampal microglia. Transcriptomic analysis revealed glycolysis as the primary dysregulated pathway. Mechanistically, hyperglycemia/AGEs induced glycolytic reprogramming and increased lactate levels, which promoted HIF-1α lactylation at lysine residues-a modification catalyzed by p300 and opposed by histone deacetylases. This posttranslational modification was associated with HIF-1α stabilisation and with enhanced transcriptional occupancy at the HK2 promoter. This established a self-amplifying feedback loop, perpetuating microglial activation and disrupting the blood-brain barrier via CXCL10 secretion, which led to CD8+ T-cell infiltration. Systemic administration of the glycolytic inhibitor 3-BP disrupted the pathogenic circuit, thereby normalizing metabolism, attenuating neuroinflammation, and restoring cognitive function. HIF-1α lactylation is associated with HIF-1α stabilisation, acting as a potential metabolic-epigenetic mechanism that links glycolytic flux to sustained microglial activation, neuroinflammation and impaired AHN in DACD. Pharmacological inhibition of this axis attenuated neuroinflammation and improved cognitive outcomes in our model, suggesting a candidate therapeutic strategy for DACD.
authors: Jiang S, Zhao Y, Zhang Q, Zhang J, Gao Z, Luo Y, Zhao N, Guo N, An C, Zhang R
overview: Diabetes-associated cognitive dysfunction (DACD) is a significant complication with few effective treatments and unclear underlying mechanism.
main: Transcriptomic analysis revealed glycolysis as the primary dysregulated pathway.

title: Association of metabolic insulin resistance with white matter hyperintensity burden and plasma proteomic signatures in the UK Biobank.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Metabolic insulin resistance is closely related to cardiometabolic dysfunction and vascular injury. Its association with subclinical cerebral small vessel disease, and the circulating molecular signals that may accompany this association, remain incompletely characterised. METHODS: We analysed 59,826 UK Biobank participants with brain magnetic resonance imaging to examine the association between the metabolic score for insulin resistance (METS-IR) and white matter hyperintensity (WMH) burden. Associations were evaluated using multivariable linear regression and restricted cubic spline analysis, with spline models restricted to participants with complete covariate data. Proteomic data were available for 6,790 participants. Protein-wide association analyses, functional annotation and LASSO prioritisation explored circulating protein links between METS-IR and WMH burden, followed by exploratory mediation models in 1,309 participants with complete model data. RESULTS: Higher METS-IR was associated with greater WMH burden after adjustment for demographic, socioeconomic, lifestyle and vascular risk factors. Complete-case spline analysis suggested a nonlinear association, with steeper fitted slopes at higher METS-IR values. Proteomic screening identified 1,266 proteins associated with METS-IR and 122 proteins associated with WMH after false discovery rate correction, yielding 119 overlapping proteins. These proteins were enriched for immune-inflammatory processes and cell adhesion. LASSO prioritisation selected eight candidate proteins, and exploratory mediation models yielded indirect-effect estimates for selected proteins, with GAL showing the largest estimated proportion mediated. CONCLUSIONS: METS-IR was associated with WMH burden after adjustment for measured covariates in this large UK Biobank analysis. Integrated plasma proteomic analyses identified immune-inflammatory and cell-adhesion signals that may help characterise molecular correlates of metabolic insulin resistance and cerebral small vessel disease burden.
authors: Si X, Qi X
overview: BACKGROUND: Metabolic insulin resistance is closely related to cardiometabolic dysfunction and vascular injury.
main: RESULTS: Higher METS-IR was associated with greater WMH burden after adjustment for demographic, socioeconomic, lifestyle and vascular risk factors.

title: Btbd11 regulates glutamatergic synapse organization in GABAergic inhibitory interneurons.
abstract: The mechanisms that underlie glutamatergic synapse organization and function in GABAergic inhibitory interneurons (INs) are not well described, despite evidence that impaired glutamatergic excitation of INs is implicated in psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia and anxiety. Glutamatergic synapses received by INs have unique basal transmission properties and exhibit distinct synaptic plasticity compared to those received by excitatory neurons, likely due to cell-type specific differences in postsynaptic density (PSD) composition and maintenance mechanisms. In the present study, we show that the interneuron-specific protein Btbd11 regulates excitatory synapse transmission in mixed-sex primary cultured rat and mouse hippocampal interneurons through promotion of phase separation and support of postsynaptic nanoarchitecture. Btbd11 forms a phase separated protein complex with Psd-95 and TARPγ2 and impacts the stability of TARPγ2 and GluA1 within glutamatergic IN synapses in an expression- and phase separation-dependent manner. Using super resolution imaging, we show that Btbd11 displays nanoscale clustering properties within IN synapses that correlate with Psd-95 nanostructure. Furthermore, genetic deletion of Btbd11 decreases PSD protein expression, reduces synapse size, and disrupts Psd-95 nanocluster organization. These effects manifest as a drastic reduction in glutamatergic synaptic transmission onto INs when Btbd11 is deleted. Together, these data provide insights into a novel cell type-specific synaptic regulatory mechanism in an understudied synapse population.Significance Statement Although glutamatergic excitation of GABAergic inhibitory interneurons (INs) is essential for maintenance of balanced signaling in the brain and dysregulation has been linked to neuropsychiatric disorders, the molecular mechanisms underlying IN-specific glutamatergic transmission are not well characterized. Using protein modeling, molecular biology, live-cell and super-resolution imaging, we describe a unique mechanism of glutamatergic synapse organization in INs by Btbd11, an IN-specific synaptic protein. Btbd11 promotes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and regulates PSD protein mobility, the abundance of key synaptic proteins, and nanoscale synaptic organization. Collectively, this is critical for glutamatergic synaptic transmission within INs. Understanding Btbd11's role at the synapse highlights the importance of synaptic LLPS, providing insight into the regulatory mechanisms in an understudied synapse with psychiatric disease relevance.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
authors: Boyer MB, Zhang S, Levy AD, Schamber P, Hartman HM, Blanpied TA, Bygrave AM
overview: The mechanisms that underlie glutamatergic synapse organization and function in GABAergic inhibitory interneurons (INs) are not well described, despite evidence that impaired glutamatergic excitation of INs is implicated in psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia and anxiety.
main: In the present study, we show that the interneuron-specific protein Btbd11 regulates excitatory synapse transmission in mixed-sex primary cultured rat and mouse hippocampal interneurons through promotion of phase separation and support of postsynaptic nanoarchitecture.

title: The immunological subtypes of cone photoreceptors in mouse and primate retinas.
abstract: We studied cone photoreceptors in adult mouse and baboon retinas for their structure and diversity with immunomarkers and confocal microscopy. In mouse retinas, L/M-opsin and S-opsin antibodies labeled regular cones primarily in the outer segment (OS). In dark-adapted conditions, S-opsin-positive OSs (152,941/retina) showed a Gaussian distribution with a density range of 40,245-150/mm2 ventrodorsally and 19,072-184/mm2 temporonasally. ~ 10% somas of L/M-opsin-positive cones were attached as pairs. 7.6% of L/M-opsin-expressing cones and 5.7% of S-opsin-positive cones showed higher opsin levels in soma and axon, and we named them lm-cones or ss-cones, respectively, which possessed single or dual OS(s), indicating the presence of double-cones and more color-sensitive subtypes. Unlike regular cones, lm-cones had significantly smaller OSs and shorter inner segments (ISs), and ss-cone somas resided in rod soma rows with a much longer IS-soma distance. Retrogradely labeling of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) revealed two photoreceptor-RGC hybrids with OSs. Peanut agglutin (PNA) identified two OS calibers: 1) 1-2 μm with two intertwined continuous PNA-positive strings and 2) 2-3μm with 3-4 PNA-positive strings, which preferred the central or peripheral retina and matched one or two OS compartments, respectively. PNA-positive strings were thinner in ISs. In monkey cones, the OS disk region was positive for PNA (89.5%) or calcium-binding protein 5 (10.5%). OS surface was covered by vertical PNA-positive grids, which were thinner in ISs, absent in fovea cone OSs, and multi-barrel-like in other cones. PNA-positive sheath contained up to ~10-12 parallel grids of similar thickness, distance, and immunoreactivity, likely serving as the wall of cones.
authors: Pang VY, Yang Z, Wu SM, Pang JJ
overview: We studied cone photoreceptors in adult mouse and baboon retinas for their structure and diversity with immunomarkers and confocal microscopy.
main: Retrogradely labeling of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) revealed two photoreceptor-RGC hybrids with OSs.

title: A Structured Workflow for Four-Plex Chromogenic Immunohistochemistry Panel Design, Validation, and Digital Imaging for Immune Cell Quantification.
abstract: PURPOSE: To support immune profiling of solid tumors using brightfield microscopy and digital image analysis, this study aims to develop an analytically validated workflow to design and implement a four-plex chromogenic IHC panel targeting CD8, CD20, CD68, and pan-cytokeratin. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We developed a stepwise approach combining antibody optimization, chromogen selection, and qualitative evaluation using microscopy, digital image analysis, and red-green-blue histograms (RGB). After testing 15 dual-stain combinations and three four-plex panel designs, we found that the panel comprising CD8-DAB, CD20-Teal, CD68-Purple, and pan-cytokeratin-Yellow provided optimal stain separation and consistent performance. RESULTS: Using this approach, we established a reliable and effective method to analyze immune cell densities in solid tumors. This panel was validated across 12 solid tumor types, including carcinomas, neuroendocrine neoplasms, and sarcomas, demonstrating consistent efficacy in quantifying immune cell densities. CONCLUSION: Our study presents a structured validation workflow for brightfield multiplex immunohistochemistry panel design and digital image analysis integration. The validated four-plex panel enabled accurate immune profiling across tumor types and was compatible with standard pathology procedures, supporting its utility in translational research and its potential for future clinical implementation.
journal: Laboratory investigation; a journal of technical methods and pathology
authors: Salvatierra ME, Serrano AG, Lu W, Jiang M, Khan K, Haymaker C, Solis Soto LM
overview: PURPOSE: To support immune profiling of solid tumors using brightfield microscopy and digital image analysis, this study aims to develop an analytically validated workflow to design and implement a four-plex chromogenic IHC panel targeting CD8, CD20, CD68, and pan-cytokeratin.
main: After testing 15 dual-stain combinations and three four-plex panel designs, we found that the panel comprising CD8-DAB, CD20-Teal, CD68-Purple, and pan-cytokeratin-Yellow provided optimal stain separation and consistent performance.

title: Semi-automated histomorphometric quantification of acetabular labral surface roughness.
abstract: Histopathologic surface changes, including fibrillation, fraying, undulation, and disruption, are important indicators of tissue wear and acetabular labral degeneration. Surface assessment, however, commonly relies on descriptive or semiquantitative grading and may be partly observer-dependent when applied to naturally curved fibrocartilaginous surfaces. This study developed and evaluated a semi-automated histomorphometric workflow for quantifying acetabular labral articular surface roughness using histologic images. Sixteen human hemipelves from nine embalmed cadavers were divided into eight anatomical segments and grouped into superior, anterior, inferior, and posterior quadrants. Sections were stained with haematoxylin and eosin and Safranin O/Fast Green, scanned at high resolution, and analysed using Fiji/ImageJ and Python. The labral articular surface was isolated, skeletonised into a one-pixel-wide line, and exported as coordinates. A specimen-specific LOWESS-smoothed reference contour was generated, and roughness percentage was calculated from the mean absolute pointwise deviation between the original and smoothed profiles. Roughness percentage did not differ significantly across anatomical quadrants. In contrast, it differed significantly across histopathologic surface severity levels, with severely degenerated surfaces showing higher values than normal, mild, and moderate surfaces. Intra- and inter-observer reliability was excellent, with intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.994 and 0.962, respectively. This workflow provides a reproducible quantitative extension to conventional histopathologic grading with potential future application to other curved, load-bearing fibrocartilaginous tissues.
authors: Alomiery AA, Shaheen S, Almajed YA, Alanazi G, Alashkham A
overview: Histopathologic surface changes, including fibrillation, fraying, undulation, and disruption, are important indicators of tissue wear and acetabular labral degeneration.
main: Roughness percentage did not differ significantly across anatomical quadrants.

title: Fluid eMTBR-tau243 as a Biomarker of Mixed 3-Repeat and 4-Repeat Tau Pathology.
abstract: IMPORTANCE: Neurodegenerative diseases with abnormal tau protein aggregation in the brain (ie, tauopathies) can be classified by the tau isoform that accumulates: 3-repeat (3R), 4-repeat (4R), or mixed 3R/4R tauopathies, which include chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), some forms of frontotemporal lobar degeneration, and Alzheimer disease (AD). The endogenously cleaved form of tau microtubule binding region containing the residue 243 (eMTBR-tau243) can be detected in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and blood and has been associated with AD tau pathology, but its specificity and biological interpretation in non-AD tauopathies remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate biofluid eMTBR-tau243 in a range of tauopathies. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This case-control study included 4 biorepositories based in the US that contributed CSF and plasma samples from participants with and without tauopathies, many of whom had antemortem biofluid samples paired with autopsy or genetically defined neuropathology. Samples were analyzed between August 2023 and December 2025. Data analysis occurred from August 2024 to July 2026. EXPOSURE: CSF and plasma eMTBR-tau243 concentrations measured using a mass spectrometry-based assay. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Outcomes included mixed 3R/4R tauopathy (eg, AD and CTE) based on autopsy, frontotemporal lobar degeneration with MAPT variants (FTLD-MAPT), and CTE stage. Differences in biomarker levels between groups were evaluated using analysis of variance or analysis of covariance, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was calculated to evaluate the discriminative performance of fluid eMTBR-tau243. RESULTS: Among the 229 participants (196 with CSF samples and 55 with plasma samples [22 with both]), mean (SD) age at fluid sample collection was 63 (13) years and 108 (47%) were female. Median (IQR) CSF eMTBR-tau243 was increased in 10 patients with AD (0.459 [0.246-0.801] fmol/mL) compared with 29 cognitively unimpaired controls (0.002 [0.001-0.005] fmol/mL) (adjusted P < .001), but other autopsy-confirmed non-AD tauopathies (which included 52 individuals with conditions including progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration) did not demonstrate an increase (0.015 [0.008, 0.039] fmol/mL). Six symptomatic FTLD-MAPT variant carriers with mixed 3R/4R tauopathy (R406W, V337M, and G389R) had increased median (IQR) CSF eMTBR-tau243 (0.140 [0.055-0.174] fmol/mL) compared with 15 4R tauopathy variant carriers including N279K and P301L (0.004 [0.001-0.044] fmol/mL) (P = .001). Median (IQR) plasma eMTBR-tau243 was increased in 11 patients with CTE (1.93 [0.42-3.68] fmol/L) compared with 20 cognitively unimpaired controls (0.29 [0.05-0.62] fmol/L) (adjusted P = .007), but did not increase as high as among 14 patients with AD (11.25 [2.29-19.38] fmol/L). Plasma eMTBR-tau243 distinguished CTE stage III and IV from controls (AUC, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.92-1.00), but not CTE stage I from controls (AUC, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.32-0.97). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: This study found that plasma and CSF eMTBR-tau243 were increased in mixed 3R/4R tauopathies including AD, high-stage CTE, and a subset of genetic FTLD-MAPT, compared with cognitively unimpaired controls. Further validation in larger cohorts is needed to determine the clinical utility of eMTBR-tau243 as a potential diagnostic biomarker for CTE and other tauopathies beyond AD.
authors: Horie K, Koppisetti RK, VandeVrede L, Asken BM, Li Y, Yen D, Ghoshal N, Paterson RW, Lario Lago A, Seeley WW
overview: IMPORTANCE: Neurodegenerative diseases with abnormal tau protein aggregation in the brain (ie, tauopathies) can be classified by the tau isoform that accumulates: 3-repeat (3R), 4-repeat (4R), or mixed 3R/4R tauopathies, which include chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), some forms of frontotemporal lobar degeneration, and Alzheimer disease (AD).
main: MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Outcomes included mixed 3R/4R tauopathy (eg, AD and CTE) based on autopsy, frontotemporal lobar degeneration with MAPT variants (FTLD-MAPT), and CTE stage.

title: Lepr Haploinsufficiency Accelerates Alzheimer-like Neurodegeneration via CDK5 Hyperactivation.
abstract: Leptin receptor (LEPR) signaling plays a critical role in neuronal survival and synaptic function and is increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis. Beyond its metabolic actions, leptin regulates β-amyloid homeostasis, tau phosphorylation, and synaptic plasticity. While the neurological consequences of homozygous leptin receptor (Lepr) mutations are well characterized, the impact of heterozygous Lepr deficiency on brain aging and neurodegeneration remains unclear. To address this, we analyzed heterozygous leptin receptor mutant (db/+) mice at 6 and 12 months of age using metabolic, behavioral, biochemical, neuropathological, and transcriptomic approaches. Young db/+ mice were comparable to controls, whereas aged db/+ mice developed obesity, impaired glucose tolerance, and insulin resistance, accompanied by deficits in spatial learning and motor coordination. Aged db/+ brains exhibited elevated amyloid-β42 levels, increased CDK5 kinase activity, and hyperphosphorylation of tau at Ser396 and Thr231. Although total LEPR protein levels were unchanged, phosphorylation of STAT3 at Tyr705 was significantly reduced, indicating impaired downstream LEPR signaling. Transcriptomic profiling revealed downregulation of genes involved in synaptic signaling and plasticity, including Gabrb2, Brsk1, Camk2a, Syn1, and Syngap1, along with alterations in neurotransmitter and oxidative phosphorylation pathways. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that leptin receptor haploinsufficiency promotes age-dependent metabolic dysfunction, synaptic failure, and CDK5-mediated tauopathy, leading to Alzheimer-like neurodegeneration and identifying LEPR as a potential genetic risk factor and therapeutic target.

title: Genetic Susceptibility, Neurodevelopmental Abnormalities, and Neuroimmune Interactions Across Major Psychiatric Disorders.
abstract: Major psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, and autism spectrum disorder, share overlapping genetic, neurodevelopmental, and neuroimmune underpinnings that challenge traditional diagnostic boundaries. This review synthesizes evidence across three interconnected domains: convergent genetic risk affecting synaptic and immune pathways, neurodevelopmental vulnerabilities shaped by early-life insults, and neuroimmune crosstalk involving blood-brain barrier dysfunction, sustained inflammation, and complement-mediated pathology. We propose a multidimensional developmental-immune framework in which genetic liability, environmental exposure timing, and peripheral immune status jointly shape transdiagnostic trajectories. This framework reframes psychiatric disorders as dynamic interactions among stable trait-like susceptibilities and fluctuating biological states, offering a roadmap for biomarker-driven stratification and early immune-targeted interventions.

title: PPARγ at the Nexus of Lipid Metabolism and Neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's Disease: A Longitudinal Multi-omics Analysis.
abstract: Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) has emerged as an important regulator linking lipid metabolism and neuroimmune responses in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Increasing evidence suggests that disruption of the lipid-immune axis contributes to disease progression and may underlie the heterogeneous therapeutic responses observed with PPARγ-targeted interventions. Experimental studies indicate that PPARγ activation influences multiple biological processes relevant to AD, including lipid homeostasis, mitochondrial function, inflammatory signaling, and amyloid-β clearance. However, the translation of these findings into consistent clinical benefit remains limited by challenges such as poor blood-brain barrier penetration, systemic adverse effects, and disease stage-dependent therapeutic responses. Recent advances in multi-omics technologies and single-cell transcriptomics have provided new insights into the context-dependent roles of PPARγ in different neural cell populations, highlighting dynamic interactions between lipid metabolism, neuroinflammation, and cellular function throughout AD progression. These findings suggest that PPARγ-associated pathways may represent an important regulatory interface linking metabolic and inflammatory processes, while emphasizing the complexity of their temporal and cell-specific regulation. This review synthesizes current evidence from experimental studies, human multi-omics investigations, and clinical research to provide an updated perspective on the role of PPARγ in coordinating lipid metabolism and neuroinflammation in AD. In addition, we discuss the major translational challenges and emerging therapeutic strategies, including selective PPARγ modulation, improved central nervous system delivery, and precision treatment approaches tailored to disease stage.
authors: Huixuan H, Ruizhe W, Chunrong H, Na W, Tianwai D, Ludan Y, Wenzhe L, Xiaofang S
overview: Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) has emerged as an important regulator linking lipid metabolism and neuroimmune responses in Alzheimer's disease (AD).

title: PINK1‑regulated mitophagy dysfunction in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease (Review).
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder, characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and the accumulation of misfolded α‑synuclein forming Lewy bodies. Emerging evidence highlights mitochondrial dysfunction as an important and early event in PD pathogenesis. Among the key regulators of mitochondrial quality control, PTEN‑induced kinase 1 (PINK1) plays a pivotal role by initiating mitophagy, the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria. Under physiological conditions, PINK1 is rapidly degraded, whereas mitochondrial depolarization stabilizes PINK1 on the outer mitochondrial membrane, where it recruits and activates Parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, to promote mitophagy. Loss‑of‑function mutations in PINK1 also disrupt this process, leading to the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria, oxidative stress, abnormal calcium homeostasis and neuronal apoptosis. Furthermore, PINK1 deficiency has been shown to exacerbate α‑synuclein aggregation, impair synaptic transmission and activate neuroinflammatory pathways, collectively accelerating dopaminergic neurodegeneration. Therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring or enhancing PINK1‑mediated mitophagy through pharmacological activation, gene delivery or modulation of parallel pathways‑represent a promising avenue for PD intervention. Continued elucidation of the molecular functions of PINK1 will provide critical insights into mitochondrial homeostasis and novel therapeutic targets for PD.

title: Disruption of cell-type-specific molecular programs of striatal spiny projection neurons in autism.
abstract: Rare genetic variants contribute substantially to autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet the regulatory logic of vulnerable subcortical cells is poorly understood. In a 16p11.2 deletion mouse model, lineage tracing across five brain regions revealed prominent striatal changes. In the human putamen from ASD and neurotypical donors, single-nucleus multi-omics showed transcriptional alterations concentrated in D1 striosome spiny projection neurons (SPNs), affecting synaptic and energy metabolism genes, with altered synapse-supporting programs in astrocytes. Gene regulatory network analysis integrating chromatin accessibility and expression identified EGR1 and EGR3 as key regulators of these programs, with reduced activity in D1 striosome SPNs. Deleting EGR1 or EGR3 in human striatal organoids produced partially overlapping transcriptional changes. These findings establish the striatum as a site of molecular convergence in ASD and provide a multi-omic resource for dissecting subcortical mechanisms.

title: Spatial mTOR biology: From organelle localization to biomolecular condensates and metabolic control.
abstract: The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) coordinates cell growth, metabolism, protein synthesis, autophagy, and survival by integrating nutrient availability, growth factors, energy status, mechanical cues, and cellular stress. Beyond classical biochemical cascades, mTOR signaling specificity is fundamentally governed by subcellular localization, temporal recruitment, and microenvironmental context. This review synthesizes current insights into the spatial architecture of mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) across lysosomes, endosomes, plasma-membrane microdomains, organelle contact sites, neuronal processes, the nucleus, and biomolecular condensates. We examine how physical principles-including membrane composition and curvature, molecular confinement, macromolecular crowding, scaffold-mediated multivalent interactions, organelle positioning, mechanical tension, and localized translation-dictate signaling outcomes. Furthermore, we contrast membrane-anchored molecular assemblies with three-dimensional biomolecular condensates, detailing their interplay during stress adaptation. Spatial constraints in specialized cell geometries, such as neuronal compartments and developing tissues, illustrate how identical signaling machinery yields divergent functional outputs under altered diffusion environments. We also evaluate how advances in spatial multi-omics and super-resolution imaging extend these subcellular paradigms to tissue-scale heterogeneity. Finally, we highlight major translational hurdles, including the trade-off between spatial resolution and dynamic temporal tracking in current technologies, as well as the inability of conventional pharmacotherapies to selectively target discrete subcellular mTOR pools. Establishing spatial organization as a primary determinant of mTOR signaling clarifies context-dependent physiological outputs and provides a roadmap for developing next-generation spatially targeted therapeutics.

title: A coronavirus protease activates sensory neurons via TRPA1 to drive sneeze, cough, and pain.
abstract: Sneezing, coughing, and pain are common symptoms of respiratory viral infection. These responses are initiated by airway-innervating nociceptors that detect noxious stimuli, but how SARS-CoV-2 activates these neurons remains unclear. Here, we show that the coronavirus papain-like protease (PLpro) directly activates airway-innervating nociceptors in mice and human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived nociceptors. PLpro triggers sneezing, coughing, acute pain, and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) release in the airways. Both the proteolytic activity of PLpro and the host ion channel transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) are required for neuronal activation and sneezing. Infection with the mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 or the murine coronavirus MHV-A59 also induces sneezing in mice, and MHV-A59-evoked sneezing is TRPA1-dependent. SARS-CoV-2 infection of the trigeminal ganglia altered transcriptional programs associated with nociception, including upregulation of the TRPA1-CGRP signaling pathway activated by PLpro. Together, these findings reveal a direct mechanism by which SARS-CoV-2 triggers pain and airway reflexes and identify PLpro and TRPA1 as potential therapeutic targets for COVID-19.

title: multiVIB: A unified probabilistic contrastive learning framework for atlas-scale integration of single-cell multi-omics data.
abstract: Integrating heterogeneous single-cell datasets requires aligning shared biological features while preserving meaningful variation across modalities, studies, and species. Here, we present multiVIB, a unified framework combining the variational information bottleneck with probabilistic contrastive learning for horizontal, vertical, and mosaic integration of single-cell multi-omics data. Across diverse benchmarks, multiVIB achieves competitive integration performance while minimizing spurious alignments. Applied to BRAIN Initiative atlas-scale datasets, multiVIB enables incremental integration of nine molecular modalities in the mouse primary motor cortex and cross-species integration of primate basal ganglia transcriptomes, recovering conserved cell identities and species-specific molecular programs. Together, these results establish multiVIB as a versatile framework for scalable, biologically faithful construction and expansion of comprehensive brain cell atlases.

title: An integrated single-cell and epigenomic resource for comparative analysis of the basal ganglia from BICAN.
abstract: The basal ganglia regulate motor, cognitive, and affective behaviors, and their dysfunction underlies diverse neurological and psychiatric disorders. Comprehensive, accessible multi-omics resources are needed to understand the regulatory mechanisms governing basal ganglia cell types. Here, we present an open, interactive web-based platform for exploring single-cell multi-omics datasets from basal ganglia, generated using 10X Multiome, single-nucleus methylome and chromatin conformation sequencing (snm3C-seq), and Paired-Tag technologies by the BICAN (NIH BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network) consortium. The platform is available at https://basalganglia.epigenomes.net/and enables integrated visualization of gene expression, chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, histone modifications, and chromatin conformation across cell types and human, macaque, marmoset, and mouse species, with direct genome browser support and comparative epigenomic functionality. Representative analyses demonstrate cell-type-specific regulatory landscapes, conserved and species-specific regulatory elements, and links between epigenomic regulation and transcription. This resource provides a scalable, community-oriented foundation for advancing basal ganglia biology and interpreting regulatory mechanisms relevant to brain function and disease.

title: Human neocortical glutamatergic neurons revealed through multimodal profiling.
abstract: The human neocortex underlies higher cognition, yet our understanding of its neuronal diversity is limited by sparse access to viable tissue, inconsistent cell-type definitions, and limited multimodal data. Although single-cell transcriptomics has transformed our understanding of cell type diversity, transcriptomic data alone cannot explain neuronal function. Here, we introduce a multimodal patch sequencing (patch-seq) resource of human neocortical glutamatergic neurons spanning cortical layers 2-6. Combining morphoelectric features with spatial transcriptomic data to provide laminar context, we sampled 39 of 42 transcriptomically defined glutamatergic neuron types. This systematic approach enabled the identification of unique phenotypes for understudied populations in the human neocortex including L4 intratelencephalic, L5/6 near-projecting, and diverse L6 neurons. Human, macaque, and mouse comparisons of transcriptomically homologous L5 neurons reveal that morphoelectric differences across species were subclass specific. This dataset provides a unified multimodal reference for studying human cortical circuitry and neuronal diversity.

title: An integrative single-cell epigenomic atlas annotates the regulatory genome of the adult mouse brain.
abstract: Histone modifications underpin the cell-type-specific gene regulatory programs that drive the remarkable cellular diversity of the mammalian brain. Here, we jointly profiled four histone modifications and the transcriptome in 2.5 million nuclei from the adult mouse brain. By integrating these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, and three-dimensional genome organization, we constructed a unified epigenomic atlas spanning over 100 brain cell subclasses and assigned active, primed, and repressive chromatin states across 81% of the genome. Active chromatin states marked by combinatorial histone modifications better nominate candidate enhancers with functional support than chromatin accessibility alone, while H3K27me3- and H3K9me3-marked chromatin states delineate distinct modes of cell-type-specific gene repression. Finally, this multimodal resource enables the development of deep learning models that predict cell-type-specific epigenomic features and gene expression from DNA sequence, providing a comprehensive framework for annotating the brain regulatory genome and interpreting non-coding disease risk variants.

title: A single-cell and spatial 3D multi-omic atlas of developing human basal ganglia.
abstract: Human basal ganglia (BG) neurons and inhibitory interneurons originate in the ganglionic eminences (GEs), transient structures in the ventral prenatal brain. This study delineates the specification and maturation of GEs and GE-derived neurons using single-nucleus methyl-3C sequencing (snm3C-seq), spatial transcriptomics, and single-molecule chromatin + RNA imaging, and we found heterogeneous temporal progression across GE subregions. Spiny projection neurons (SPNs), the principal cells of the BG, acquire distinct subtypes through synchronized 3D-epigenomic remodeling, in contrast to the asynchronous maturation of other neuron types. Oligodendrocyte differentiation involves a transient short-range chromatin state during infancy, showing that the short-range and long-range chromatin conformations previously linked to terminal glial and neuronal fates can also be transient. The temporal cortex matured epigenomically faster than other cortical regions during this period. Lastly, SPNs were enriched in genetic risk for neuropsychiatric disease. Our study extends findings on unique 3D-epigenomic dynamics during human brain development.
authors: Heffel MG, Xu H, Pastor-Alonso O, Li X, Baig MS, Ghoor RI, Li R, Kern C, Kum J, Zhang Y

title: Circuit-aligned specialization of human basal ganglia astrocytes.
abstract: Astrocytes shape synapses and circuits, yet their diversity within the human basal ganglia remains poorly defined. Integrating single-nucleus transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling with spatial transcriptomics, we identify three anatomically organized astrocyte subgroups-striatal gray matter (GM), extra-striatal GM, and white matter (WM)-distinguished by neurotransmitter transporter expression and synapse-associated programs that reflect afferent input. These molecular distinctions generalize brain-wide, separating telencephalic from non-telencephalic astrocytes, with LHX2 marking telencephalic astrocyte identity across species. Within the striatum (STR), dorsal and ventral populations align with distinct microcircuits; a ventral population maps to the nucleus accumbens mediodorsal shell alongside specialized neuronal subtypes, a pattern conserved in nonhuman primates. A deep learning sequence model identifies subgroup-specific enhancer codes and recovers established transcription factor motif logic from published enhancer-AAV datasets, providing a foundation for targeted viral vector design. These findings define intersecting axes of human astrocyte specialization and offer a framework for cell-type-specific dissection of basal ganglia circuits.
authors: Fu Y, Kempynck N, Ding W, Turner MA, Garcia AD, Schmitz MT, Close J, Kapen I, Hewitt M, Seeman SC

title: Multiscale spatial atlas of human basal ganglia cell types and communities.
abstract: The human basal ganglia comprise functionally varied nuclei, but their cell-type composition and spatial organization have not been comprehensively resolved. We generated a multi-region, subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomic atlas by integrating multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH)+ and spatiotemporal enhanced-resolution omics sequencing (Stereo-seq) across four neurotypical donors. The datasets profiled ∼7.9 million cells across the caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens, and globus pallidus, resolving 60 transcriptionally distinct cell types. We identify region-selective molecular and spatial diversification of spiny projection neurons and non-neuronal populations. Subcellular RNA localization captures somatic size and projection-inferred signatures, reflecting direct- and indirect-pathway topology. Cellular community analyses reveal astrocyte and oligodendrocyte subclusters enriched at striosome-matrix borders, while primate-expanded interneurons are confined to matrix territories. Cross-species comparisons reveal conserved and species-specialized organization, including orthologous striosome-matrix architecture and conserved dorsolateral-to-ventromedial transcriptional gradients. Together, this multi-centimeter-scale human basal ganglia atlas links cell types, spatial architecture, and subcellular transcript topography across scales.

title: Single-cell analysis of chromatin state and transcriptome in the human basal ganglia.
abstract: The basal ganglia are central to motor control, learning, emotion, and reward processing, and their dysfunction contributes to many neurological and psychiatric disorders. Here, we generated a single-cell multi-omic atlas of histone modifications and transcriptomes across eight basal ganglia regions from neurotypical human donors. This atlas resolved cell-type- and region-specific landscapes of active and repressive candidate cis-regulatory elements and delineated gene regulatory networks underlying cell identity. We found that the combinatorial expression of homeobox transcription factors provides distinctive molecular descriptors of neuronal cell identities in the basal ganglia. Integration with matched MERFISH spatial transcriptomics further uncovered regional heterogeneity in epigenomic and transcriptional programs. Finally, we used this atlas to interpret noncoding risk variants associated with neuropsychiatric disorders and to construct a deep-learning model that predicts gene regulatory activities and variant effects. Together, this work provides a multimodal regulatory framework for understanding human basal ganglia organization, evolution, and disease genetics.
authors: Chang L, Li K, Xie Y, Zhong G, Rink JA, Báez-Becerra CT, Lie A, Indralingam HS, Loe T, Dong K
overview: The basal ganglia are central to motor control, learning, emotion, and reward processing, and their dysfunction contributes to many neurological and psychiatric disorders.
main: We found that the combinatorial expression of homeobox transcription factors provides distinctive molecular descriptors of neuronal cell identities in the basal ganglia.

title: Multimodal single-cell epigenomic and 3D genome atlas of the human basal ganglia.
abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) underlie motor control, reward processing, and many neurological and psychiatric disorders, yet cell-type-resolved epigenomic and 3D genome maps of the human BG remain limited. Here, we present a multimodal single-cell atlas of DNA methylation (261,331 nuclei) and 3D chromatin conformation (229,286 nuclei) from eight subregions, harmonized under the BG consensus taxonomy and integrated with matched data across multiple regulatory layers. We identify millions of differentially methylated regions across cell types, enriched for distinct transcription factor motifs, and link them to disease-associated heritability. We characterize the POU6F2+ STR D2 SMYD2-HTR7 spiny projection neuron (SPN) subtype, with concordant signatures across multiple modalities, and reveal region-specific methylation and contact gradients. Integrative gene regulatory networks (GRNs) predict cell-type-resolved enhancer-promoter interactions, nominating candidate regulatory mechanisms for Parkinson's disease (PD) risk variants at SNCA. Finally, multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH) profiling combined with cross-species Patch-seq identifies a neuronal subtype, STR FS PTHLH-PVALB GABA, with electrophysiological differences across the striatal matrix-striosome (MS) boundary.

title: Mesoscale molecular architecture of the striatum across cell types and adult aging.
abstract: The human striatum governs diverse motor, cognitive, and affective behaviors yet lacks the obvious cytoarchitectural boundaries defining functional territories elsewhere in the brain. Using Slide-tags single-nucleus spatial transcriptomics, we profiled 1.1 million cells across 19 postmortem donors to uncover the striatum's spatial organization. These data revealed a consistent subdivision of the striatum into six zones, each defined by molecularly distinct populations of spiny projection neurons (SPNs) and featuring spatially coordinated neuron-astrocyte interaction networks. To determine their structural relevance, we generated a companion mouse spatial atlas that identified four homologous zones that aligned with territories defined by brain-wide afferent projections. Finally, imputing zonal identities onto a 131-donor single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) cohort revealed that dorsal zones exhibit the greatest age-related transcriptional change and that the expression differences defining zonation attenuate with age. This resource establishes a conserved mesoscale spatial framework for the mammalian striatum, linking single-cell molecular identity to structural connectomics and aging.
authors: Kraft AW, Lee M, Gao H, Mohsin A, Rayan NA, Lawler AJ, Kim G, Milidantri J, Vanderburg C, Balderrama K
overview: The human striatum governs diverse motor, cognitive, and affective behaviors yet lacks the obvious cytoarchitectural boundaries defining functional territories elsewhere in the brain.

title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals molecular organization of human and nonhuman primate basal ganglia.
abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) are interconnected subcortical nuclei with a complex topographical organization that orchestrate goal-directed behaviors and are implicated in neurodegenerative movement disorders. We generated a cellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics atlas of the BG in human, rhesus macaque, and common marmoset, sampling over one million cells in each species. By integrating spatial data with a cross-species consensus single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) cell-type taxonomy, this atlas reveals principles of molecular organization within and across structures. Extensive spatial sampling across the rostral-caudal axis illuminates complex, yet highly stereotyped, multi-axis gene expression gradients superimposed onto discrete compartments of the striatum. Additionally, we identify core-shell organization of the internal globus pallidus. This unified, cross-species spatial transcriptomics atlas will be a foundational resource for characterizing the molecular and functional organization of the BG and their roles in health and disease.
authors: Hewitt MN, Turner MA, Johansen N, McMillen DA, Dan S, DeBerardine M, Ruiz A, Huang M, Quon J, Fu Y
overview: The basal ganglia (BG) are interconnected subcortical nuclei with a complex topographical organization that orchestrate goal-directed behaviors and are implicated in neurodegenerative movement disorders.
main: This unified, cross-species spatial transcriptomics atlas will be a foundational resource for characterizing the molecular and functional organization of the BG and their roles in health and disease.

title: Toward an integrated framework for a human and mammalian brain cell atlas.
abstract: The NIH BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) is developing a standardized, integrated reference framework for classifying and studying brain cell types across human, macaque, marmoset, and mouse. We present a cross-species, multimodal atlas of the basal ganglia, a group of subcortical nuclei central to motor control, adaptive behavior, and neurological disease. Built from large-scale single-cell transcriptomic classification and integrated with epigenomic, spatial genomic, multiomic, and developmental datasets, the atlas provides a curated, data-driven taxonomy with standardized nomenclature, extensive phenotypic characterization, and community-informed annotation. Cell types are mapped into species-specific anatomical reference frameworks and linked across species through structural ontologies. Realizing this resource required coordinated standards for tissue acquisition and processing, harmonized donor metadata, anatomical registration, sequencing pipelines, data infrastructure, visualization, mapping tools, and interoperable metadata. The BICAN basal ganglia atlas demonstrates how pipelines and standards can be implemented, validated, and scaled toward a whole-brain human and mammalian cell-type reference.

title: Stepping (hi)stones: Charting a single-cell multiomic path toward understanding the human brain.
abstract: In this issue of Cell, two single-cell multiomic atlases jointly profile transcription and histone modifications across different regions of the adult human brain, revealing cell-type-specific regulatory landscapes, developmental epigenetic memory, and improved interpretation of neurological variants. These studies establish a framework for understanding human brain cell identity, evolution, and pathology.

title: NeuroBase: A Web-Based Transcriptomic Resource and R Package for Cross-Disorder Analysis of Neurodegenerative and Neuropsychiatric Diseases.
abstract: Neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder, Parkinson's disease, and schizophrenia, are highly prevalent and biologically complex conditions that remain difficult to diagnose and treat. This study aimed to develop NeuroBase, a web-based transcriptomic resource that supports exploratory comparison of shared and disorder-specific gene expression features across these disorders. Fourteen human brain bulk RNA sequencing datasets (262 total samples) were processed using a standardized pipeline, followed by differential gene expression analysis with DESeq2, edgeR and limma-voom for broad exploratory discovery, complemented by a multi-method sensitivity analysis to define a method-concordant core gene set, protein-protein interaction network analysis using STRING with downstream exploration in Cytoscape, and functional enrichment analysis. Principal component analysis and clustering-based visualizations were used to summarize similarities and differences in transcriptomic patterns among disorders. Differential expression analysis identified dataset-level significant genes within each disorder using DESeq2 for one dataset per disorder (FDR ≤ 0.05), including 38 genes in Alzheimer's disease, 6,704 in autism spectrum disorder, 3,559 in bipolar disorder, 687 in Parkinson's disease, and 2,750 in schizophrenia; a stricter multi-method intersection analysis yielded method-concordant Core Intersection sets in the most informative datasets (983 core DEGs in autism spectrum disorder, 505 in bipolar disorder, 281 in schizophrenia, and 234 and 151 in two Parkinson's disease datasets; only two core genes (SPP1 and CHST3) were found in Alzheimer's disease). A unified strict-threshold reanalysis (FDR ≤ 0.05, |log₂FC|≥ 1) revealed disorder-level DEG burdens ranging from 34 (Alzheimer's disease) to 2,812 (autism) deduplicated genes, but only 24 genes were reproducible across independent cohorts of the same disorder, highlighting the limited cross-cohort reproducibility characteristic of bulk brain transcriptomics. Enrichment analyses identified significantly enriched signaling pathways in autism spectrum disorder and nominally enriched synapse-related pathways in Alzheimer's disease. Representative high-signal genes included SPP1 in Alzheimer's disease, NRGN in one Parkinson's disease dataset, and BEST1 in autism spectrum disorder. Cross-disorder comparison identified 465 differentially expressed genes shared between the neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorder groups, and principal component analysis showed that sample variation was dominated by dataset and tissue of origin. NeuroBase is a publicly accessible, web-based transcriptomic database and companion R package (neurobaseR) that enables standardized, cross-disorder exploration of bulk brain gene expression profiles across neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders, supporting comparative analysis, programmatic data access, and hypothesis generation through interactive visualization and pathway-level summaries.

title: Singapore grouper iridovirus VP018 exploits FTR86 to promote viral replication through Tollip-mediated degradation of the STING-TBK1 axis.
abstract: Members of the tripartite motif (TRIM) family have been demonstrated to exert crucial roles in immune defense against pathogens. However, functions of the fish-specific TRIM subfamily (FTR), which lacks mammalian orthologues, remains poorly understood. In the current study, we investigated the potential roles of grouper FTR86 (EcFTR86) on innate immune response and its actions during fish virus infection. EcFTR86 was found to localize to lysosomes, and its transcription was significantly up-regulated in grouper spleen cells upon Singapore grouper iridovirus (SGIV) infection. Notably, the exogenous expression of EcFTR86 markedly enhanced SGIV replication, whereas knockdown of endogenous EcFTR86 significantly attenuated viral infection, demonstrating that EcFTR86 functions as a pro-viral factor against virus infection. EcFTR86 negatively regulated type I interferon signaling triggered by STING-TBK1 and interacted with the key molecules of STING-TBKl axis. Mechanistically, EcFTR86 degraded STING or TBK1 via an autophagy-lysosome-dependent pathway. Moreover, autophagic cargo receptor Tollip was identified to interact with EcFTR86, and was involved in EcFTR86-mediated degradation of STING or TBK1. In addition, EcFTR86 was verified to interact with SGIV viral proteins, including VP018 and VP075, whereas only VP018 exploited EcFTR86 to accelerate the degradation effects on STING and TBK1, thereby abrogating the interferon response. Collectively, our findings firstly showed that FTR86 functioned as a negative regulator of interferon response, and was exploited by fish iridoviral proteins to promote viral replication via Tollip-mediated autophagic degradation of the STING-TBK1 axis.

title: RORα contributes to melatonin-mediated neuroprotection in cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury by promoting microglia/macrophage M2 polarization through the AMPK-mTOR signaling pathway.
abstract: Cerebral ischemia/reperfusion (CI/R) injury is a neurological disorder in which microglia and macrophages regulate repair by switching M1/M2 phenotypes. RORα, a regulator of circadian rhythm and a mediator for melatonin effects, has an unclear role in CI/R injury and melatonin-mediated neuroprotection, particularly in microglial/macrophage polarization. An in vivo transient middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion model was established in C57BL/6J mice, and in vitro oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R) models were developed for BV-2 and HT22 cells. In vivo, Flag-tagged RORα overexpression lentivirus were intracranially injected and melatonin (10 mg/kg) was injected intraperitoneally; in vitro, BV2 cells were exposed to 200 µM melatonin and infected with an RORα-overexpressing lentiviral vector, while HT22 cells were cultivated in conditioned medium. Western blot, immunofluorescence, TTC staining, and ELISA were used to evaluate RORα expression, neurological function, microglia/macrophage M2 polarization, inflammatory responses, and cellular apoptosis, respectively. The role of the AMPK-mTOR pathway was confirmed using the AMPK inhibitor Compound C in vitro. The viability, apoptosis, and ROS levels of HT22 cell were assessed using CCK-8 assay, TUNEL staining, and flow cytometry, respectively. In both in vivo and BV-2 cell in vitro models, RORα levels gradually decreased within 24 h, followed by a gradual recovery. Melatonin reduced neurological scores and enhanced blood-brain barrier protection, promoting M2 microglia/macrophage polarization and inhibiting subsequent inflammatory responses, with RORα overexpression further amplifying these effects. In an HT22 cell model, RORα overexpression enhanced the protection by melatonin against OGD/R-induced reductions in cell viability, as well as against increased apoptosis and elevated ROS levels. Mechanistically, RORα overexpression promoted M2 microglial polarization via activation of the AMPK-mTOR pathway, thereby amplifying the melatonin-mediated neuroprotection. RORα enhanced neuroprotection by melatonin against CI/R injury through promoting microglia/macrophage M2 polarization, suggesting a possible treatment target for CI/R injury.

title: Irosustat and STX140 improve cognitive function and modulate amyloid, oxidative stress, and inflammatory pathways in experimental Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is currently the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder affecting the geriatric population. The pathology of AD has been described as neuronal loss caused by the accumulation of beta-amyloid plaques and the formation of neurofibrillary tangles resulting from tau protein phosphorylation. This study aimed to investigate the therapeutic potential of steroid sulfatase inhibition using two drugs, the clinical steroid sulfatase inhibitor Irosustat and the multi-targeting preclinical candidate STX140, in scopolamine-induced AD in male Wistar rats compared to Donepezil as a standard drug. Behavioral tests such as the Open Field Test, Elevated Plus Maze Test, and Morris Water Maze Test were conducted to confirm the disease state and assess any improvement. At the end of the study, the animals were dissected to collect blood and brain samples for morphological, histological, immunohistochemical, biochemical, quantitative polymerase chain reaction and western blotting analyses. Treatment with Irosustat or STX140 improved learning, memory, and cognitive function compared with the disease group. The treated groups showed lowered brain tissue Aβ-40 & 42 levels, acetylcholinesterase activity, oxidative stress, and inflammatory markers. Morphological assessments showed that the drugs protected against brain atrophy and neuronal loss. Irosustat and STX140 are therefore promising therapeutic candidates for the management of Alzheimer's Disease.

title: Amyloid and tau display distinct patterns across Alzheimer's in anterior caudate.
abstract: The anterior caudate shows a pattern of Alzheimer's disease pathology that differs from the more extensively studied cortex. Across 41 donors, we found mostly diffuse amyloid beta plaques in gray matter and phosphorylated tau threads associated with white matter. Combining digital pathology with single-nucleus and spatial gene expression data, we detected no significant loss or gain in neuronal cell-type abundance with increasing pathology. However, we did observe increases in an FLT1+/IL1B+ microglial population with tau burden. Fast-spiking PTHLH-PVALB interneurons showed changes in genes related to ion channels, cellular trafficking, and phosphorylation. These findings offer a cellular-resolution reference for investigating how Alzheimer's disease affects subcortical brain regions.

title: Molecular Insights into the Aβ-42 Tetramer-Induced Disruptive Effects on a Model Phospholipid Membrane.
abstract: Formation of pores in neuronal membranes by amyloid-β (Aβ) oligomers is believed to be the origin behind neurotoxicity in Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, despite significant efforts, high-resolution characterizations of the pore-forming Aβ oligomers from experimental studies have been hindered due to structural heterogeneity of such aggregated oligomers. Consequently, efforts have been made to characterize the aggregated oligomers that develop within a membrane environment. Attempts have been made in this study to probe the microscopic properties of the three-dimensional structure of an Aβ oligomer, specifically an Aβ-42 tetramer present in a membrane-mimicking environment. The tetramer comprises of eight antiparallel β strands forming an Aβ-42 barrel. Atomistic molecular dynamics simulations at constant temperature and pressure (NPT) have been carried out on a fully hydrated liquid-crystalline lamellar phase of dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) lipid bilayer with an Aβ-42 tetramer embedded into it forming a pore. The results were compared with that of a fully hydrated pure DPPC bilayer system. Based on the calculations, we have been able to successfully quantify the disruptions in the bilayer structure caused by the peptide tetramer through conformational rearrangements of the lipid hydrocarbon chains. We believe that the results presented can quantitatively provide fundamental molecular-level insights into the detrimental effects of pore-forming Aβ-42 on membrane environment, which in turn, may have important implications on Alzheimer's disease.
