title: Serum Exosomes from Subacute Phase Post-cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Promote Microglial Pro-inflammatory Phenotype Polarization and Exacerbate Blood-Brain Barrier Disruption in Mice.
abstract: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) restores circulation but induces cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury characterized by blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption and microglial-mediated neuroinflammation. Exosomes circulate systemically following CPR, yet their temporal profiles and specific roles remain poorly understood. C57BL/6 mice (n = 5/group) underwent asphyxial cardiac arrest and CPR. BBB permeability was assessed longitudinally (3 h to 14 d) using Evans blue extravasation. Serum exosomes were isolated at 1 d and 3 d post-CPR and characterized. To determine immunomodulatory effects, exosomes were administered via intracerebroventricular injection into recipient mice, and BBB integrity and microglial polarization (CD86, CD206) were evaluated by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry. Additionally, primary cultures of microglia cells isolated from CPR mice were exposed to exosomes in vitro (n = 3/group), and pro-inflammatory phenotype/anti-inflammatory phenotype markers and inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, iNOS, TGF-β, Arg1, IL-10) were quantified. CPR induced transient BBB disruption peaking at 3 d post-resuscitation. Serum exosomes isolated at both 1 d and 3 d exhibited characteristic cup-shaped morphology. Intracerebroventricular administration of post-CPR exosomes significantly exacerbated BBB leakage and skewed microglial polarization toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype (elevated CD86⁺; reduced CD206⁺), with 3-day exosomes eliciting more potent detrimental effects than 1-day exosomes. In vitro, exposure to 3-day exosomes similarly produced stronger pro-inflammatory transcriptional responses and increased nitric oxide (NO) production compared with 1-day exosomes. Serum exosomes derived from post-CPR mice exhibit pro-inflammatory activity, aggravating BBB disruption and promoting microglial pro-inflammatory phenotype polarization upon central delivery. These findings suggest that circulating exosomes may contribute to post-resuscitation neuroinflammatory injury, and highlight exosome-related pathways as candidate targets worthy of further investigation.

title: Effects of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus on the Offspring's Neurodevelopment.
abstract: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is a major global health concern that affects up to 14% of pregnancies. Traditionally, it has been characterized by hyperglycemia and insulin resistance. However, GDM can also lead to long-term health consequences in offspring, particularly affecting neurodevelopment. It has been associated with an increased risk of cognitive deficits, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and emotional dysregulation in GDM-exposed offspring. Findings from human and experimental studies suggest that GDM disrupts cortical and hippocampal architecture, impairs synaptic plasticity, and induces epigenetic alterations in key neurodevelopmental genes. These mechanistic pathways include oxidative stress, inflammation, apoptosis, and altered neurotrophin expression and receptor signaling. Maternal metabolism, diet, and genetic background may negatively affect neurotrophin expression, which could impact fetal brain development. Lower levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and nerve growth factor (NGF) in maternal blood, placental tissue, and cord blood have been linked to poor neurodevelopmental outcomes. This suggests that neurotrophins could be considered potential biomarkers. This narrative review compiles the latest evidence on the effects of GDM on fetal brain development, emphasizing the role of neurotrophins, especially BDNF and NGF, as critical mediators in this process. Emerging data also suggest that glycemic control during pregnancy may partially restore neurotrophin levels and improve neurodevelopmental outcomes. Understanding the interaction between maternal glucose metabolism and fetal brain signaling pathways is essential for pregnancy care and the design of neuroprotective strategies.

title: Spontaneous Neuronal Activity in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Insights from Human and Animal Studies.
abstract: Developmental spontaneous neuronal activity (SNA) plays an instrumental role in the generation of precise brain circuits. Spontaneous activity patterns guide neuronal differentiation, synaptic refinement, and circuit formation; consequently, perturbations in these activity patterns can profoundly influence brain network organization. Growing evidence suggests that mutations in autism-associated genes lead to alterations of the SNA pattern during early brain development, thereby giving rise to the behavioral features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This review integrates findings from neuroimaging studies, which reveal widespread alterations in neuronal excitability in individuals with ASD. Regional homogeneity and functional connectivity analyses consistently demonstrate region-specific abnormalities, including hyperactivity in higher-order cortical regions, hypoactivity in sensorimotor areas, and disrupted long-range connectivity. These functional alterations are closely linked to the underlying molecular and cellular mechanisms such as excitation-inhibition (E/I) imbalance, impaired GABAergic signaling, glutamatergic dysregulation, and abnormalities in calcium-dependent signaling pathways. Identification of activity-based biomarkers, together with advanced neuroimaging techniques and computational and machine learning (ML) approaches, may facilitate early diagnosis of ASD. Understanding the origin and consequences of alterations in SNA provides a unifying framework for identifying novel targets for designing pharmacological intervention strategies.

title: The Cxcl14 chemokine defines pioneer axon guidance and early circuit assembly in the inner ear.
abstract: The nervous system wiring requires the precise coordination of axon guidance, neuronal migration, and target cell recognition. Here, we show that inner ear circuit formation relies on pioneer cells extending an axonal scaffold that selectively targets early-born hair cells. High spatiotemporal imaging of pioneer axons reveals how they navigate through the cranial environment, establishing dynamic cell-cell contacts with other axons to finally stabilize in target cells. These pioneer axons are required not only for follower axon growth but also for coordinated migration of follower neurons, revealing a cellular hierarchy underlying circuit assembly. We identify the chemokine Cxcl14 as a novel instructive guidance cue regulating pioneer axon extension, turning, and fasciculation at discrete cellular decision points. Loss of Cxcl14 disrupts axonal navigation, compromises synaptic organization in hair cells, and impairs mechanosensory-based behavior. Together, our findings establish a new chemokine-based mechanism linking pioneer axon guidance to early sensory circuit assembly necessary for building mechanosensory networks.

title: Antisense oligonucleotide silencing rescues neurodevelopmental deficits in AMPA receptor gain-of-function mice.
abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are essential for neuronal development and brain function. We investigated the role of a recurrent AMPAR GluA1 variant (GRIA1 p.A636T) identified in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using a Gria1-A636T knock-in mouse model, we show that this variant is sufficient to produce core ASD/ID-like behaviors and cause selective hippocampal vulnerability characterized by progressive dendritic atrophy and neuronal loss. Despite a reduction in GluA1-containing complexes, synaptic AMPARs exhibit hyperexcitability and fail to transition from calcium-permeable to calcium-impermeable AMPARs during development, resulting in persistent excitotoxicity. To explore potential therapeutic interventions, we developed an allele-specific antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) to selectively silence the mutant transcript. A single neonatal ASO dose prevents hippocampal pathology and rescues behavioral deficits. These findings define a mechanism of developmental excitotoxicity driven by a GRIA1 gain-of-function channelopathy and support RNA-targeted precision therapy for AMPAR-related neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Altered dynamic brain states and potential transcriptomic correlates in autism spectrum disorder.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is associated with widespread alterations in functional brain networks, but its transient dynamic brain states and potential transcriptomic correlates remain unclear. We applied Leading Eigenvector Dynamics Analysis (LEiDA) to resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 110 individuals with ASD and 110 healthy controls (HCs) from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange I (ABIDE I) dataset. Five recurrent phase-locking states were identified, and dynamic brain state metrics were compared between groups. Compared with HCs, individuals with ASD showed reduced fractional occupancy (FO) of State 5, which was predominantly characterized by the visual network with additional involvement of the sensorimotor network. Exploratory analyses within the ASD group revealed nominal negative associations between State 4 FO and ADOS total and social scores. To investigate potential transcriptomic correlates, we derived an ROI-wise ASD-HC State 5 weighted beta map and related it to Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA) gene expression data and SFARI ASD risk gene sets. SFARI ASD risk gene sets showed a consistent pattern of negative spatial associations with the ASD-related State 5 imaging phenotype, but these associations did not reach statistical significance after BrainSMASH testing and FDR correction. Exploratory rank-based Gene Ontology (GO) analysis implicated biological functions related to neuronal structure, synaptic function, and the regulation of neuronal excitability. These findings identify alterations in dynamic brain state organization in ASD and provide exploratory transcriptomic clues to their potential biological context.

title: Endosomal signalling of protease-activated receptor-2 amplifies histamine-induced pain of irritable bowel syndrome.
abstract: BACKGROUND.: Proteases and histamine, co-secreted by mast cells and bacteria, sensitize colonic nociceptors and contribute to irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) pain. OBJECTIVE.: To determine whether irreversible proteolytic cleavage of protease-activated receptor-2 (PAR2) and its continued activity in endosomes amplify and sustain otherwise transient pronociceptive actions of histamine receptors (HRs) to cause recurrent pain, the defining symptom of IBS. DESIGN.: We investigated PAR2 and H1R coexpression in nociceptors using RNAscope and assessed the consequences of coactivation using electrophysiological assays of nociceptor sensitization and biophysical measurements of receptor and effector activity. RESULTS.: PAR2 and H1R were coexpressed by human and mouse dorsal root ganglion nociceptors. Intracolonic infusion of fecal supernatants from IBS patients with elevated histamine and proteolytic activity enhanced mechanosensitivity of colonic nociceptors in mice. Antagonists of PAR2 or H1R abolished this response. Combined administration of subthreshold concentrations of trypsin and histamine replicated the effects of fecal supernatant and caused hyperexcitability of isolated nociceptors. Pre-activation with trypsin sensitized histamine-induced hyperexcitability in nociceptors from wild-type but not Par2−/− mice. Endocytosis inhibitors prevented this hypersensitivity, consistent with sustained endosomal signaling of PAR2 and persistent nociceptor hyperexcitability. Trypsin amplified histamine-induced activation of H1R and β-arrestin2 and Gαq effectors at the plasmalemma and in endosomes. Conversely, histamine did not sensitize trypsin-induced hyperexcitability of neurons, in line with the inability of histamine to induce sustained nociceptor hypersensitivity. CONCLUSIONS.: By amplifying and maintaining the otherwise transient actions of H1R and possibly other pain receptors, persistent PAR2 endosomal signaling makes a dominant contribution to IBS-related colonic pain.

title: APC regulates NSLIT2-induced internalization and signaling of the chemorepellent receptor, ROBO1.
abstract: The SLIT-Roundabout signaling pathway regulates axon guidance and cell migration, and ROBO1 is a receptor for SLIT ligands. ROBO1 undergoes constitutive endocytosis, which is enhanced upon NSLIT2 binding, but the molecular mechanisms and functional consequences of this process are not well understood. Using pharmacologic inhibitors and molecular techniques, we found that clathrin-mediated endocytosis is necessary for NSLIT2-induced inhibition of cell spreading. To explore the underlying mechanisms, we performed proximity-dependent biotin identification to identify ROBO1-interacting proteins whose association with the cytoplasmic domain of ROBO1 is differentially regulated by NSLIT2. We discovered that adenomatous polyposis coli, a multifunctional tumor suppressor, is in close proximity to ROBO1 but dissociates upon binding of NSLIT2 and that this dissociation is necessary for clathrin-mediated endocytosis of ROBO1 and subsequent effects on cell morphology. These findings provide new insights into the functional mechanisms by which NSLIT2 binding to ROBO1 affects changes in actin cytoskeletal architecture.

title: Cell adhesion molecule-related proteins signal to promote cytoneme elongation from Sonic Hedgehog-producing cells.
abstract: Tissue morphogenesis and postdevelopmental homeostasis rely on efficient information exchange between communicating cells. Cytonemes are actin-based protrusions that contribute to precise information flow by facilitating contact-mediated directional transport of diverse signaling cargoes. How pathway-specific cytonemes are formed is poorly understood, as are the molecular mechanisms promoting actin organization for elongation and stability of the dynamic cellular extensions. We investigated biogenesis of Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) cytonemes, revealing functional repurposing of cell adhesion molecule-related proteins Brother of CDON (BOC) and Cell adhesion molecule-related, Down-regulated by Oncogenes (CDON) into recruiters of actin regulators FARP1 and Cdc42 for cytoneme elongation. Loss of BOC and CDON function blunts protrusion-localized Cdc42 activity, reducing cytoneme lengths and occurrence in SHH-expressing cells. Live imaging of developing murine spinal cords reveals that CDON loss in SHH-expressing cells reduces the frequency of neuroepithelial cytonemes and alters neuronal cell fate specification. These results inform a model whereby SHH-binding proteins promote ligand transport through stimulating formation of long cytonemes.

main: These results inform a model whereby SHH-binding proteins promote ligand transport through stimulating formation of long cytonemes.

title: Neuronal cell-cycle re-entry stratifies clinical trajectories in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
abstract: The clinical heterogeneity of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) remains a fundamental barrier to effective therapy. While cell cycle re-entry in post-mitotic neurons is a known precursor to neurodegeneration, its role in defining patient-specific outcomes has never been established. Here, we integrate large-scale transcriptomic profiling from the AnswerALS cohort with mechanistic studies in human iPSC-derived spinal motor neurons to define how cell-cycle re-entry shapes disease heterogeneity in ALS. We identify a transcriptionally distinct patient subgroup with the highest expression of G1 or G2-phase cyclins that exhibit significantly slower functional decline (ALSFRS-R), whereas the engagement of S-phase markers correlates with accelerated disease progression. Nucleocytoplasmic transport dysfunction, a hallmark of ALS and related disorders, disrupts the spatial distribution of key regulatory proteins and may contribute to maladaptive cell-cycle activation. Our recent evidence suggests that impaired nuclear import may initiate, rather than merely accompany, neuronal cell-cycle re-entry. Using iPSC-derived motor neurons, we show that impaired nuclear import initiates TDP-43 pathology and global nuclear/cytoplasmic mis-localization of key ALS-related proteins. This nucleocytoplasmic transport dysfunction triggers a transient wave of cell-cycle activity immediately preceding neuronal cell death. Crucially, we show that DNA-replication initiation is a pathological inflection point of no return, as neurons entering S-phase accumulate replication-associated DNA damage and undergo cell death. Selective inhibition of CDK4/6 prevents S-phase entry and confers potent neuroprotection. Our findings demonstrate that impaired nuclear import drives maladaptive cell-cycle reactivation in ALS and that the depth of cell-cycle engagement stratifies neuronal fate and patient trajectories.
authors: Plessis-Belair J, Sher RB
overview: The clinical heterogeneity of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) remains a fundamental barrier to effective therapy.
main: Using iPSC-derived motor neurons, we show that impaired nuclear import initiates TDP-43 pathology and global nuclear/cytoplasmic mis-localization of key ALS-related proteins.

title: Transcriptional boosting and buffering during neurodevelopment by shifts in mRNA instability.
abstract: The contribution of mRNA half-life is commonly overlooked when examining changes in mRNA abundance during development. mRNA levels are regulated by transcription rate or mRNA half-life, but combinations of both could boost or buffer the final steady-state. We measured transcription rate and mRNA half-life changes during human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neuronal development using RATE-seq. The most prevalent mode of gene regulation during transitions to neuronal progenitors and neurons was transcriptional buffering. Less prevalent modes consisted of transcriptional boosting events, transcription rate only shifts, or mRNA half-life only shifts. Buffered and novel boosted gene sets were enriched in RNA-binding protein (RBP) motifs and microRNA sites. Global mRNA half-life decreased two-fold in neurons. microRNA copy number per cell increased during neurodevelopment coincident with destabilization of a subset of short isoforms that contributed to increased average 3'UTR length. Our findings identify mRNA instability mechanisms that regulate transcript levels and 3'UTR isoform abundance, and provide a precedent for transcriptional boosting or buffering during development of other human tissues.

main: Global mRNA half-life decreased two-fold in neurons.

title: PPP1R1B differentially modulates alcohol intake and emotional comorbidity through distinct prefrontal circuits.
abstract: Excessive alcohol consumption frequently co-occurs with anxiety and depression in alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet the specific neural circuits and molecular mechanisms coordinating these comorbid conditions remain poorly defined. The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), particularly its prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) subregions, projects to key reward and emotion centers like the nucleus accumbens (Nac) and basolateral amygdala (BLA), but the functional heterogeneity of these projections is unclear. Using chemogenetics, retrograde tracing, electrophysiology, spatial proteomics, and cell-type-specific gene editing in mice subjected to a 4-wk intermittent access to alcohol (IAA) paradigm, we selectively manipulated glutamatergic projections from the PL and IL to the Nac core, Nac shell, and BLA and assessed alcohol intake, anxiety-like, and depression-like behaviors. Chemogenetic activation of PL-Nac core projections reduced short-term alcohol intake, anxiety-, and depression-like behaviors, while IL-BLA activation decreased alcohol consumption and anxiety-like behaviors only. Retrograde tracing revealed mirror-image anatomical segregation of projection-defined neuronal subpopulations within PL/IL linking spatial organization to functional divergence. IAA induced pathway-specific synaptic adaptations. Spatial proteomics nominated protein phosphatase 1 regulatory subunit 1B (PPP1R1B) as a candidate molecule in PL-Nac core neurons. Independent immunostaining confirmed PPP1R1B downregulation, and circuit-specific knockout recapitulated alcohol-related and affective phenotypes, whereas overexpression reversed them. In IL-BLA neurons, PPP1R1B manipulation modulated alcohol intake and anxiety, but not depression. These findings define a subregion- and projection-specific organizational logic in the mPFC for differentially regulating alcohol consumption and emotional comorbidity, with PPP1R1B as a key molecular determinant. This provides a neural pathway-molecule framework for targeted intervention in AUD.

title: Autophagy- and Ferroptosis-Related Responses and SIRT1/mTOR Signaling in Nucleus Pulposus Cells Under Fluid Shear Stress.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: To characterize duration-dependent responses of Nucleus Pulposus Cells (NPCs) to Fluid Shear Stress (FSS) and identify candidate pathways associated with autophagy- and ferroptosis-related changes relevant to Intervertebral Disc Degeneration (IVDD). METHODS: Primary NPCs isolated from male Sprague-Dawley rats were exposed to 12 dyn/cm² FSS for 0, 30, 60, 90, or 120 minutes. Cellular morphology, proliferation, apoptosis, mitochondrial function, autophagy-related structures, and protein expression were assessed. Chloroquine, erastin, and ferrostatin-1 were used in pharmacological comparisons. Network pharmacology, Mendelian randomization, transcriptomic analyses, machine learning, human single-cell analysis, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations supported candidate prioritization. RESULTS: Among the conditions tested, 60 min of FSS produced the most favorable cellular response, with improved proliferation and reduced apoptosis. This response was accompanied by increased autophagy-related structures, increased abundance of GPX4 and SLC7A11, and decreased abundance of ACSL4. A longer exposure of 120 minutes produced an adverse response. Network analysis identified 12 candidate hub genes, and integrated transcriptomic screening identified eight IVDD-associated candidates: ACSL1, KDM6B, MAPK14, TLR4, ALOX5, ATG7, PHF21A, and SIRT1. Human single-cell analysis provided their cellular expression context. SIRT1 was the only panel member assessed experimentally by Western blotting under FSS. Its abundance increased, and mTOR phosphorylation decreased after 60 min, with the opposite pattern after 120 minutes. Docking and simulations characterized predicted ligand-protein interactions involving SIRT1/mTOR. DISCUSSION: The cellular and computational findings support SIRT1/mTOR signaling as a candidate pathway linking the observed responses, while functional dependence and autophagy- ferroptosis coupling require validation. CONCLUSION: FSS elicited duration-dependent responses in NPCs, providing a basis for targeted mechanistic investigation and future phenotype-based screening relevant to IVDD.

title: A2A Receptor Intervention Protects Astrocytes Against 6-Hydroxydopamine-Induced Oxidative and Mitochondrial Stress via the p38 MAPK Axis, Alleviating Inflammation in an In Vivo Model of Parkinson's Disease.
abstract: INTRODUCTION/OBJECTIVE: Astrocytic mitochondrial dysfunction and redox imbalance contribute to Parkinson's Disease (PD) pathogenesis, but the role of adenosine A2A receptor (A2AR) antagonism in maintaining astrocytic homeostasis remains unclear. This study investigated whether the selective non-purine A2AR antagonist IDPU protects against 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA)-induced astrocytic stress and improves behavioural, neurochemical, and inflammatory outcomes in an experimental model of PD. METHODS: Primary cortical astrocytes were exposed to 6-OHDA (100 μM) and subsequently treated with IDPU (0.5-1 μM) or ZM241385. Cell viability, apoptosis, Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS), intracellular Ca²⁺, Mitochondrial Membrane Potential (MMP), BDNF, and p38MAPK/DRP1/Parkin signalling were assessed. In vivo efficacy was evaluated in adult male Sprague-Dawley rats with unilateral 6-OHDA lesions following 14 days of treatment with IDPU (6 or 9 mg/kg) or ZM241385 (5 mg/kg), using behavioural, dopamine, and TNF-α assessments. RESULTS: 6-OHDA reduced astrocyte viability, increased apoptosis, ROS production and intracellular Ca²⁺ levels, and disrupted MMP. IDPU treatment improved cell viability, reduced apoptosis, oxidative stress and Ca²⁺ overload, and partially restored MMP and BDNF levels. These effects were accompanied by reduced phosphorylation of p38MAPK and DRP1 and restoration of Parkin expression. In vivo, IDPU improved motor performance and depressive-like behaviour, partially restored dopamine levels, and reduced TNF-α expression in 6-OHDA-lesioned rats. DISCUSSION: These findings indicate that A2AR antagonism may mitigate astrocytic stress by modulating redox balance, calcium homeostasis, mitochondrial dynamics, and inflammatory signalling. The observed regulation of the p38MAPK-DRP1-Parkin axis supports a potential mechanistic link between astrocytic mitochondrial dysfunction and neuroinflammatory outcomes in PD. CONCLUSION: IDPU-mediated A2AR antagonism demonstrated protective effects against 6-OHDA-induced astrocytic and Parkinsonian alterations, supporting A2AR antagonism as a potential non-dopaminergic, astrocyte-targeted therapeutic approach. Further studies are required to establish its effects on dopaminergic neuronal survival and long-term therapeutic efficacy.

title: UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss.
abstract: TDP-43 nuclear depletion is a defining pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia that induces widespread cryptic splicing defects in hundreds of transcripts1-8. Despite this, whether TDP-43 loss affects synaptic function has remained unclear. Here we show that TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact but suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication. Genetic correction of a single cryptic splicing event in UNC13A was sufficient to rescue these deficits. We developed splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides that correct UNC13A cryptic splicing in human cortical and spinal motor neurons and in a humanized mouse model. In human neurons this intervention restored spontaneous and evoked synaptic vesicle release, release probability at individual synapses and wider network synchrony. Together, this establishes UNC13A splice correction as a mechanistically defined and genetically validated therapeutic strategy relevant to roughly 97% of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and roughly 50% of patients with frontotemporal dementia with TDP-43 pathology.

title: Thalamic Reticular Nucleus Excitability and Cholinergic Signaling are Disrupted in a Mouse Model of Alzheimer's Disease Neuropathology.
abstract: The thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) forms powerful GABAergic connections with thalamic nuclei that regulate sleep, attention, and sensory processing. TRN neurons receive dense cholinergic innervation from the basal forebrain and brainstem, dynamically shaping TRN function across brain states. We previously showed reduced TRN activity and sleep deficits in amyloid precursor protein transgenic mice (APP mice), implicating TRN dysfunction as an early contributor to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathophysiology. Here, using slice electrophysiology in mice of both sexes, we determined whether changes in intrinsic membrane properties or cholinergic synaptic transmission contribute to TRN hypoactivity in APP mice. We found that TRN neurons located in the inner core and outer shell regions undergo substantial increases in excitability after the first postnatal month. In mature animals, core neurons exhibited higher firing rates and diverse firing patterns, including persistent firing, whereas shell neurons fired at lower rates and displayed more homogeneous firing patterns without persistent activity. Firing diversity in core neurons was mediated in part by low-threshold T-type Ca²⁺ channels. Cholinergic synaptic activation, mediated predominantly by basal forebrain afferents, produced biphasic excitatory-inhibitory postsynaptic responses in both core and shell neurons, with the ratio of postsynaptic excitation and inhibition varying across postsynaptic targets. Overall, cholinergic activation suppressed TRN firing. In APP mice, core neurons showed reduced intrinsic excitability and cholinergic afferents evoked postsynaptic responses with a larger muscarinic receptor-mediated inhibitory component, leading to delayed TRN firing. Together, these findings identify both intrinsic and cholinergic synaptic mechanisms that may contribute to TRN dysfunction during early AD.Significance Statement Alzheimer's disease (AD) is typically diagnosed after cognitive symptoms emerge when treatments are less effective, highlighting the need to understand preclinical disease mechanisms. Cholinergic signaling and slow-wave sleep are disrupted before symptom onset, but the mechanisms underlying these changes remain poorly understood. Because the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) receives strong cholinergic input and mediates sleep-related rhythms, it is well positioned to contribute to early AD pathophysiology. We previously found reduced TRN activity and disrupted sleep in an AD mouse model. Here, we show that intrinsic excitability and cholinergic synaptic signaling are altered in TRN neurons during preclinical AD. These changes may contribute to thalamic dysfunction and sleep disturbances, providing a potential circuit mechanism linking early AD pathology to disease progression.

title: Incomplete synaptic vesicle priming functionally disconnects CA1 pyramidal cells.
abstract: The hippocampal CA1 area is perceived as a nonrecurrent neuronal network, i.e., CA1 pyramidal cells (CA1PCs) within the CA1 area innervate mainly γ-aminobutyric acid-releasing interneurons but not each other. Here, we performed an unbiased examination of the functional properties of local CA1PC output synapses using in vitro two-photon glutamate imaging. Fluorescent transients measured with iGluSnFR3 in individual boutons displayed extraordinary heterogeneity in their amplitudes and short-term plasticity patterns upon a complex train of presynaptic action potential firing. Post hoc electron microscopy of the imaged boutons demonstrated that distinct postsynaptic structure-innervating boutons display different functional properties. Approximately 25% of the boutons innervate CA1PC spines, which either release glutamate with very low release probability or completely fail to release. Phorbol 12,13-dibutyrate and elevated calcium (2+) concentration, manipulations that enhance synaptic vesicle priming and fusion, convert these silent into properly functioning synapses. Our results provide evidence that CA1PCs are interconnected with structurally and molecularly intact glutamatergic synapses, but incomplete synaptic vesicle (SV) priming precludes SV release.

title: A Correlative Light and Electron Microscopy Workflow for Nanoscale Three-Dimensional Reconstruction of Synaptic Projections From the Thalamic Reticular Nucleus.
abstract: Correlative light and electron microscopy (CLEM) combines molecular specificity with nanoscale ultrastructural resolution and has become an important approach for investigating neural circuit organization. However, ultrastructural reconstruction of long-range projection terminals remains technically challenging. This study aimed to develop a CLEM workflow for the identification, localization, three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction, and ultrastructural characterization of thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN)-derived presynaptic terminals in the mouse thalamus. TRN presynaptic terminals were selectively labeled by stereotaxic injection of rAAV-hSyn-Synaptophysin-mCherry. Confocal microscopy was combined with serial section scanning electron microscopy (ssSEM) to achieve fluorescence-guided ultrastructural imaging and 3D reconstruction of labeled axonal boutons and synaptic contacts. The CLEM workflow enabled fluorescence-guided identification of presynaptic terminals within serial EM datasets. 3D reconstruction of a representative TRN axon segment revealed multiple en passant boutons along continuous axonal shafts. Ultrastructural analysis demonstrated synaptic contacts with multiple postsynaptic dendritic profiles, together with distinct vesicle distributions and mitochondrial organization within presynaptic boutons. This study presents a practical CLEM-based workflow for nanoscale reconstruction of long-range synaptic projections. Application of this method to the TRN-to-thalamus pathway illustrates the spatial organization of presynaptic boutons and their postsynaptic contacts in the thalamic neuropil. The workflow provides a methodological framework for ultrastructural studies of defined neural projections in the mammalian brain.

title: The people behind the papers - Pavel Tomancak and Jean-Yves Tinevez.
abstract: Segmenting cells and tracking their internal structures remains a complex image-analysis challenge in cell and developmental biology. In their work, Johannes Girstmair, Tobias Pietzsch, Pavel Tomancak, Jean-Yves Tinevez and colleagues demonstrate how Mastodon, an existing Fiji/ImageJ plugin, can visualise and analyse cell lineages and track cells in 3D within large microscopy datasets. To learn more about their work, we talked to the two corresponding authors, Pavel Tomancak, Principal Investigator at the Max Planck Institute of Molecular Cell Biology and Genetics, Germany, and director of the Central European Institute of Technology, Czech Republic, as well as Jean-Yves Tinevez, founder and leader of the Image Analysis Facility, Institute Pasteur, France.

title: Integrating Cytoskeletal Systems in Neurons and Glia: Dynamic Orchestration of Structure and Function.
abstract: Neurons and glia form the circuitry of our nervous system, allowing nerve cells to communicate with each other and other cell types throughout the body in a highly specific manner to integrate sensory, motor, and cognitive functions. The ability of these cells to do this is profoundly dependent on an elaborate and dynamic cytoskeleton which allows these cells to adopt complex shapes and specialized structures such as myelin sheaths, the blood-brain barrier, axonal growth cones, dendritic spines, nodes of Ranvier, synapses, and elaborate sensory organs. The cytoskeleton is also critical for morphogenetic movements, the migration of neuronal precursors, and axon growth, which together establish the organization and wiring pattern of the central and peripheral nervous system during development. This review provides a primer on our current understanding of the cytoskeleton of neurons and glia, with an emphasis on how the protein polymers of the cytoskeleton-microtubules, actin filaments, intermediate filaments, and septins-work together to orchestrate the remarkable shapes and functions of these cells. We also highlight key questions and challenges for the field and technological advances that may help address them.

title: Brain organoids: Experimental access to human-specific brain development.
abstract: Human cerebral cortical development includes species-divergent cellular programs and unusually prolonged trajectories that remain difficult to investigate experimentally. These processes support human-specific cognitive abilities and are thought to be associated with vulnerability to neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders. Human brain organoids provide a tractable system for studying these processes across developmental time and under controlled perturbation. Here, we review how cortical organoids model human-specific features of progenitor biology and cell diversification, as well as progressive cellular maturation and circuit formation. We consider the limitations that constrain later-stage maturation and how approaches including the addition of missing cell types, the use of assembloids, and transplantation can extend the developmental processes accessible to study. Finally, we examine how patient-derived, isogenic, chimeric, and perturbation-based organoid systems are being used to investigate neurodevelopmental disorders and, in turn, reveal mechanisms of typical human development.

title: Beyond Transcriptomes and Dissociated Cells: Spatial Proteomics for Mechanistic Neurobiology.
abstract: Single-cell transcriptomic studies have revealed remarkable molecular heterogeneity across neuronal and glial populations during development, aging, and disease. However, dissociation-based approaches disrupt tissue architecture, and RNA measures alone incompletely capture cellular function. These limitations are particularly relevant in neurodegenerative diseases, where pathology develops within cellular microenvironments and diseased cells progressively lose canonical cell-state identity markers. Spatial proteomic approaches are beginning to address this critical gap by enabling high-dimensional molecular profiling within the intact tissue, preserving the spatial relationships between vulnerable cells and their surrounding cellular environments across scales ranging from subcellular single-cell imaging to large-volume three-dimensional mapping. Here, we discuss emerging spatial proteomic technologies and their applications in aging and neurodegeneration, emphasizing how integration with complementary modalities, including transcriptomics, glycomics, three-dimensional genome architecture, and quantitative neuropathology, is providing new insight into disease biology. We further highlight how these approaches are beginning to accelerate therapeutic target validation, biomarker discovery, and treatment response monitoring. Realizing the full potential of spatial proteomics will require continued advances in cross-platform harmonization, analytical standardization, and computational methods capable of integrating increasingly complex, multimodal datasets.

title: The neuroprotective efficacy of cholecalciferol: Targeting oxidative stress and NF-κB-mediated neuroinflammation in a valproic acid-induced autism model.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a multifactorial neurodevelopmental condition characterized by repetitive behaviors, heightened anxiety and altered exploratory motivation, which are closely linked to oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and glial dysfunction. Although vitamin D₃ (cholecalciferol) exhibits promising neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory properties that may counteract these effects, comparative evidence evaluating whether early prophylactic supplementation provides superior neuroprotection compared to late therapeutic administration, as well as its precise modulation of the cerebral NF-κB/glial axis, remains lacking. AIM: This study aimed to evaluate and compare the prophylactic versus therapeutic effects of vitamin D₃ against valproic acid (VPA)-induced oxidative, neuroinflammatory, and apoptotic alterations in the frontal cortex of rat pups, correlating these neuromolecular changes with behavioral performance. METHODS: Forty male albino rat pups were randomly divided into five groups (n = 8/group): Control, Vit. D, Val. A., Vit. D + Val. A, and Val. A. + Vit. D. Vitamin D₃ (80,000 IU/kg, i.m.) was administered on postnatal days (PND) 7 and 14 in the protective group, and on PND 21 and 28 in the therapeutic group, while VPA (400 mg/kg, s.c.) was given as a single dose on PND 14. Behavioral, biochemical, molecular (qPCR), histopathological, and immunohistochemical studies were done to assess cortical oxidative stress, NF-κB-mediated neuroinflammation, glial activation, and neuronal integrity. RESULTS: VPA-exposed rats exhibited increased repetitive behavior, heightened anxiety-like responses, and reduced central exploration in the open field test, along with elevated MDA levels, and reduced SOD activity, along with upregulation of pro-inflammatory and pro-apoptotic genes (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, BAX, and Caspase-3). Histological examination revealed neuronal degeneration, glial activation, and NF-κB immunoreactivity in the frontal cortex. Vitamin D₃ administration, both preventively and therapeutically, significantly mitigated these behavioral, biochemical, molecular, and histological alterations with significantly more pronounced neuroprotection observed in the early prophylactic group (Vit. D + Val. A.). CONCLUSION: Vitamin D₃ exerts protective and restorative effects against VPA-induced autistic-like alterations in the developing rat frontal cortex through attenuation of oxidative stress, suppression of the NF-κB inflammatory cascade, inhibition of glial activation, and promotion of neuronal survival and neurogenesis. Importantly, the extent of neuroprotection is highly timing-dependent, emphasizing the critical value of early prophylactic supplementation during key postnatal neurodevelopmental windows.

title: Transdiagnostic variation in age-related patterns of rich-club organization across neurodevelopmental and related mental health conditions.
abstract: Rich-club organization is a topographical property of functional brain networks where highly connected regions are more densely interconnected. The rich-club has been shown to be vital for supporting cognitive functioning, and differences have been associated with a wide range of mental health and developmental conditions. This type of organization undergoes complex changes across development, and we have previously shown that males and females have strikingly distinct age-related changes. While disruptions in its development have been related to neurodevelopmental conditions and related mental health conditions such as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), the diagnostic- and sex-specific age-related patterns remain unexplored. These conditions also have heterogeneous and overlapping neurobiology and phenotype, and thus transdiagnostic approaches may be most suitable for addressing the complexities. Here, we combine the temporal advantages of magnetoencephalography (MEG) with a data-driven, transdiagnostic approach to parse the heterogeneity of age-related variation in rich-club organization in 386 neurodivergent (116 ADHD, 231 autism, 39 OCD) and 231 neurotypical children and youth, stratified by biological sex. In males and females, subgroups with distinct age-related patterns of rich-club organization did not align cleanly with the diagnostic categories. These patterns were frequency specific, separating the female subgroups in the alpha and gamma bands and the male subgroups in the theta, alpha, beta, and high gamma bands. While the female subgroups differed in their proportions of autistic and neurotypical individuals, all diagnostic categories were represented across the subgroups. The female subgroups also differed in intelligence, while the male subgroups differed in hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms. Together, our findings indicate that frequency-specific, age-related variation in rich-club organization is largely shared across neurotypical and neurodivergent children and youth, rather than delineating diagnostic categories, and highlight the importance of considering sex when studying the biological constructs underlying neurodivergence.

title: Expression of the neurodevelopmental disease susceptibility genes CADM1 and CADM2 in the early human fetal forebrain.
abstract: CADM1 and CADM2 are cell-adhesion molecules with likely roles in cell migration, axon guidance and synapse formation. Both are considered potential susceptibility genes for various neurodevelopmental disorders. However, their expression patterns in early human brain development have not been explored. Here we employed transcriptomics, RNAScope in situ hybridisation (ISH) and immunofluorescence (IF) to determine the time course and location of expression in the human cerebral cortex and thalamus between 7.5-17 postconceptional weeks (PCW). In the cerebral cortex, tissue RNAseq revealed both to be highly expressed throughout this period. CADM1 exhibited very high expression which declined slightly with age. CADM2 exhibited high expression which increased over time. Single-cell RNA-seq and ISH revealed that both genes were co-expressed in most cells; however, IF revealed different patterns of cellular localisation. At 8 PCW, expression for both CADMs was similar throughout the cortex and predominantly located in the cytoplasm/cell surface in the cortical plate (CP) but with stronger expression of CADM1 in the subventricular zone. However, from 10 PCW onwards, the strongest immunoreactivity for CADM1 was in the cell nucleus with weak cytoplasmic localisation, whereas CADM2 was expressed on the cell surface and increasingly in axons with age. By 17 PCW, CADM2 exhibited strong immunoreactivity in the thalamocortical and callosal corticocortical axons but was weakly expressed in corticofugal pathways. In the thalamus, CADM2 expression in posterior and lateral projection neurons contributing to thalamocortical pathways was confirmed. CADM1 and CADM2 show differential expression in the thalamus and associated nuclei, suggesting a role in their segregation; CADM1 favouring anterior and medial thalamic nuclei and the ventromedial subthalamus, CADM2 the lateral habenula, lateral and posterior thalamus and dorsolateral subthalamus. CADM1 and CADM2 may play important and varied roles in early fetal human forebrain development, guiding cell migration and aggregation, and axon guidance and fasciculation.

title: ER-mitochondria contacts orchestrate mitochondrial transport via C19orf12.
abstract: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-mitochondria contact sites facilitate lipid transfer, calcium signaling, and mitochondrial division; however, their role in mitochondrial transport remains unclear. Here, we identify hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP)-associated protein C19orf12 as an ER-anchored regulator of mitochondrial trafficking. The loss of C19orf12 leads to perinuclear mitochondrial clustering in cells, impaired anterograde transport in neurons, and progressive locomotor dysfunction in mice that recapitulates key features of HSP in humans. Mechanistically, C19orf12 forms a discrete complex with the mitochondrial Rho GTPase Miro1 and the Kinesin-1 motor Kif5b, thereby providing a molecular link between ER-mitochondria contacts and microtubule-based anterograde transport. Ca2+ also modulated C19orf12-Miro1 behavior in vitro and showed a biphasic association with mitochondrial motility in live cells. Therefore, our findings establish ER‒mitochondria contact sites as logistical hubs for Kinesin-1 motor loading and highlight the importance of the Ca2+-tunable C19orf12 scaffold in sustaining directional mitochondrial transport, providing a mechanistic framework for how C19orf12 loss may contribute to neurodegeneration.

title: Neuronal and mitochondrial phenotypes in iPSC-derived bipolar disorder models with and without a family history of mitochondrial disease.
abstract: Psychiatric disorders frequently accompany primary mitochondrial diseases (PMDs), suggesting shared biological pathways between mitochondrial function and psychiatric vulnerability. In this exploratory study, we investigated whether bipolar disorder (BD) occurring in the context of a family history of primary mitochondrial disease is associated with differences in neuronal and mitochondrial phenotypes. We generated induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), neural progenitor cells (NPCs), and cortical neurons (CNs) from three non-psychiatric controls, three individuals with BD without a family history of mitochondrial disease, and three individuals with BD who did not themselves have mitochondrial disease but had relatives with clinically diagnosed mitochondrial (BD-FHMD). Our primary endpoints were distinguished network activity and cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca2+ dynamics, complemented by measurements of mitochondrial and cellular function and metabolomic profiles across differentiation. Across neurodifferentiation, we assessed neuronal network activity, calcium dynamics, mitochondrial and cellular health, and metabolomic signatures. BD neurons exhibited sustained hyperexcitability with increased firing and burst activity. In contrast, BD-FHMD neurons showed lower network activity with enhanced cytosolic calcium responses and prolonged mitochondrial calcium transients. BD-FHMD also exhibited stage-dependent mitochondrial alterations, while BD and BD-FHMD showed distinct developmental metabolic signatures. Together, these findings identify two distinct mitochondrial-associated phenotypes within BD. BD is characterized by a hyperexcitable neuronal phenotype associated with altered developmental metabolic programming, whereas BD-FHMD exhibits calcium dysregulation and altered mitochondrial developmental trajectories consistent with increased bioenergetic vulnerability. These findings suggest that BD occurring in the context of a family history of primary mitochondrial disease may be characterized by a distinct pattern of neuronal and mitochondrial dysfunction. Replication in larger, independently characterized cohorts will be important to determine whether this family-history-defined phenotype can contribute to biologically informed subtyping and therapeutic approaches in BD.

title: scMINA: an interpretable workflow for paired scRNA-scATAC multiome integration and regulatory prioritization.
abstract: Single-cell multiomic technologies that jointly profile transcriptomic and epigenomic states provide unprecedented opportunities to investigate cellular heterogeneity and gene regulatory mechanisms in complex diseases. However, analysis of paired single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) and chromatin accessibility (scATAC-seq) data remains computationally challenging due to modality-specific technical variation, integration complexity, and limited interpretability of downstream regulatory inference. Here, we present scMINA (single-cell Multimodal Integration and Network Attribution), a modular and interpretable analytical workflow for the analysis of paired single-cell multiome datasets. scMINA comprises coordinated modules for multimodal integration, technical covariate correction, and regulatory feature prioritization, enabling systematic characterization of cellular states across transcriptomic and epigenomic modalities. In addition, scMINA incorporates explainable artificial intelligence-based attribution strategies to prioritize candidate genes and transcription factors associated with cell-state heterogeneity and disease-related regulatory alterations. We applied scMINA to the single-cell multiome data from the Seattle Alzheimer's Disease Brain Cell Atlas, where the workflow robustly resolved major glial cell populations and identified regulatory features associated with Alzheimer's disease pathology. By coupling multimodal integration with interpretable regulatory prioritization, scMINA provides a practical workflow for systematic analysis and biological interpretation of paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq datasets.

title: A pKa-Guided BBB-Permeable NIR Fluorescent Probe for Tracking Lipid Droplets in Microglia with Neuroinflammation and Alzheimer's Disease.
abstract: Abnormal accumulation of lipid droplets (LDs), accompanied by altered microenvironmental polarity within the microglia, is closely associated with neuroinflammation and also has been increasingly recognized as an early and dynamic indicator of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Herein, a LD-targeting polarity-sensitive blood-brain barrier (BBB)-permeable near-infrared (NIR) probe, BTDN, was screened by tuning the electron-donating substituents to modulate the pKa values of benzothiadiazole-based derivatives. Endowed with the donor-acceptor-donor (D1-A-D2) architecture and strong intramolecular charge-transfer (ICT) characteristics, the BTDN probe exhibited high sensitivity to polarity change. The BTDN probe displayed suitable physicochemical properties such as a pKa of 7.47 and lipophilicity with a log P of 3.72 for favorable BBB-penetrating efficiency with a permeability percentage of 24.23%. In addition, the BTDN probe showed advantages for fluorescence imaging including NIR emission from 643 to 770 nm with the increased polarity, Stokes shift larger than 308 nm, comparable two-photon absorption capacity with an absorption cross-section of 10 GM at 870 nm, good biocompatibility, and robust photostability. Using this multifunctional BTDN probe, the dynamic fluorescence imaging of accumulation behaviors of LDs in BV2 microglia with neuroinflammation was performed, demonstrating that LD formation may serve as a potential biomarker for neuroinflammation. Furthermore, overproduced LDs within microglia were directly observed in vivo and in tissue sections from the brains of AD mice. This work not only provides an imaging tool for dynamically characterizing LD accumulation in microglia but also provides insights into the relationship between LD accumulation in microglia and AD pathogenesis.

title: Platelet lysates ameliorate impaired neuronal autophagy in Parkinson's Disease: correlative evidence for ROS/Akt signaling.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder and represents a growing global health challenge. Platelet lysates (PLs) are enriched in growth factors, cytokines, and bioactive proteins with known tissue-regenerative and neurorestorative properties; however, their neuroprotective efficacy and molecular mechanisms in PD remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the neuroprotective effects of PLs in PD models and to explore the underlying mechanisms. METHODS: SH-SY5Y cells exposed to 6-OHDA, MPP⁺, or rotenone were used as in vitro PD models. Cell viability, morphological injury, ROS levels, TH expression, and p-α-syn (Ser129) levels were assessed. Autophagosome formation was evaluated using an Ad-GFP-LC3 transduction assay, and autophagic flux was further verified by bafilomycin A1-mediated lysosomal blockade. Mechanistic studies employed SC79 (Akt activator) and N-acetylcysteine (NAC, ROS scavenger). In vivo, MPTP-induced and A53T transgenic mouse models of PD were used to evaluate nigrostriatal dopaminergic neuronal protection, Nissl body preservation, p-α-syn accumulation, and motor function. RESULTS: PLs ameliorated neurotoxin-induced morphological injury, increased cell viability, reduced intracellular ROS levels, upregulated TH expression, and decreased p-α-syn (Ser129) accumulation in SH-SY5Y cells. Ad-GFP-LC3 assays showed that PLs promoted autophagosome biogenesis, and bafilomycin A1-based flux assays further confirmed that PLs rescued neurotoxin-impaired autophagic flux across all three toxin models. Mechanistically, PLs consistently reduced ROS and enhanced Akt phosphorylation. In MPP⁺- and 6-OHDA-injured cells, this was accompanied by ATG5/LC3-II upregulation and restoration of autophagic degradation; however, in the rotenone model, the toxin-induced ATG5 reduction was not significantly reversed despite effective attenuation of oxidative stress and p62 accumulation, suggesting ATG5-independent protective mechanisms. In vivo, PLs administration protected nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons, preserved Nissl bodies, reduced p-α-syn (Ser129) immunoreactivity, and improved motor function in both MPTP-induced and A53T transgenic mouse models of PD. CONCLUSION: PLs attenuate neurotoxin-induced neuronal injury and improve pathological and behavioral phenotypes in PD models. The ROS/Akt signaling axis appears to be one plausible mechanistic correlate of PLs-mediated neuroprotection, with toxin-specific divergence in downstream autophagy mechanisms. These findings support further investigation of PLs as a potential intervention for PD-related pathological phenotypes.

title: Neuroprotective potential of EGF-treated bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells in trimethyltin-induced neurodegeneration: in vitro and in vivo studies.
abstract: UNLABELLED: Background: Neurodegenerative diseases are progressive, debilitating, and often life-threatening disorders of the nervous system. Bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cells are considered a promising therapeutic strategy for different diseases, including neurodegeneration. EGF has been reported to promote neuron-like characteristics and neurotrophic responses in BM-MSCs. This study was conducted to assess the role of EGF-treated Bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells in a neurodegenerative rat model (a novel approach). Methods: In vitro analysis was performed to evaluate the specific dose and cell viability using MTT and Crystal Violet assays and morphology under a microscope. For the in vivo study, forty rats were randomly allocated into four groups: Control, Injury, injury + Bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells (BM-MSCS), and injury + EGF-treated Bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells (BM-MSCs). A neurodegenerative rat model was developed with the use of trimethyltin chloride. Following TMT induction, BM-MSCs and EGF-treated BM-MSCs were administered via the intrathecal route. Behavioral performance, Histopathological alteration, protein expression, and gene expression were evaluated. The assessed biomarkers included TNF-α (inflammation), NFL (neuronal injury), MAPT (Tau gene expression), the neurotrophic factors BDNF and NGF, together with the progenitor-associated marker Nestin. Findings: In vitro, BM-MSCs treated with 10 ng/mL EGF maintained cell viability comparable to untreated controls, as confirmed by MTT and Crystal Violet assays, while exhibiting pronounced neuron-like morphological characteristics. In vivo, transplantation of EGF-treated BM-MSCs significantly improved spatial learning, memory, and neuromuscular performance compared with both the TMT-induced injury group and the untreated BM-MSC group. Histopathological analysis demonstrated improved preservation of hippocampal architecture following EGF-treated BM-MSC transplantation. Furthermore, EGF-treated BM-MSCs significantly reduced the expression of TNF-α, neurofilament light chain (NFL), and phosphorylated Tau (p-Tau), while significantly increasing the expression of BDNF, NGF, and Nestin at both the protein and gene levels. Overall, EGF preconditioning enhanced the neuroprotective and recovery associated effects of BM-MSCs in the TMT-induced neurodegenerative rat model. Conclusion: EGF-preconditioned BM-MSCs attenuated TMT-induced neurodegenerative changes by improving behavioral performance, reducing neuroinflammatory and neuronal injury-associated responses, preserving hippocampal cellular and tissue integrity, and enhancing neurotrophic support. These findings suggest that EGF preconditioning may potentiate the neuroprotective and immunomodulatory effects of BM-MSCs and may represent a promising strategy for the treatment of neurodegenerative disorders. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s10616-026-01109-1.

title: J-Aggregation-Reshaped pKa in a Spirocyclic BODIPY Enables Ratiometric Lysosomal pH Sensing and Super-Resolution Imaging.
abstract: Ratiometric fluorescent pH probes typically rely on complex intramolecular energy/charge transfer, rendering the design strategies increasingly rigid. We report a conceptually distinct ratiometric probe based on pH-driven J-aggregate disassembly utilizing a spirocyclic BODIPY platform. Strategic installation of β-Cl and α-3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenylvinyl substituents on BODIPY synergistically drives J-aggregate formation via directional X···π, F···H, and π···π interactions. The resulting J-aggregates and the corresponding monomer displayed markedly different pKa values (4.69 vs. 7.54, ΔpKa = 2.85). As pH increases, spirocyclization is triggered, driving the cooperative disassembly of the J-aggregates, while monomer emission remains constant, thereby enabling a robust ratiometric readout (I714/I654) with excellent reversibility. This supramolecular J-aggregate enables quantitative lysosomal pH detection in cells, diagnosis of acute gastritis in mice, and self-blinking super-resolution lysosomal imaging without exogenous additives. This work establishes a new paradigm for ratiometric probe design via aggregation control and stimulus-responsive supramolecular disassembly.

title: International Multicenter Retrospective Study on UBTF-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: UBTF encodes the upstream binding transcription factor (UBTF), a protein essential for rRNA synthesis. Dominantly acting pathogenic variants, either de novo or inherited, have been associated with a broad clinical childhood-onset neurodegenerative/neurodevelopmental spectrum whose genotype-phenotype correlation has not been accurately defined yet. This multicenter study aims to conduct a retrospective analysis of a large cohort of patients with pathogenic variants in the UBTF gene to refine diagnostic criteria and identify clinically relevant outcome measures for future trials. METHODS: Clinical centers provided clinical, molecular, and neuroimaging data on patients carrying pathogenic or predicted pathogenic UBTF variants, consistent with the clinical phenotype. Data were collected using an human phenotype ontology-based standardized electronic case report form and included unreported cases or updated information on patients reported in the literature from January 2017 to December 2024. RESULTS: A cohort of 49 patients (23 previously unreported) was included in the study. The disease typically presented at ≤3 years (89.6%) with neuroregression in 71.4% of cases, either in a child with preexisting neurodevelopmental delay (42.9%) or after previously normal psychomotor development (28.6%). Less frequently, neurodevelopmental delay occurred in isolation (26.5%). During disease progression, patients developed behavioral abnormalities (81.6%), movement disorders (78.3%), autonomic manifestations (50.0%), and epilepsy (34.7%). At the last follow-up (mean age 13 years and 6 months), only 2 patients were deceased (4.1%). The main neuroimaging findings included white matter hyperintensity (68.1%), cerebral (66.0%) and cerebellar (51.1%) atrophy, and thinning of the corpus callosum (38.3%). However, brain MRI findings were reported as normal in 21.3% of cases. We identified 7 novel UBTF variants (c.271G>C; c.349A>T; c.495C>A; c.517G>A; c.761A>G; c.1048-2A>G; and c.1625_1626+15del). Genotype-phenotype analysis led to the distinction of 2 allelic, clinically distinct disorders: a childhood-onset neurodegenerative disease due to gain-of-function variants, characterized by the triad of neuroregression, movement, and behavioral disorders, and a neurodevelopmental disorder with a milder clinical course associated with loss-of-function/hypomorphic variants. DISCUSSION: The results from our deep-phenotyping analysis suggest the classification of UBTF-related disease into 2 main clinical syndromes impacting the natural history of the disease with a different degree of severity and complexity. This novel observation should be considered in the management and prognosis of patients and will be fundamental in the design of targeted therapies.

title: Reduced hypoxanthine Ameliorates LPS-triggered autism-like stereotyped behaviors in intestinal Tlr4 knockout mice via the DRN ROS-5-HT axis.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) involves social deficits and severe stereotyped behavior. While central serotonin (5-HT) systems and Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) activation are known to be implicated in ASD, how gut TLR4 affects central 5-HT and stereotyped behavior remains unknown. This study demonstrated that prenatal lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced social deficits in offspring of both intestinal Tlr4 knockout (Tlr4△IEC) and Tlr4fl/fl mice. However, the stereotyped behaviors and the inhibition of dorsal raphe nuclei (DRN) 5-HT were reduced in Tlr4△IEC-LPS mice compared with those in Tlr4fl/fl-LPS mice. By intersecting metabolites present in both colonic and cerebrospinal fluid, and selecting those exclusively changing in the colon of Tlr4fl/floffspring, hypoxanthine was identified as a metabolite that can cross the blood-brain barrier and mediate the effects of intestinal Tlr4 knockout on DRN 5-HT signaling. Remarkably, hypoxanthine and xanthine oxidase were increased in the serum of ASD children compared to typical development (TD) children. In vivo and in vitro experiments confirmed that hypoxanthine increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reduced 5-HT production, thereby promoting 5-HT neuron apoptosis. The inhibition of both the PI3K/AKT and 5-HT pathways in H2O2-treated PC12 cells was rescued by glutathione pretreatment in vitro. Meanwhile, the above LPS-induced DRN changes were significantly different in the Tlr4fl/fl offspring, and were reversed in the Tlr4△IEC mice after LPS exposure. Collectively, intestinal Tlr4 knockout reduces LPS-induced stereotyped behaviors, and the mechanism involves reduced hypoxanthine production and ROS-mediated inhibition of PI3K/AKT signaling, thereby decreasing 5-HT neuronal apoptosis by elevating the 5-HT level in DRN.

title: Microglial Cofilin-1 Regulates Neuroinflammatory Responses and Behavioral Outcomes Following Intracerebral Hemorrhage.
abstract: Cofilin-1, an actin-binding protein, modulates cytoskeletal dynamics and cellular motility. Although its role in conditional neuron knockout (KO) and neuronal injury has been well studied, the specific deletion of cofilin-1 in microglia and its role in neuroinflammation after intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) remains unknown. This study aimed to characterize the effects of microglia-specific cofilin-1 deficiency on microglial morphology, homeostasis, behavioral phenotypes, and neurobehavioral and neuroinflammatory outcomes following ICH in male and female mice. A conditional KO mouse model was generated by crossing cofilinfl/fl (Flx) mice with CX3CR1-Cre drivers to achieve microglia-specific deletion. Baseline behavioral performance, microglial morphology, and homeostatic markers were evaluated in both sexes. ICH was then induced by intra-striatal collagenase injection, and neurobehavioral function, brain edema, hematoma volume, microglial activation, and peripheral immune responses were evaluated three days post-injury. Microglial deletion of cofilin-1 was associated with reduced TMEM119 expression, increased IBA1 immunoreactivity, and morphological transformation toward an activated phenotype. Female KO mice showed pronounced hyperlocomotion and decreased anxiety-like behavior, whereas both sexes exhibited impaired neuromuscular performance in the wire hang test. After ICH, KO mice had significantly larger hematoma volumes, enhanced microglial activation, and increased peripheral leukocyte counts compared with Flx controls. Notably, these changes were more severe in female KO mice, indicating a sex-dependent vulnerability. Our findings establish cofilin-1 as a key regulator of microglial homeostasis and immune balance within the brain. Deficiency of microglial cofilin-1 predisposes to worse secondary brain injury after ICH in a sex-dependent manner.

title: Caltubin regulates microtubule stability through tubulin interaction favouring neurite regrowth.
abstract: Microtubule regulation is highly controlled in nerve regeneration. Caltubin, a novel Lymnaea stagnalis protein, contains putative EF-hand calcium-binding motifs and promotes neuronal outgrowth in Lymnaea and mouse. Here, we generated cell-permeable caltubin proteins to investigate mechanisms underlying this effect. We observed increased neurite extension and regrowth following acute neurite injury in CaT-Tat-treated embryonic mouse cortical neurons compared to vehicle controls. Purified caltubin bound the L391-V405 region of α-tubulin, promoting microtubule assembly. Caltubin reduced the association of tubulin tyrosine ligase with tubulin, which catalyzes tubulin retyrosination, and increased the ratio of detyrosinated to tyrosinated tubulin. Crystal structure analysis confirmed that caltubin has a calmodulin-like fold with four EF-hand motifs which also coordinate Sr2+. These findings identify caltubin as a direct modulator of tubulin assembly and tubulin tyrosination state. While this may represent an essential mechanism of axonal regulation, the present functional assays were performed in embryonic neuronal cultures and do not directly test calcium dependence or in vivo regeneration, and future studies should evaluate CaT-Tat in mature neuronal and in vivo injury models.

title: Exosome-associated cargo is linked to familial Alzheimer's disease-associated phenotypes in vitro.
abstract: The propagation of pathological proteins such as tau and amyloid-beta (Aβ) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is poorly understood. Here, we developed a human-relevant in vitro conditioned medium (CM)-based model using human neural progenitor ReN cells carrying Familial AD (FAD) mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP Sw/Lo) and presenilin 1 (PSEN1ΔE9). Healthy ReN-derived neurons and astrocytes treated with FAD-CM for nine weeks exhibited AD features, including cellular toxicity, neuro-glial alterations, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Exogenous Aβ42 further induced neuroglial and mitochondrial damage. Exosomes released by FAD cells and -to a lesser extent- by CM-treated healthy cells showed elevated Aβ42/40 ratios. Proteomic analysis also revealed that exosomes from FAD-cells carried a distinct content, including overrepresentation of proteins linked to inflammation, extracellular matrix remodelling, synaptic dysfunction, and Aβ processing, as well as Calmodulin-like protein 3. Moreover, exosomes were actively internalized by healthy cells through an actin-dependent mechanism. In summary, these findings support a model based on FAD-associated APP/PSEN1 mutations in which exosome-associated cargo alongside soluble and non-vesicular factors contribute to the transfer of AD-associated cellular phenotypes.

title: CellScore: an open-source image-based pipeline for automated cell quantification in microalgae.
abstract: Accurate quantification of microalgal cell density is essential for both basic research and industrial applications, as it directly reflects culture growth, productivity, and physiological status. There are existing methods routinely used to measure cell counts, although many are limited by high cost, labor-intensive workflows, or steep technical barriers. To address these limitations, we developed CellScore, a rapid and accessible image-based pipeline for microalgal cell counting implemented in ImageJ, a widely adopted open-source platform in the biological sciences ( https://github.com/shijieh/imageJ-annotate ). By leveraging the broad user base and ease of installation of the software, CellScore enables researchers to obtain reliable cell counts from standard microscopy images with minimal specialized equipment. Although the workflow has only been tested with three microalgae species of similar morphologies, the pipeline balances automation with user control and includes practical troubleshooting strategies to facilitate adoption by new users. Thus, CellScore has the potential to be used broadly across other species, however, broader validation across diverse morphologies is required. Overall, CellScore provides a cost-effective, user-friendly, and reproducible solution for routine microalgal cell quantification in both laboratory and applied settings.

title: Rab GTPases and the Rabopathy framework: from synaptic trafficking to neurodegeneration via LRRK2-driven pathology.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and Huntington's disease (HD) show significant differences in their clinical manifestations, but they all seem to share a common upstream problem: malfunction in the membrane transport controlled by Rab GTPases. This review introduces the concept of Rabopathy, a framework that connects developmental synaptic maturation defects with late-onset protein aggregation. The LRRK2-Rab phosphorylation axis is emerging as a potential common amplifying mechanism across these disorders, with the strongest mechanistic support in PD and growing implications in AD and HD. When Rab substrates are excessively phosphorylated at specific sites, vesicular transport is impaired or arrested, leading to progressive depletion of the reserve pool of synaptic vesicles and the surface pool of receptors, and severe compromise of the autophagy-lysosome flux. The failure of distinct Rab sub-networks also produces disease-specific signatures, including Rab5-driven endosomal congestion in AD, Rab35-mediated α-synuclein secretion in PD, and Rab11/Rab7 trafficking collapse in HD. Restoration of Rab flux may be a therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative diseases, which can be achieved through calibration of LRRK2 activity, modulation of selective Rab subtypes, and rescue of the trafficking network at the systems level.

title: SHANK3 drives abnormal neurodevelopment in iPSC-derived 2D and 3D brain models of Phelan-McDermid Syndrome.
abstract: Phelan-McDermid Syndrome (PMDS) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by 22q13.3 deletion involving SHANK3. While SHANK3 is critical for synapses, its role in early human neurodevelopment remains elusive. Here, we generated induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived 2D neuronal cultures and 3D cerebral organoids from two twin Phelan-McDermid syndrome patients with a 1.7 Mb 22q13 deletion encompassing SHANK3 gene. PMDS organoids showed reduced volume due to impaired neural progenitor cells (NPCs) proliferation. PMDS NPCs exhibited biased differentiation with decreased excitatory neurons but increased GFAP+ astroglia and GABAergic neurons. PMDS neurons displayed simplified morphology, reduced synapse density and diminished excitability. Importantly, lentiviral-mediated SHANK3 overexpression largely rescued these defects. Our findings identify SHANK3 as a key regulator of early neurodevelopment and provide mechanistic insights into PMDS pathogenesis.

title: An Optimized Stem Cell Secretome Proteomics Platform: Application to Progranulin-Deficient iPSCs.
abstract: Stem cells secrete diverse extracellular proteins that regulate pluripotency, differentiation, and cell-cell communication, making them powerful model systems for studying development, disease mechanisms, and regenerative medicine. However, robust stem cell secretome analysis remains technically challenging. Unlike many other cell types, pluripotent stem cells cannot tolerate serum starvation or growth factor deprivation, while low-abundance secreted proteins are often masked by media-derived proteins and intracellular contamination. Here, we systematically optimized the secretome proteomics workflow in induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) by evaluating culture medium composition, conditioned-media collection time, cell plating density, media harvest and preparation methods, LC-MS acquisition methods, and data analysis strategies. Full-strength Essential 8 medium, 48 h media collection, 80% cell confluency, two-step centrifugation, and data-independent acquisition (DIA)LC-MS/MS provided the optimal secretome proteomics data quality. We then applied the optimized platform to an isogenic iPSC disease model to investigate how progranulin deficiency reshapes the extracellular and intracellular proteomes. Progranulin-deficient iPSCs showed a coordinated reduction of extracellular lysosomal hydrolases despite relatively modest intracellular proteome changes, suggesting altered lysosome trafficking and possible impairment of lysosomal exocytosis. Together, this work establishes a robust and standardized workflow for stem cell secretome proteomics and demonstrates its utility for investigating extracellular proteome remodeling in human disease models.

title: PRKN-independent mitophagy regulators in dopaminergic neurons identified by genome-wide CRISPR screening.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Genetic and epidemiological studies have suggested that mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in the development of PD. PRKN/Parkin is known to play an essential role in mitochondrial quality control and mitophagy. Indeed, mutations and inactivation of this gene are associated with hereditary and idiopathic forms of PD. Despite extensive studies on PRKN-dependent mitophagy, the molecular regulators of PRKN-independent mitophagy in dopaminergic neurons remain incompletely understood. We generated a PRKN knockout iPSC-derived dopaminergic neuronal line expressing the fluorescent mitophagy biosensor mito-SRAI, which reports the delivery of mitochondria to lysosomes as an increase in the TOLLES/YPet fluorescence ratio. We used this cell line to conduct a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen to reveal genetic regulators involved in PRKN-independent mitophagy. Dozens of genes were identified whose knockout increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in an uncoupler-dependent manner. Of these, several genes emerged as candidates with potential therapeutic implications, one of which was Cathepsin F (CTSF). CCCP treatment increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in neurons with siRNA-mediated CTSF knockdown, and CTSF knockdown partially preserved the proportion of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons after paraquat exposure. These results suggest that CTSF is a candidate regulator of PRKN-independent mitophagy and that this lysosomal enzyme may represent a potentially druggable candidate target for PD.

overview: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta.
