title: Epitope-dependent acute inhibition and potentiation of N-methyl-d-aspartate receptors by GluN1 autoantibodies.
abstract: Transfer of autoantibodies targeting ionotropic N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptors from patients with autoimmune encephalitis to mice induces characteristic disease signs. The long-term effects of pathogenic antibodies include immunoglobulin G (IgG)-induced cross-linking and receptor internalization. We investigated the direct and immediate impact of two specific pathogenic patient-derived monoclonal autoantibodies (IgG #003-102 and #007-168) on NMDA receptor (NMDAR) function. We performed cell-attached recordings from cells transfected with the GluN1-3a and GluN2A subunits of NMDARs. IgG #003-102 binds to the R2 lobe of the amino-terminal domain (ATD) of the glycine-binding GluN1 subunit. It significantly reduced the number of simultaneous NMDAR openings compared to controls at both low and high concentrations of glutamate and glycine. Closer examination revealed that IgG #003-102 rapidly reduced the number of open receptors and shortened receptor-opening bursts. However, antigen-binding fragments of IgG #003-102 did not reduce receptor openings. By contrast, IgG #007-168, which binds to the top of the R1 lobe of the GluN1-ATD, potentiated the NMDAR response. In conclusion, patient-derived IgG #003-102 inhibits NMDARs within seconds, before receptor internalization, and the full IgG is required for this acute inhibitory effect. This suggests that monovalent IgG #003-102 constructs could be a new treatment strategy to shield a pathogenic epitope on NMDARs. KEY POINTS: N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptors (NMDARs) are ionotropic glutamate receptors central to brain development and function. Anti-NMDAR encephalitis is the most common cause of non-viral autoimmune brain inflammation and is characterized by psychosis, dyskinesias, autonomic dysfunction and seizures. Symptoms are considered to result from autoantibodies that internalize surface NMDARs on neurons. Using patch clamp recordings, we tested the acute effects of two monoclonal anti-GluN1 autoantibodies and the Fab fragment of one of them on NMDARs. The autoantibody (IgG #003-102), which binds to the R2 lobe of the GluN1-amino-terminal domain (ATD), inhibits receptors within seconds. The entire IgG is required for this inhibition. By contrast, IgG #007-168, which binds to the top of the R1 lobe of the GluN1-ATD, potentiates receptor responses. By capitalizing on the null phenotype of a Fab from IgG #003-102, we propose monovalent constructs as a potential new treatment strategy to prevent pathogenic antibodies from causing receptor dysfunction.

overview: Transfer of autoantibodies targeting ionotropic N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptors from patients with autoimmune encephalitis to mice induces characteristic disease signs.

title: Evaluation of the effect of p38γ gene delivery using exosomes derived from mesenchymal stem cells on Alzheimer's rat model.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dementia, memory loss, and cognitive decline. This study investigated the therapeutic potential of delivering the p38γ gene via exosomes derived from adipose-derived stem cells (ADSC-Exos) in a rat model of streptozotocin (STZ)-induced AD. METHODS AND RESULTS: After the AD model was established, the rats were administered via intraperitoneal injections of p38γ, Exo, or p38γ-loaded ADSC-Exo (Exo+p38γ). Cognitive and memory assessments were performed via novel object recognition (NOR), passive avoidance, elevated plus-maze (EPM), and the Barnes maze (BM). Histological techniques were used to evaluate cell density and beta-amyloid (Aβ) plaque accumulation, while quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT‒PCR) was used to measure the transcription levels of neuronal nuclei (NeuN), glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), nerve growth factor (NGF), and sex-determining region Y-box 2 (SOX2). Additionally, the expression of GDNF, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), SOX2, and malondialdehyde (MDA) was analyzed via an ELISA kit. The Exo and Exo+p38γ groups demonstrated significant improvements in STZ-induced memory deficits across various assessments. However, no significant differences in the protein expression levels of GDNF, BDNF, SOX2, and MDA or the gene expression levels of SOX2, NeuN, GDNF, and NGF were detected between STZ-treated rats that received Exos+p38γ and those that received Exos alone. CONCLUSIONS: Taken together, this study demonstrates that ADSC-derived exosomes effectively improve cognitive deficits in an AD rat model; Although Exo+p38γ was associated with a significant increase in SOX2 gene expression compared with the AD group, the direct comparison between Exo+p38γ and ADSC-Exos did not demonstrate a statistically significant additional effect.

title: Live-cell imaging of inter-organelle contacts using an integrated dimerization-dependent fluorescent protein reporter.
abstract: Organelles communicate with each other by building membrane contact sites (MCSs) via specialized protein-protein and/or protein-membrane interactions. Conventional light microscopy cannot distinguish organelles connected by MCSs from those merely juxtaposed. In addition, organelle contacts are dynamic, yet only a limited number of tools are available to monitor MCSs in living cells. In this study, we developed a series of reporters based on dimerization-dependent fluorescent proteins (ddFP) to visualize, quantify and follow inter-organelle contacts. We first generated an integrated system specifically designed to study contacts between late endocytic compartments (late endosomes and lysosomes) and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). This system utilizes a single plasmid coding for the two complementary ddFP components: green A (GA) and green B (GB) targeted to the ER and late endosomes and lysosomes (LE/Lys), respectively. This construct enabled the generation of a stable reporter cell line suitable for semi-quantitative imaging. The ddFP reporter, which we called ddFP LELYS-ER, did not perturb endogenous LE/Lys-ER contacts in stable cells, and detected changes in the number of LE/Lys-ER contacts, for example, upon downregulation of the ER-resident VAP tether protein family, or under conditions of lysosomal damage. Moreover, live-cell imaging revealed that LE/Lys-ER contacts have distinct shapes, mobilities and lifetimes. Finally, using the same vector design, we generated two additional integrated reporter systems adapted to the study of contacts between the ER and the plasma membrane, and between the ER and mitochondria.

title: CelFDrive - multimodal deep learning-assisted microscopy for automated detection of rare events.
abstract: The emergence of automated microscopy has enabled the collection of large datasets of rare biological events, accelerating discovery in biology. However, most existing methods cannot be readily integrated into microscopy setups or are limited to a single microscope type. We present CelFDrive, a software package that automatically detects rare events of interest and automates high-resolution three-dimensional imaging of target cells by integrating deep learning-assisted cell classification of auxiliary low-magnification fluorescence images. We show that CelFDrive reduced the mean time required to nominate a mitotic prophase candidate for high-resolution light-sheet imaging by over 30-fold relative to manual expert selection. This approach can be used to define the order of kinetochore assembly upon nuclear envelope breakdown. The trained CelFDrive detector demonstrated transferability by retaining mitotic cell detection capability in an independently generated dataset using a different cell line, DNA marker and imaging setup. As datasets grow and models improve, CelFDrive offers a clear path toward intelligent imaging systems that not only accelerate data collection, but also fundamentally enhance how biological questions are explored.

title: Tubulin polyglutamylation modulates Golgi morphodynamics and neurite branching during neuronal morphogenesis.
abstract: Neurons establish functional networks through morphological remodeling during neuronal differentiation. Microtubule polyglutamylation is a key microtubule post-translational modification that is highly enriched during this process and plays an important role in differentiation. However, how remodeling of organelle features such as morphology, distribution and interactions depends on tubulin polyglutamylation during neuronal differentiation remains unclear. Here, we employed multispectral imaging combined with quantitative three-dimensional organelle analysis to comprehensively profile eight organelles simultaneously in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons. We discovered that depletion of tubulin polyglutamylation induces pronounced alterations in somatic Golgi morphology and associated organelle interactions. In addition, Golgi-derived compartments in proximal neurites exhibited altered morphology and dynamics, namely, decreased anterograde transport together with less efficient movement. These changes were accompanied by increased neurite branching and tortuosity. Together, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for tubulin polyglutamylation in coordinating organelle organization with neurite architecture, providing a mechanistic link between tubulin post-translational modifications, Golgi morphology, dynamics and neuronal morphogenesis.

title: Analysis of motor-based transport in primary cilia by dynamic mode decomposition of live-cell imaging data.
abstract: Kinesin-3 motor proteins are increasingly recognized for their important roles in cilia. The mammalian kinesin-3 motor KIF13B moves bidirectionally in primary cilia and regulates ciliary content, but its relationship to the intraflagellar transport (IFT) machinery is unclear. Here, we combine quantitative live-cell imaging with a new kymograph analysis based on dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) to separate mobile from immobile protein populations in primary cilia. This approach simplifies extraction of molecular velocities from kymographs and improves directional analysis of molecular tracks using the Fourier and Radon transforms. Our novel analysis reveals that a KIF13B deletion mutant only retaining the motor domain and part of the forkhead-associated domain does not alter steady-state IFT velocity or frequency. However, when retrograde dynein-2 function is inhibited by ciliobrevin D or tanespimycin, both anterograde and retrograde IFT velocities decrease in parental cells, as expected, but remain unchanged in KIF13B mutant cells. Structured illumination, confocal and stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy further show that KIF13B localizes to the ciliary membrane and concentrates at the periciliary membrane region and the centriolar subdistal appendages, below the distal appendage marker FBF1. Our improved kymograph approach provides new insight into KIF13B ciliary function and simplifies the quantitative analysis of ciliary protein transport.

title: Making smart microscopy deployable in imaging core facilities.
abstract: Smart microscopy, in which real-time image analysis enables microscopes to adapt their acquisition dynamically, is becoming central to biological imaging. However, deploying such workflows in imaging facilities remains challenging. The computers that control microscopes in a facility are shared, governed by institutional policies, often offline and run vendor-specific software. As a result, installing custom software environments for the workflow of each user is both unsafe and unsustainable. We argue that smart microscopy requires a practical deployment strategy that links open-source bioimage analysis with commercial acquisition software without turning acquisition computers into development platforms. Using our recently developed tools, NucleiSky and LabConstrictor, as examples, we demonstrate how microscope control and external image analysis can be integrated while keeping the custom Python environment separate from the vendor-managed environment. The deployment strategy might vary - for instance, a USB drive, a facility workstation, a server or a network share - but the underlying principle remains the same: smart-microscopy workflows must be straightforward to approve, launch, reuse, audit and remove. Smart microscopy will become routine only when it is both powerful and deployable.

title: Lipid homeostasis and cellular metabolism in neurodegenerative diseases: A maturing framework to guide therapeutic development.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and dementia with Lewy bodies have long been viewed through the lens of protein aggregation. Emerging evidence, however, highlights lipid transfer, load, metabolism, and cellular homeostasis as upstream drivers of pathology. This perspective integrates established neurobiological, genetic, and mechanistic evidence of lipid dysfunction and outlines how these pathways can guide patient stratification, biomarker discovery, and therapeutic development. Of critical importance, lipid transport and lysosomal and trafficking networks are at the center of cholesterol regulation, glycosphingolipid clearance, endolysosomal function, and neuron-glia lipid exchange across genetic and sporadic neurodegenerative diseases. We present an integrated framework where correcting lipid imbalances and metabolic dysregulation may complement or obviate protein-targeted approaches, creating more precise clinical trials and combination strategies. By re-centering the therapeutic focus on lipid and cellular metabolism, we aim to catalyze translational advances in neurodegenerative disease treatment.

title: Alcohol use disorder - progress in mechanism discovery and new pharmacotherapy design.
abstract: The systematic use of alcohol is a frequent behaviour on a world-wide scale. Some of the users develop an abuse pattern of consumption and an alcohol use disorder (AUD). This is considered as a major psychiatric disorder causing significant suffering for the individual and society. As yet, there are no satisfactory and broadly working treatment options for AUD available, which has sparked research in a better understanding of neurobiological mechanism of alcohol and AUD and the search for an evidence-based treatment rational. Here we review the development of neuropharmacological insights focusing on selected brain mechanisms that have recently experienced significant progress and which give rise to new pharmaco-development ideas for AUD. Those include alcohol action and AUD mechanisms in the actin cytoskeleton system, in the nociceptin/orphanin system, and in the endocannabinoid system. Besides progress in pharmacotherapeutic targets, there are developments in how this therapy may be better applied in a personalized and addiction phase-sensitive way. This embraces new technologies like Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) for near real-time AUD symptom diagnosis, treatment allocation, and success monitoring. Emergence and future potential of this combination are discussed here. Altogether, current research in alcohol and AUD shows significant progress in our understanding of disease mechanisms and may spark the implementation of a new generation of technology supplemented pharmacotherapies of AUD.

title: αvβ3 integrin recycling is associated with the intracellular trafficking and efflux of cRGDfK-modified PLGA nanoparticles.
abstract: Understanding the cellular transport mechanisms of active-targeting nanocarriers is essential for improving their therapeutic performance. In this study, cRGDfK-modified poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) nanoparticles (cRGDfK-PLGA-NPs) were developed as an αvβ3 integrin-targeted delivery system, and their cellular uptake, intracellular trafficking, and efflux behaviors were systematically investigated in HeLa cells. Confocal laser scanning microscopy and HPLC analyses demonstrated enhanced cellular uptake of cRGDfK-PLGA-NPs compared with non-modified nanoparticles in HeLa cells. The uptake advantage was associated with αvβ3 integrin targeting, while pathway-inhibition studies suggested contributions from clathrin-mediated endocytosis and macropinocytosis. Following internalization, cRGDfK-PLGA-NPs were rapidly transported to early endosomes (EE), followed by redistribution to the endocytic recycling compartment (ERC) and gradual accumulation in late endosomes (LE). Real-time and fixed-cell colocalization analyses suggested three intracellular trafficking routes: the EE-LE pathway, a proposed EE-ERC-slow efflux pathway, and an EE-fast efflux pathway. Efflux studies indicated a two-stage kinetic process, with an initial rapid efflux phase (∼5 min) and a subsequent slower phase (∼10 min). To further elucidate the underlying mechanism, the intracellular trafficking behavior of the αvβ3 integrin receptor was investigated using an ELISA-based method, revealing a cyclical pattern of endocytosis and recycling with a periodicity of approximately 5 min. Comparative analysis using a cRGDfK fluorescent probe demonstrated that its rapid efflux behavior closely paralleled receptor recycling dynamics, suggesting that the fast efflux pathway of cRGDfK-PLGA-NPs is associated with αvβ3 integrin-mediated recycling, whereas the slower efflux pathway may involve ERC-mediated transport. Overall, this study provides insights into the potential relationship between target-receptor trafficking dynamics and the intracellular fate of active-targeting nanoparticles. These findings offer a theoretical basis for the rational design and optimization of active-targeting nanocarriers and contribute to improving their therapeutic efficacy.

title: Lysosome-targeted near-infrared fluorescent probe ROCL enables dynamic hypochlorous acid imaging in living cells and a mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Hypochlorous acid (HClO) plays critical roles in oxidative stress and is strongly implicated in the progression of Parkinson's disease (PD). Here, we report ROCL, a new lysosome-targeted near-infrared fluorescent probe for sensitive and selective detection of HClO in living systems. ROCL displays rapid response, excellent selectivity, and a low detection limit of 49 nM, based on an HClO-induced spirolactam ring-opening mechanism. The probe enables real-time imaging of exogenous and endogenous HClO in SH-SY5Y and PC12 cells, exhibits low cytotoxicity, and effectively visualizes elevated HClO levels in MPTP- and rotenone-induced PD models. ROCL also shows favorable blood-brain barrier permeability and allows noninvasive in vivo HClO imaging in PD model mice. These results establish ROCL as a valuable tool for probing HClO-associated oxidative stress in neurodegenerative diseases.
journal: Spectrochimica acta. Part A, Molecular and biomolecular spectroscopy

main: These results establish ROCL as a valuable tool for probing HClO-associated oxidative stress in neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Cofilin hyperphosphorylation triggers TDP-43 pathology in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
abstract: Pathological forms of TAR-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), involving its aberrant mislocalization to the cytoplasm, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, are present in ∼45%-50% frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease individuals and most (97%) amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases. Hence, identifying mechanisms that induce TDP-43 pathology are central to neurodegeneration and developing new therapeutic targets in these conditions. Cofilin is a multifunctional protein with a crucial role in regulating the actin cytoskeleton. Actin has important neuronal-specific activities in dendritic spines, axonal growth cones and synapses and it is in constant equilibrium between two forms: monomeric globular actin (G-actin) and polymeric filamentous actin (F-actin). Cofilin controls actin dynamics by depolymerizing and severing actin filaments. When cofilin is phosphorylated (at serine-3, Ser3) by LIM kinase1 (LIMK1), it becomes inactive, leading to production of more F-actin. Defects in cofilin are well described in other neurodegenerative disorders, unlike in ALS. We examined phosphorylation of cofilin and actin dynamics in post-mortem spinal cord tissue from sporadic ALS (SALS) patients, the TDP-43 rNLS8 transgenic mouse model and NSC-34 motor neuronal cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. F-actin was pharmacologically stabilized to mimic cofilin hyperphosphorylation and TDP-43 pathology was assessed. Neuronal cells were treated with a non-phosphorylatable cofilin S3A peptide (MAAGVAVSDGVIKVFN) and TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis were evaluated. Here, we show that cofilin is hyperphosphorylated in human ALS and disease models compared to controls. This was detected in spinal motor neurons from SALS patients and a TDP-43 mouse model (rNLS8) displaying key ALS phenotypes, and in motor neuronal NSC-34 cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. Supporting this observation, more F-actin relative to G-actin was present in cortical/spinal cord lysates from SALS patients and TDP-43 rNLS8 mice, and NSC-34 cells expressing TDP-43. We also show that mimicking cofilin hyperphosphorylation by pharmacological stabilization of F-actin induced TDP-43 pathology: cytoplasmic mislocalization, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, and promoted its recruitment into stress granules (SGs). Furthermore, we detected increased levels of LIMK1 phosphorylation and tropomyosin isoforms 4.1 and 4.2 in SALS patients. These findings reveal aberrant cofilin hyperphosphorylation disrupts actin dynamics, triggering TDP-43 pathology and SG recruitment in SALS. They imply that preventing cofilin phosphorylation is a novel therapeutic strategy applicable to most ALS cases. Treatment of neuronal cells with the S3A peptide prevented features of TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis compared to control peptides. These findings thus describe a novel pathogenic mechanism producing TDP-43 pathology, applicable to most ALS cases and other neurodegenerative diseases.

title: P2RX7 drives inflammatory microglia and pathogenic extracellular vesicle secretion in tauopathy.
abstract: P2X purinoreceptor 7 (P2RX7), an ATP-gated ion channel, contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that genetic disruption of P2rx7 mitigates brain atrophy, tau accumulation, and cognitive impairment in PS19 mice. Microglia-specific, but not astrocyte-specific, deletion of P2rx7 suppresses tau propagation. Single-cell RNA sequencing identifies a previously unrecognized first-responding microglial state (FRM) with prominent P2rx7 expression. P2RX7 promotes the transition from FRM to an inflammatory microglial state enriched in extracellular vesicle (EV) biogenesis. P2RX7 increases EV loading of tau and of mitochondrial proteins and DNA, which activate cytosolic DNA sensing and interferon signaling in recipient microglia. Tau-containing microglial EVs disrupt neuronal endolysosomal integrity and facilitate endosomal tau escape and phosphorylation. Thus, P2RX7 regulates the FRM branch point, driving inflammatory microglial transition and EV-mediated spread of tau and toxic mitochondrial molecules and highlighting the P2RX7-EV axis as a therapeutic target in AD.

title: The role of ZC3H14 (MSUT2) in neurodevelopment and tauopathies.
abstract: The processes of neurodevelopment and neuropathology can be influenced by RNA binding proteins. The RNA binding protein ZC3H14 (also referred to as MSUT2) is of particular interest for two reasons. First, homozygous loss-of-function alleles in ZC3H14 are associated with an inherited form of intellectual disability. Second, in model systems, loss of ZC3H14 can suppress the toxicity of tau aggregates, which are hallmark diagnostic features of Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative diseases referred to as 'tauopathies'. In this review, we discuss both the normal functions of ZC3H14 and how alterations in these functions may affect cognitive function or tau pathology. Although not fully understood, an emerging theme is that alterations in RNA regulation attributable to ZC3H14 loss can affect neuronal function.
authors: Shelby G, Corbett AH, Parker RR
overview: The processes of neurodevelopment and neuropathology can be influenced by RNA binding proteins.
main: Although not fully understood, an emerging theme is that alterations in RNA regulation attributable to ZC3H14 loss can affect neuronal function.

title: Hagen-Poiseuille distributed-pressure model of osmotically-driven cytoplasmic flow in severed axons.
abstract: Repair (sealing) of traumatic plasmalemmal lesions involves the formation, movement, and accumulation of vesicles at the injury site by active transport and by passive bulk flow of cytoplasm. We show that hypotonic and hypertonic salines affect the direction and rate of vesicle movement in severed crayfish medial giant axons (CMGAs), presumably because osmotically-driven changes in intracellular pressure alter bulk cytoplasmic flow along the axon and at the lesion site. We develop a general Hagen-Poiseuille pressure-cable biophysical model of bulk cytoplasmic flow to predict direction and relative rate of cytoplasmic influx and efflux for CMGAs and other axons modeled as fluid-filled cylinders with distributed osmotic water permeability. Although our general-model applies to axons of any length, this model simplifies for a short-cable model in which the axonal length is much shorter than the hydraulic length constant, i.e., axons like CMGAs. Both General- and Shortcable-Models predict that hypotonic extracellular conditions drive transmembrane water flux into an axon, elevating intracellular pressure that is relieved by cytoplasmic efflux at the injury site. Conversely, hypertonic conditions drive transmembrane water flux out of the axon that is relieved by extracellular fluid influx at the severed end. Our data from CMGAs show that active transport involving molecular motors associated with microtubules and actin in CMGAs is the predominant contributor to vesicle movement towards severed end. Bulk cytoplasmic flow - as assessed by the movement of vesicles and cellular debris that persist when active transport is inhibited - is a lesser contribution to vesicle movement whose extent depends on the difference between extracellular and intracellular osmolarity. Our Hagen-Poiseuille distributed-pressure Model accurately predicts the direction and approximate rate of movement of vesicles and cellular debris under all osmotic conditions tested. Our Model should also account for vesicle behavior in other axons and cylindrical cytoplasmic processes of various diameters and lengths.

title: Mechanistic study on neurotoxicity induced by neodymium oxide exposure via TNT-mediated transfer of damaged mitochondria.
abstract: The health issues caused by the global mining, processing, and utilization of rare earth elements are receiving increasing attention. This study examined the molecular mechanisms mediating damaged mitochondria transfer via TNTs during neodymium oxide (Nd2O3)-induced neurotoxicity. Adult Sprague-Dawley rats were administered Nd2O3 by gavage, and effects on spatial learning and memory were assessed in the Morris water maze. Primary astrocytes and whole brain tissues from SD rats were extracted to identify differentially expressed genes via RNA-seq, and qRT-PCR and Western blotting were employed to perform targeted analyses of genes and proteins involved in blood-brain barrier (BBB) maintenance, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and mitochondrial dynamics. Alterations in calcium homeostasis, oxidative stress markers, and mitochondrial metabolism were measured using dedicated assay kits. TNT formation and mitochondrial migration were examined in co-cultures of primary astrocytes with HT22 neuronal cells by fluorescence staining under laser confocal microscopy. The stability of the F-actin-Myo19-Miro1 complex was evaluated using Co-IP and molecular docking, and the effects of Nd2O3 exposure on mitochondrial transport carriers and the number of TNTs were assessed. Finally, the role of TNTs in damaged mitochondria transfer was demonstrated by co-culturing astrocytes and neurons in a Transwell system and performing mitochondrial membrane potential detection. Neuronal damage was verified using TUNEL staining. Exposure to Nd2O3 caused dose-dependent spatial learning and memory impairment, reduced neural expression of core BBB genes, disrupted intracellular calcium homeostasis, induced oxidative stress, reduced OXPHOS, and promoted mitochondrial fragmentation. Astrocytes exposed to Nd2O3 formed TNTs with neurons, and damaged mitochondria were transported through TNTs containing the F-actin-Myo19-Miro1 complex, ultimately aggravating the degree of neuronal damage. We conclude that neodymium neurotoxicity involves mitochondrial oxidative stress and kinetic damage. Neodymium acts as a promoting factor through the F-actin-Myo19-Miro1 complex, transferring damaged mitochondria from astrocytes to neurons via TNTs and ultimately causing nerve damage.

overview: The health issues caused by the global mining, processing, and utilization of rare earth elements are receiving increasing attention.
main: Finally, the role of TNTs in damaged mitochondria transfer was demonstrated by co-culturing astrocytes and neurons in a Transwell system and performing mitochondrial membrane potential detection.

title: Tubulin autoregulation mediator TTC5 regulates neuronal morphology and migration.
abstract: Microtubule dynamics are essential for neuronal development, yet how neurons regulate tubulin levels remains poorly understood. Tetratricopeptide repeat domain 5 (TTC5) mediates tubulin autoregulation, the co-translational degradation of tubulin transcripts in response to excess soluble tubulin, and TTC5 mutations cause cerebral atrophy with speech and motor impairment. Here, we show that tubulin autoregulation is active in induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cortical neurons and depends on TTC5. TTC5 loss, or structure-guided mutations that disable autoregulation suppress microtubule polymerization, axonal outgrowth, and arborization, while enhancing cellular motility. Motility changes extend to non-neuronal cells, where they alter focal adhesion dynamics and can be rescued by manipulating soluble tubulin levels. Furthermore, downregulation of TTC5 interactor and autoregulation mediator S-phase cyclin A-associated protein in the endoplasmic reticulum (SCAPER) also suppresses neurite outgrowth and enhances motility. In vivo, TTC5 loss in mouse cortical projection neurons disrupts axon and dendrite arborization and causes hypermigration, recapitulating the cellular phenotypes observed in vitro. Patient-derived TTC5 disease mutants phenocopy this motility dysregulation, directly linking loss of TTC5 function to neurological deficits seen in patients. Together, these findings establish TTC5 as an essential regulator of neuronal morphogenesis and connectivity, with direct implications for TTC5-associated neurodevelopmental disease.
authors: Sarbanes SL, Ziak J, Sacks DC, Qi YA, Kolodkin AL, Roll-Mecak A
overview: Microtubule dynamics are essential for neuronal development, yet how neurons regulate tubulin levels remains poorly understood.
main: Here, we show that tubulin autoregulation is active in induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cortical neurons and depends on TTC5.

title: Tubulin autoregulation factors recruit γ-tubulin to non-centrosomal MTOCs for neuronal microtubule nucleation.
abstract: Neuronal function and survival depend on stereotyped non-centrosomal microtubule (MT) arrays. How these arrays form remains poorly understood. Here, we found that two factors previously implicated in tubulin mRNA turnover control neuronal MT content through γ-tubulin-dependent nucleation. In C. elegans neurons, loss of scaper, ttc5, or both reduced MT numbers to a similar degree as depletion of γ-tubulin, the main MT nucleator. Using conditional single-cell degradation alleles and endogenous tagging, we find that scaper and ttc5 are required to recruit γ-tubulin to non-centrosomal MT organizing centers (MTOCs). SCAPER is also instructive, as its overexpression raises γ-tubulin levels at nucleation sites and increases MT density. SCAPER, TTC5, and γ-tubulin are dispensable for developmental axon growth but play essential roles during regeneration, where SCAPER recruits γ-tubulin to a growth-cone-localized MTOC to orient MT nucleation. Last, SCAPER is required for activity-dependent MT nucleation in rat hippocampal neurons, suggesting a conserved role. These findings reveal mechanisms governing neuronal cytoskeleton assembly and function and suggest potential crosstalk between tubulin autoregulation and MT nucleation.

title: Restoration of BDNF/TrkB signaling rescues presynaptic dysfunction in GM1 gangliosidosis iPSC-derived neurons.
abstract: GM1 gangliosidosis is a lysosomal storage disease characterized by progressive neurodegeneration and severe central nervous system (CNS) dysfunction. Although the abnormal intracellular accumulation of GM1 ganglioside is recognized as a major pathological feature, the molecular mechanisms underlying neuronal dysfunction remain unclear. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) plays essential roles in CNS development and the maintenance of synaptic function and plasticity; however, its contribution to the pathology of lysosomal storage diseases remains unclear. We previously identified a marked impairment of neurotransmitter release in GM1 gangliosidosis neurons, accompanied by reduced expression of synapse-related molecules. In this study, we investigated the potential involvement of endogenous BDNF signaling in synaptic dysfunction using human iPSC-derived neurons. We found that endogenous BDNF expression was significantly reduced in GM1 gangliosidosis neurons, accompanied by a marked decrease in full-length tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), a key mediator of BDNF signaling. Further, the gene expression of synapse-related molecules involved in neurotransmitter release, including SNAP25 and VAMP2, was reduced. Importantly, exogenous BDNF supplementation ameliorated presynaptic dysfunction and substantially restored the expression of synapse-related molecules, which were reduced in disease neurons. Furthermore, 7,8-dihydroxyflavone (7,8-DHF), a selective TrkB agonist, markedly reversed presynaptic dysfunction. These findings suggest that impaired BDNF/TrkB signaling contributes to presynaptic dysfunction in GM1 gangliosidosis and identify the enhancement of this pathway as a potential therapeutic strategy.

title: Multi-omics profiling suggests deep brain stimulation-associated expansion of CLIC3+ NK cells attenuates neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) alleviates Parkinson's disease (PD) symptoms, but its immunomodulatory mechanisms remain elusive. Through integrating microarray (GSE23676), single cell/nucleus RNA-seq (GSE184950, GSE202210, GSE223138, GSE243639; after quality control (mitochondrial gene content <25%, gene number >200) 616,076 high-quality cells were included), and GWAS data, we identified CLIC3 as a DBS-associated, potential protective implications in PD. CLIC3 was selectively up-regulated in a distinct natural killer cell subset (NK_CLIC3), which secreted TGFB1 to restrain neuroinflammation. CellChat and immunohistochemistry revealed that NK_CLIC3 cells communicated with PD-relevant neuronal populations: excitatory (SLC18A2+), inhibitory (SLC18A2+), oligodendrocyte (SLC18A2+), and astrocytic (SLC18A2+) cells via THY1-ADGRE5 and GZMA-PARD3 axes. Immune infiltration analysis (GSE114517; n = 75) suggested NK infiltration and deficient M2 macrophage recruitment in PD brains, underscoring an inadequate anti-inflammatory response. We further isolated CLIC3-positive NK cells (from a healthy donor) by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) and confirmed their ability to degrade α-synuclein, the pathological protein in Parkinson's disease, supporting the potential NK(CLIC3+) cells' protective function in PD. Our findings suggest DBS may expand NK_CLIC3 cells to suppress neuroinflammation through TGFB1 mediated immune-neuronal crosstalk, positioning CLIC3 as a prospective therapeutic target for PD.

title: Subcellular compartment determines signal dominance: Endosomal cAMP overrides concurrent plasma membrane RhoA activation from a single receptor.
abstract: Cells convey information not only via the identity of activated signaling pathways but also through the subcellular location where those signals originate. Whether spatially distinct signals from a single activated receptor compete to determine net cellular output has remained unclear. Here, we demonstrate this principle for a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), showing that endosomal and plasma membrane signals from a single activated receptor are not merely distinct but functionally opposed, with endosomal signaling predominating to reverse the net cellular output. Using the adhesion GPCR GPR64/ADGRG2 as a model system, we show that ligand activation engages two spatially distinct G-protein pathways that are not just additive but functionally opposed: plasma membrane G13/RhoA activation and Gs/cAMP production that persists from endosomes following receptor internalization. The endosomal cAMP pool actively overrides concurrent plasma membrane RhoA activation, resulting in net RhoA inactivation, an outcome that is completely reversed by pharmacological blockade of endocytosis or endosomal Gs inactivation. In parathyroid cells, where GPR64 is highly expressed, this endosomal signal dominance suppresses parathyroid hormone secretion independently of extracellular Ca2+ levels. These findings support a model in which the subcellular compartment, rather than pathway identity, determines the dominant signal and the overall cellular response of a single activated receptor, with implications for understanding the complexity of GPCR signaling.

title: Redox-dependent remodeling of mitochondrial nucleoids contributes to bioenergetic decline during neuronal aging.
abstract: Why mitochondria progressively fail in aging neurons remains a fundamental question in neurobiology. Although bioenergetic decline and oxidative stress are hallmarks of aging, whether redox signaling remodels mitochondrial nucleoids (mt-nucleoids) to impair neuronal bioenergetics remains unclear. Using aged mouse neurons and human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons, we demonstrate that redox-driven mt-nucleoid remodeling underlies reduced mtDNA transcript abundance and bioenergetic decline. Combining minimal photon fluxes (MINFLUX) nanoscopy with single-molecule transcription mapping, we identify distinct mt-nucleoid architectures governed by mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM)-mediated mtDNA compaction. Aging-associated oxidative stress drives mt-nucleoid remodeling from compact, transcriptionally active structures toward decompacted forms with reduced mtDNA transcript abundance and impaired mitochondrial ATP production. This remodeling involves species-specific TFAM redox mechanisms: cysteine oxidation promotes human TFAM polymerization, whereas methionine oxidation weakens mouse TFAM-mtDNA interactions. Notably, expressing an oxidation-resistant TFAM variant restores mt-nucleoid organization, mtDNA transcript abundance, and ATP production in aged neurons, identifying mt-nucleoid architecture as a potential target for preserving neuronal bioenergetics during aging.

title: A rare TMEM175 mutation drives Parkinson's disease pathology by disrupting proton gating and lysosomal acidification.
abstract: Transmembrane protein 175 (TMEM175), implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD) risk, has been variably proposed to function as a background K+ "leak" channel or a proton-activated proton channel in lysosomes. Here, we identified the rare TMEM175 variant p.L275R in a patient with early onset PD. Electrophysiological analyses revealed that TMEM175-L275R mutant proteins retain normal lysosomal expression and K+ "leak" activity, but specifically lose proton- and agonist-dependent activation gating. In skin fibroblasts isolated from the patient with PD harboring the monoallelic p.L275R mutation (TMEM175+/L275R), and in derived induced pluripotent stem cells and induced dopaminergic neurons, lysosomal H+ flux, acidification, and degradation were impaired. These lysosomal defects were corrected upon genome editing to produce the isogenic WT allele (+/+Cor), but appeared when the mutant allele was introduced onto a WT background (+/L275RMut). Pathological α-synuclein aggregation was facilitated in patient-derived (+/L275R) and mutation-introduced (+/L275RMut) neurons. Consistent with these genetic findings, pharmacological activation of TMEM175 with small-molecule agonists restored lysosomal functions and reduced α-synuclein aggregation in TMEM175+/L275R neurons. In in-vivo studies, equivalent-site-mutation knock-in mice demonstrated synucleinopathy and PD-like motor phenotypes. Collectively, our work provides genetic and pharmacological evidence that severe loss-of-function mutations may contribute causally to the onset age and pathogenesis of PD and identifies lysosomal proton channels and transporters as potential therapeutic targets for PD intervention.

title: SSH1 knockdown increases autophagosome formation through ATG9A recruitment and promotes MAPT/tau protein degradation.
abstract: Pathological accumulation of MAPT/tau protein is a defining feature of Alzheimer disease (AD) and related tauopathies, highlighting the need to identify druggable regulators of MAPT/tau clearance. Using Drosophila behavioral assays focused on cytoskeletal remodeling pathways dysregulated in AD, we identified genes whose genetic modulation mitigates MAPT/tau-induced behavioral deficits. These modifiers were validated by histopathology and mechanistically examined in human tauopathy cell models to determine their impact on autophagy-dependent MAPT/tau degradation. Autophagic flux, ATG9A trafficking, and autophagosome biogenesis were further analyzed. Across models, reduction of the phosphatase SSH1 consistently lowered steady-state MAPT/tau levels by enhancing autophagic flux through a mechanism distinct from its canonical regulation of CFL1. Mechanistically, SSH1 functions as a negative regulator of early autophagosome formation: SSH1 depletion promotes ATG9A mobilization to the endoplasmic reticulum-phagophore assembly site (ER-PAS), thereby accelerating autophagic vesicle biogenesis. Importantly, the MAPT/tau-lowering effect of Dmssh attenuation was abolished in flies haploinsufficient for DmAtg9, demonstrating that SSH1-mediated MAPT/tau clearance requires ATG9 function. Consistent with a direct regulatory interaction, in vitro phosphatase assays revealed that recombinant SSH1 decreases ATG9A phosphorylation in the presence of actin, identifying an SSH1-ATG9A regulatory axis controlling autophagosome initiation. These findings position SSH1 as a nodal inhibitor of autophagy initiation whose inhibition enhances MAPT/tau proteolysis. Notably, SSH1 haploinsufficiency also reduces SNCA/α-synuclein accumulation in vivo, indicating broader relevance to neurodegenerative proteopathies. By integrating in vivo functional screening with mechanistic studies in human cells, this work identifies SSH1 as a druggable phosphatase that constrains autophagy at the level of ATG9A-dependent vesicle formation.Abbreviations: Aβ: amyloid-beta; AD: Alzheimer disease;AMP-AD: Accelerating Medicines Partnership-Alzheimer's Disease; ANOVA: analysis of variance;ATG9A: autophagy related 9A; BDSC: Bloomington Drosophila stock center; BSA: bovine serum albumin; CFL1: cofilin 1; DIOPT: DRSC Integrative Ortholog Prediction Tool; DmAtg9: Drosophila ortholog of ATG9; DMEM: Dulbecco's modified Eagle medium; DMSO: dimethyl sulfoxide; Dmssh: Drosophila ortholog of SSH1; Dmtsr: Drosophila ortholog of CFL1 and CFL2; ER-PAS: endoplasmic reticulum-phagophore assembly site; ESCRT: endosomal sorting complexes required for transport FC: fold change; FTD: frontotemporal dementia; HeLa: Henrietta Lacks; LIMK: lim domain kinase; MTOR: mechanistic target of rapamycin kinase; ND: neurodegenerative disease; NFE2L2/Nrf2: nuclear factor, erythroid derived 2, like 2; PBS: phosphate-buffered saline PD: Parkinson disease; PFA: paraformaldehyde; PHF-1: paired helical filament 1; RNAi: RNA interference; ROSMAP: The Religious Orders Study and Memory and Aging Project; SDS-PAGE: sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis; snRNA-seq: single nucleus RNA-sequencing; SQSTM1/p62: sequestosome 1; SS inhibitor: SAR405 + SBI-0206965 inhibitors; SSH1: slingshot protein phosphatase 1; ULK1: unc-51 like kinase 1; WT: wild type.

title: RBM42 couples alternative splicing to cytoskeletal organization to direct cortical development.
abstract: Alternative splicing coordinates gene expression programs that shape the developing cerebral cortex. Here, we used nervous system-specific Rbm42 conditional knockout mice, RBM42-depleted human SH-SY5Y cells, RNA sequencing, RIP-seq, proteomics, and splice-switching rescue to define how the spliceosomal RNA-binding protein RBM42 supports cortical development. Rbm42 loss caused perinatal lethality, cortical thinning, defective lamination, reduced progenitor proliferation, increased apoptosis, and disrupted neuronal cytoskeletal organization. RBM42 bound and regulated cytoskeleton-associated transcripts, including NIN/Nin and NUMA1/Numa1, and its loss altered their splicing in human cells and mouse cortex. Restoring RBM42 corrected these splicing defects and improved proliferation and neurite growth. Selective correction of NIN exon 18 mis-splicing partially restored βIII-tubulin organization and proliferation but did not rescue apoptosis. These findings connect spliceosome-dependent isoform control with cytoskeletal remodeling during cortical development and provide a mechanistic framework for RBM42-associated neurodevelopmental disease.

title: The Path to Kinesin and Beyond.
abstract: The recognition that the components of the axon and synapse originated in the neuronal cell body and were transported to their final destinations was recognized as early as Ramon y Cajal's pioneering studies on regeneration. However, mechanisms by which this transport was accomplished remained a mystery even as information accumulated about the rates and the composition of material being transported. The challenge was a lack of knowledge about molecular motors. In the early 1980's, advances in live cell imaging in combination with a novel model for study of vesicle transport in the axon led to the discovery of a new family of molecular motors, the kinesins.

title: Isozyme-Specific Inhibition of GSK-3 Reveals Distinct Cellular Responses in Huntington's Disease Fibroblasts.
abstract: Inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3) has been implicated in alleviating Huntington's disease (HD)-associated phenotypes. However, the mechanisms linking GSK-3 to HD pathogenesis, and particularly the distinct roles of GSK-3 isozymes in regulating HD-associated cellular dysfunction, remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the cellular responses of patient-derived HD fibroblasts to selective inhibition of GSK-3α or GSK-3β using isozyme-specific inhibitors, focusing on metabolic and bioenergetic pathways. Although inhibition of either isozyme suppressed mTORC1 signaling, selective GSK-3β inhibition elicited broader cellular responses, including altered oxidative stress signaling, increased expression of proteins associated with mitochondrial fission, enhanced lysosomal activity, and mitophagy, together with lysosomal redistribution and increased α-tubulin acetylation, suggesting improved microtubule-dependent intracellular trafficking. Quantitative proteomic analysis of four independent patient-derived HD fibroblasts corroborated these findings: GSK-3β inhibition elicited a broad set of proteins involved in cytoskeletal organization, adhesion signaling, and metabolic adaptation, whereas GSK-3α inhibition produced a more restricted and heterogeneous response. Collectively, these findings identify distinct cellular responses to selective GSK-3 isozyme inhibition and reveal GSK-3β as a predominant regulator of intracellular trafficking and mitochondrial and cytoskeletal dynamics in HD fibroblasts. Thus, inhibition of GSK-3β may represent a potential therapeutic approach for modulating HD-associated cellular dysfunction.

title: A Cilia-Centered Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD+) Signaling Network Regulates Hypothalamic Lysosomal Homeostasis and Metabolic Aging.
abstract: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) is an essential metabolite that regulates diverse cellular metabolic processes. Primary cilia, hair-like organelles on the cell surface, function as critical signaling hubs. Here, we demonstrate that cellular NAD+ levels are key regulators of both primary cilia growth and lysosomal function in hypothalamic neurons. NAD+ depletion induces ciliary shortening and diminishes lysosomal activity in a cilia-dependent manner. Mechanistically, the lysosomal repair complex protein CHMP4B translocates from periciliary satellites to lysosomes during lysosomal stress, a process impaired by ciliary dysgenesis. Disrupted lysosomal recruitment of CHMP4B leads to abnormal lysosomal Ca2+ signaling and lysosomal dysfunction. Aged mice with hypothalamic NAD+ deficiency exhibit shortened cilia and lysosomal stress phenotypes, both of which are restored by calorie restriction (CR). Moreover, CR improves aging-associated metabolic dysfunction, at least in part, through hypothalamic cilia-dependent mechanisms. These findings identify a primary cilium-mediated-NAD+ signaling axis that maintains lysosomal homeostasis in hypothalamic neurons, the disruption of which drives metabolic aging.

title: MANF promotes cell fitness and attenuates bortezomib sensitivity in multiple myeloma.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a clonal plasma cell malignancy in which disease relapse and treatment resistance remain major clinical challenges. Identifying molecular dependencies that support myeloma cell fitness may reveal therapeutic vulnerabilities beyond recurrent genomic alterations. Mesencephalic astrocyte-derived neurotrophic factor (MANF) is an endoplasmic reticulum-resident, stress-responsive protein, but its clinical and biological significance in MM remains poorly defined. METHODS: Publicly available DepMap CRISPR dependency data were analyzed to identify candidate MM-preferential dependencies. MANF expression and prognostic associations were examined in the MMRF CoMMpass cohort. Single-cell RNA sequencing and in silico perturbation analyses characterized its cellular distribution and predicted functional associations. MANF knockdown and genetic rescue using an siRNA-resistant MANF construct were performed in RPMI-8226 and OPM-2 cells to assess proliferation, cell-cycle distribution, and bortezomib sensitivity. Transcriptomic profiling characterized gene expression changes following MANF knockdown, while measurements at multiple time points assessed the temporal patterns of IRE1α-XBP1s-associated readouts. RESULTS: MANF was identified as a candidate MM-preferential dependency. Higher MANF expression was associated with advanced ISS stage and inferior overall survival, with the survival association retained after adjustment for established clinical and cytogenetic risk factors. Single-cell analysis localized MANF expression predominantly to plasma cells, while virtual knockout predicted changes involving ER protein processing, proteasome function, and metabolism. MANF knockdown inhibited proliferation, increased G0/G1 accumulation, and reduced MYC/E2F-associated transcriptional programs and cell-cycle regulatory proteins. Time-course analyses revealed early enhancement followed by later attenuation in selected IRE1α-XBP1s-associated readouts. MANF knockdown also increased bortezomib-induced apoptosis and reduced its IC₅₀. MANF re-expression partially reversed proliferation and cell-cycle phenotypes, restored IRE1α-XBP1s-associated protein abundance, and attenuated bortezomib sensitization. CONCLUSION: These findings identify MANF as a previously underexplored candidate myeloma-associated dependency that supports proliferative fitness and modulates bortezomib sensitivity in the tested MM models. MANF depletion is associated with dynamic changes in IRE1α-XBP1s-related readouts. These results support further investigation of MANF as a candidate therapeutic vulnerability in MM.

title: Intranuclear localisation of KLF3-AS1 under the balance of histone acetylation and methylation in BMSCs ameliorates cerebral ischaemia‒reperfusion injury by preserving microglial mitochondrial function and inhibiting inflammatory polarisation.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Ischaemic stroke occurs when blood flow to the brain is obstructed. Rapid restoration of blood supply frequently induces cerebral ischaemia‒reperfusion injury (CIRI). Bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC)-derived exosomes exhibit promising therapeutic potential for CIRI. In-depth exploration of their therapeutic mechanisms holds crucial significance for CIRI management. METHODS: The middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO) model was established in mice. An in vitro ischaemic stroke model was established by treating BV-2 cells with oxygen‒glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R). Exosomes were isolated from BMSCs and intranasally administrated into mice or added into BV-2 cells. Neurological deficits, grasping and coordination function were evaluated. Cell viability, apoptosis, proliferation and migration were examined. The localisation of KLF3-AS1 was examined by combined staining of immunofluorescence and fluorescence in situ hybridisation. Intracellular Ca2+ and adenosine triphosphate levels, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species and membrane potential were assessed. RESULTS: KLF3-AS1 enhanced BMSC viability, proliferation and migration, accompanied by epigenetic reprogramming at its promoter characterised by increased H3K27 acetylation (H3K27Ac) and decreased H3K27 trimethylation (H3K27Me3). BMSC-derived KLF3-AS1-enriched exosomes indicated therapeutic efficacy in both in vivo and in vitro models of cerebral ischaemia. In MCAO-induced mice, these exosomes alleviated neurological deficits and shifted microglial polarisation from pro-inflammatory M1-like to anti-inflammatory M2-like phenotypes. Similar effects were observed in OGD/R-treated BV-2 microglia, where KLF3-AS1-enriched exosomes attenuated oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction while upregulating Silent Information Regulator 3 (SIRT3) expression. Mechanistically, KLF3-AS1 facilitated ETS Variant Transcription Factor 4 (ETV4) nuclear translocation to activate SIRT3 transcription in microglia, and inhibition of SIRT3 abolished the neuroprotective effects of exosomal KLF3-AS1. CONCLUSION: BMSC-derived exosomes delivering KLF3-AS1 ameliorates CIRI by preserving microglial mitochondrial function and inhibiting inflammatory polarisation, highlighting KLF3-AS1 as a critical epigenetic regulator and exosome-mediated therapeutic agent for CIRI through the ETV4/SIRT3 axis. KEY POINTS/HIGHLIGHTS: KLF3-AS1 enhances bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC) function via promoter H3K27Ac/H3K27Me3 reprogramming. KLF3‑AS1 directly binds ETS Variant Transcription Factor 4 (ETV4) to activate Silent Information Regulator 3 (SIRT3), preserving mitochondrial integrity. BMSC‑derived exosomal KLF3‑AS1 promotes M2 microglial polarisation and ameliorates cerebral ischaemia-reperfusion injury.

title: Novel NaV1.6-Mitochondrial Complexes in Retinal Astrocyte Pockets Sequester GABA.
abstract: Voltage-gated sodium channels are best known for their capacity to generate and propagate electrical currents in neurons and muscle. Their expression in glial cells may also be of great importance given these cells' involvement in various disease processes. Here we identify a previously unrecognized voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.6-enriched microdomain in mouse retinal astrocytes. Using super-resolution confocal microscopy, electrophysiology, and transcriptomic analyses, we show that NaV1.6 forms high-density clusters within intracellular compartments devoid of the calcium-binding protein, S100β, typically understood to distribute throughout the entire astrocyte. These NaV1.6 pockets are polarized, clustering only on the bilayer facing retinal ganglion cell neurons, and are packed with unusually large, anaplerotic, and relatively depolarized mitochondria that closely appose NaV1.6 puncta. These metabolic compartments also accumulate high levels of GABA. Together, our findings reveal a specialized NaV1.6-mitochondrial complex in retinal astrocytes that expands the functional repertoire of voltage-gated sodium channels beyond direct neuronal electrical excitability.

title: STMN2: Membrane-Binding Microtubule Regulator or Tubulin Effector?
abstract: STMN2, a protein implicated in motor neuron degeneration, is widely viewed as a membrane-associated microtubule inhibitor, but emerging evidence challenges whether this activity defined its cellular function. Three alternative models integrates available evidence to offer perspectives beyond microtubule regulation. The vesicle cargo adaptor model proposes that STMN2 recruits diverse cargos to transport vesicles for axonal delivery. The membrane-bound signaling messenger model links STMN2 turnover to local signaling, effector, degradation, or effector release. The traffic director model proposes that STMN2 regulates cargo routing between delivery and degradative pathways. These models are not mutually exclusive and position tubulin binding as a regulator of STMN2 function rather than its defining activity.

title: Reduced BNIP1 impairs autophagosome-lysosome fusion in hippocampal neurons and contributes to Alzheimer's disease pathology.
abstract: BNIP1 (BCL2‑interacting protein 1) belongs to the soluble N‑ethylmaleimide‑sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) family. Statistical screening based on the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) dataset GSE48350 reveals reduced BNIP1 expression in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), suggesting that BNIP1 is a potentially key regulatory protein for investigating AD pathogenesis. In this study, we detected BNIP1 protein levels in APP/PS1 transgenic mice and APP‑overexpressing HT22 hippocampal neuronal cells, screened key interacting proteins of BNIP1 via mass spectrometry, and further performed gain‑ and loss‑of‑function assays using overexpression plasmids and small interfering RNA (siRNA) to verify the protein function of BNIP1. Our findings indicate that, in these experimental models, reduced BNIP1 expression contributes to AD‑related pathological alterations by impairing autophagosome‑lysosome fusion. Restoration of BNIP1 expression enhances Rab5b‑mediated Rab7 recruitment and consequently ameliorates autophagosome‑lysosome fusion. This study suggests that reduced BNIP1 expression is involved in AD‑related pathological alterations.NIP1 (BCL2-interacting protein 1) belongs to the soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) family. Statistical screening based on the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) dataset GSE48350 reveals reduced BNIP1 expression in Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, which renders BNIP1 a potentially key regulatory protein for investigating AD pathogenesis. In this study, we detected BNIP1 protein levels in APP/PS1 transgenic mice and APP-overexpressing HT22 hippocampal neuronal cells. Mass-spectrometry analysis was performed to screen key interacting proteins of BNIP1. Gain- and loss-of-function experiments were further conducted using overexpression plasmids and small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) to verify the protein function of BNIP1. Our findings indicate that decreased BNIP1 may act as an important contributing factor mediating AD-associated autophagosome-lysosome fusion defects in these experimental models. Restoration of BNIP1 expression enhances Rab5b-mediated Rab7 recruitment and consequently ameliorates aberrant autophagosome-lysosome fusion. This study suggests that BNIP1 serves as a potentially key regulatory protein for mechanistic research into Alzheimer's disease.

title: Lipid Droplet-Associated Hsp70 Palmitoylation Drives Lysosomal Dysfunction in Ischemic Stroke.
abstract: Lipid droplet (LDs) accumulate in glial cells across neurodegenerative and ischemic brain pathologies. LDs modulate cellular stress via organelle crosstalk, particularly with lysosomes, whose dysfunction and cathepsin leakage drive glial activation after cerebral ischemia. However, the molecular link between accumulated LDs and lysosomes in pathological glial activation remains incompletely understood. Using a mouse middle cerebral artery occlusion ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) model and oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/Re) cell models, we found that both LD signal intensity and lysosomal cathepsin B leakage progressively increased from day 1 to day 14 after I/R. Etomoxir, an inhibitor of carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 A (CPT1A), the rate-limiting enzyme for fatty acid β-oxidation, aggravated I/R-induced LD accumulation and lysosomal damage in glial cells. Exogenous LDs derived from OGD/Re-treated glial cells aggravated lysosomal damage and promoted the proliferation of astrocytes and microglia. LD accumulation was associated with Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution of Hsp70 from lysosomes to the extracellular space, leading to lysosomal damage and reactive glial activation. Mechanistically, using multiple genetic and pharmacological approaches, including Plin3 knockdown, an Hsp70 palmitoylation‑site mutant, recombinant human Hsp70 (rhHsp70), as well as a pan-palmitoylation inhibitor and TLR2/4 antagonist, we consistently validated that Plin3, an LD surface protein, interacts with lysosomal Hsp70, causing Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution, and lysosomal damage. Extracellular Hsp70 activates TLR2/4 on glial cells, promoting cell proliferation and pro-inflammatory cytokine release. Collectively, these findings indicate that pathological LDs interacting with lysosomes drive Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution, causing lysosomal impairment and astrogliosis in ischemic stroke. We uncover Hsp70 palmitoylation as a potential drug target for ischemic stroke therapy.

title: Protein Quality Control Systems in Neurodegeneration-Chaperones, Cytoskeleton, and the Pathogenic Transition of Tau.
abstract: Maintenance of protein homeostasis is essential for neuronal survival, and its disruption is a defining feature of neurodegenerative diseases. Neurons are particularly vulnerable to proteostatic stress due to their post-mitotic nature, long lifespan, and dependence on cytoskeletal integrity for structural stability, intracellular transport, and synaptic function. In tauopathies and related neurodegenerative disorders, misfolded proteins and aggregation-prone proteins burden the cellular quality-control systems, leading to cytoskeletal destabilization, synaptic dysfunction, and progressive neuronal loss. This review is organized around a central question: for a given tau species, defined by its isoform, post-translational modifications, and assembly state, what determines its fate? We examine how molecular chaperone networks, including HSP100, HSP90, HSP70, J-domain proteins (JDPs), small heat shock proteins (sHSPs), and the Prefoldin-CCT pathway, regulate the folding, disaggregation, sequestration, and degradation of pathogenic tau. We highlight how these chaperone networks influence key proteostasis checkpoints, determine whether tau refolds, is degraded, or is redirected toward toxic aggregation, and how these outcomes impact microtubule stability and neuronal function. Drawing on studies in yeast, Drosophila, mammalian models, and human tissues, we develop two key conclusions. First, chaperone activity is not uniformly protective against tauopathies; its effects depend on the tau species, cellular context, and disease stage. Second, because the cytoskeleton is both a chaperone client and an essential component of intracellular clearance pathways, tau pathology and proteostasis failure can reinforce one another. Finally, we discuss emerging therapeutic strategies and challenges in targeting chaperone networks to restore proteostasis while avoiding unintended neurotoxic consequences.

title: Dynamic transcriptomics of the HPG and HPI axis reveals male pregnancy regulatory networks in the lined seahorse (Hippocampus erectus).
abstract: Male seahorses exhibit a remarkable reproductive mode among vertebrates, in which embryos are incubated within a specialized brood pouch of the male. To clarify the endocrine mechanisms underlying male pregnancy, we integrated multi-tissue transcriptomic sequencing with stage-dependent hormonal profiling across pregnancy stages in the lined seahorse Hippocampus erectus. Our results revealed pronounced stage-specific remodeling of both the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) and hypothalamic-pituitary-interrenal (HPI) axes during male pregnancy. Within the HPG axis, brain gnrh1 and gnrh2, together with pituitary lhb and fshb, were upregulated during pregnancy, whereas genes involved in testicular steroid hormone biosynthesis showed reduced expression throughout gestation. Consistently, circulating levels of estradiol-17β and 11-ketotestosterone remained low, suggesting that reduced steroidogenic activity may be associated with endocrine adaptations during male pregnancy. In the HPI axis, the cortisol-metabolizing gene hsd11b1 was highly expressed in the brood pouch during late pregnancy, coinciding with a local cortisol peak in the pouch while circulating cortisol levels remained relatively stable. This spatially restricted pattern indicates that local cortisol signaling in the brood pouch may contribute to late-pregnancy remodeling and parturition-related processes. These findings indicate that male pregnancy in seahorses involves endocrine adjustments, including altered gonadal steroidogenesis and localized activation of cortisol signaling within the brood pouch.

title: TUBA1A mutations in cerebral cortical dysplasia.
abstract: The cerebral cortex is essential for higher cognitive functions, and its structural and functional integrity relies on the precise regulation of microtubule proteins in neuronal proliferation, differentiation, axonal and dendritic growth, migration, and connectivity. The TUBA1A gene, encoding alpha-tubulin, is highly expressed during fetal brain development and is crucial for cortical maturation. Research has linked mutations in the TUBA1A gene to malformations of cortical development (MCDs), but the specific types of MCDs caused by these mutations and the underlying molecular mechanisms are not fully understood. This review compiles current research findings on the development of the cerebral cortex, the role of microtubules in cortical development, and existing studies on the TUBA1A gene. It aims to elucidate how TUBA1A regulates microtubules to influence brain development, providing key insights into the gene's role in neural development.

title: ALS-linked FUS mutation impairs GEMIN5-dependent mRNA recruitment to neuronal late endosomes.
abstract: Neurons depend on tightly regulated positioning of cellular components to maintain long-distance signaling, but the mechanisms guiding specific mRNAs to distant regions remain unclear. Here, we show that late endosomes function as selective RNA carriers in human motor neurons and uncover the molecular logic guiding their loading. Using APEX2-mediated proximity labeling, we identify the external transcriptome of RAB7A-positive endosomes and find a specific population of mRNAs enriched for endosomal, axonal, and synaptic functions. We find that mRNAs enriched in RAB7A endosomes contain evolutionarily conserved 5'UTRs that act as localization signals, and that the RNA-binding protein GEMIN5 interacts with these regions to promote endosomal RNA recruitment. Finally, we show that there is a conspicuous loss of endosome-associated transcripts in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-associated conditions, accompanied by the mislocalization of GEMIN5 from endosomes. These findings uncover fundamental principles of RNA compartmentalization and highlight endosomal mRNA loading as a vulnerable axis in neuronal homeostasis.

title: Extracellular neuroligin-ICAM5 coupling drives dendritic growth via actin remodeling.
abstract: Neuroligins (NLGNs) organize neuronal connectivity by engaging a diverse set of interaction partners, yet how extracellular recognition couples to intracellular growth programs remains unclear. Using affinity proteomics, we identify intercellular adhesion molecule-5 (ICAM5), a cell-surface protein localized to dendritic filopodia, as a NLGN interactor. Surface plasmon resonance and cell-based assays demonstrate direct binding between the ICAM5 and NLGN3 extracellular domains and reveal that ICAM5 engages all NLGN isoforms. In neurons, NLGN3 and ICAM5 preferentially colocalize at extrasynaptic, F-actin-positive dendritic sites, linking this interaction to regions of active cytoskeletal reorganization and growth. Accordingly, ICAM5 strongly enhances NLGN-induced dendritic outgrowth, but the NLGN3-ICAM5 complex does not detectably contribute to synaptogenesis. Mechanistically, ICAM5 sustains PAK-cofilin signaling and F-actin organization in growth cones, positioning it as a modulator linking NLGN engagement to actin remodeling. Together, these findings define a NLGN-ICAM5 axis that couples extracellular recognition to intracellular cytoskeletal remodeling to control neuronal structural development.

title: A chemomechanical bifurcation landscape unifies sustained growth, length homeostasis, and regenerative collapse in axons.
abstract: Axonal growth machinery is largely shared across neurons, but axons exhibit strikingly different fates depending on developmental and environmental context: sustained elongation in peripheral neurons under permissive conditions, length homeostasis in cortical neurons after target innervation, and pathological collapse into dystrophic endbulbs in injured adult central nervous system (CNS) axons. These divergent outcomes have resisted explanation by length-sensing and biomechanical models that treat long-range transport and local force generation as separate problems. We unify these phenomena through a mechanochemical model that couples bidirectional motor transport and intracellular signaling to growth-cone balance of axonal tension, actomyosin contraction, and adhesion within a single feedback loop: The lengthening axon uses its own growing transport delay to establish self-limiting mechanical feedback, as the accumulating delay reshapes signaling waveforms to progressively elevate myosin contractility against actin-driven protrusion. Two physical parameters, the transport delay and the signaling feedback strength, organize axon fate into a unified state-space landscape spanning sustained growth, length homeostasis, and pathological collapse. Reduced feedback strength weakens this self-limiting mechanical feedback by simultaneously enhancing protrusion and suppressing contractility, providing a mechanistic interpretation of axon lengthening under partial reduction of retrograde transport. Bistability in the inhibitory regime explains why mature CNS tracts persist where nascent sprouts collapse, recasting regenerative failure as a state-dependent gate rather than a capacity limit. The framework predicts that partial rather than complete inhibition of retrograde transport could shift collapsed axons across the bifurcation into a growth-permissive regime, identifying a class of interventions complementary to existing capacity-restoration strategies for nerve injury.

title: iPSC-derived RPE and retinal organoids from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients show differences in ABCA4 function.
abstract: Stargardt disease is a phenotypically heterogeneous disease caused by bi-allelic mutations in the ABCA4 gene. We generated retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, photoreceptor precursors (PhRPs), and retinal organoids (ROs) from two induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell lines derived from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients. We observed that RPE cells from the patient with peripheral affectation showed reduced ABCA4 expression, reduced phagocytosis and digestion of photoreceptor outer segments (POSs), and accumulation of lipid byproducts. ROs from both patients show stunted segments, more rods, caspase-3 activation, and lipofuscin accumulation at week 45 of maturation. Phenotypical differences seen in Stargardt disease patients are caused by their specific ABCA4 variants, but cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the process of photoreceptor degeneration are still poorly understood. Here, we suggest that peripheral phenotypes associated with these macular dystrophies can be linked to poor clearance of POSs by RPE cells, giving these cells a higher role in the pathogenesis of the disease.

title: Evaluation of deep learning-based super-resolution reconstruction in fetal brain T2-weighted single-shot fast spin-echo imaging.
abstract: PURPOSE: The study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of a deep learning-based Precise IQ Engine (PIQE) in enhancing image sharpness and quality during MRI reconstruction to enhance the image quality of fetal brain single-shot fast spin-echo (SSFSE) imaging. METHODS: Fetal brain MRI scans of 14 patients, including an SSFSE sequence, acquired between January 2024 and February 2025, were analyzed. Images were reconstructed with and without PIQE (zoom ratio of 3 from low-resolution matrices). We quantified the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and image sharpness using the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the fetal brain. Two board-certified radiologists assessed the image noise, contrast, sharpness, artifacts, and overall image quality of the two image types on a 4-point scale. We compared the quantitative and qualitative scores between the images with and without PIQE using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. RESULTS: SNRs, CNRs, and FWHM were significantly enhanced with PIQE compared to those without PIQE (SNR, CNR: p < 0.001, FWHM : p < 0.01). Qualitative scores for noise (p < 0.001), contrast (p < 0.001), sharpness (p < 0.001), artifacts (p < 0.001), and overall image quality (p < 0.001) were superior in images obtained with PIQE compared to those without it. Kappa analysis revealed moderate-to- excellent agreement for different image quality aspects: noise (κ = 0.52), contrast (κ = 0.74), sharpness (κ = 0.82), artifacts (κ = 0.61), and overall image quality (κ = 0.80). CONCLUSION: PIQE potentially enhances the image quality of fetal brain MRI using an SSFSE sequence.

title: Kinesin-12 (Kif15) in Neurons: From Mitotic Motor to Activity-Dependent Regulator of Dendritic Spines.
abstract: Kinesin-12 (Kif15) is a canonical mitotic kinesin that crosslinks parallel microtubules and suppresses microtubule catastrophe. It exists in both dimeric and tetrameric oligomerization states that are regulated by ionic conditions and binding partners. Its persistent expression in postmitotic neurons indicates that this ancestral microtubule-organizing activity has been repurposed for neuronal functions, yet the dendritic role of Kif15 has remained poorly defined. Here, we review and hypothesize KIF15 acting as a dendritic regulator. We propose that in the dendritic shaft, Kif15 exists predominantly as a tetramer crosslinker to organize the mixed-polarity antiparallel microtubule array. At the neck of the dendritic spines, perhaps due to the electrical signals, the compartmental ion concentration has changed. The dimeric Kif15 transports PSD95 along microtubule plus ends that invade dendritic spines and unloads PSD95 at the postsynaptic sites. There, synaptic activity triggers Ca2+ influx and CaMKII activation to promote Kif15 association with Myosin IIb (Myh10), forming a Kif15-Myh10 hetero-complex, which reorganizes the microtubule-actin network to facilitate mushroom-like dendritic spine formation. This framework explains why Kif15 loss impairs spine complexity, synaptic development, and mood-related behaviors without causing catastrophic disassembly of dendritic microtubules. It further links KIF15 mutations to cognitive disorders and suggests that mechanistic insights from a mitotic motor to its synaptic functions.

title: Deep brain stimulation of the nucleus basalis magnocellularis ameliorates autistic behavior in a rat model of autism via cholinergic modulation in the prefrontal cortex.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: In the present study, we investigated whether deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the nucleus basalis magnocellularis (NBM) improves autism spectrum disorder (ASD)-related behavioral abnormalities in a valproic acid (VPA)-induced rat model of autism, consistent with changes in cholinergic markers in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). METHODS: On the 12.5th day of gestation, pregnant rats ( n  = 16) received a single intraperitoneal injection of 500 mg/kg sodium valproate dissolved in 0.9% saline, while others ( n  = 5) received saline alone. Male offspring were allowed to reach 3 months of age and then were randomly assigned to one of four experimental groups: Contr - prenatally saline injected, VPA - prenatally VPA-injected, VPA/I - VPA-injected with electrode implantation in the NBM, and VPA/S - VPA-injected with electrical stimulation. DBS was initiated in rats of the VPA/S group 10 days after surgery (two consecutive hours per day, every day for 2 weeks; DBS parameters: 60 Hz, 120 µs, and 50 µA). RESULTS: The prenatally VPA-exposed rats demonstrate deficits in social behavior, increased locomotor activity, and reduced anxiety levels. Immunohistochemical evaluation shows a decrease in the number of acetylcholinesterase-immunoreactive neurons in the mPFC and choline acetyltransferase-immunoreactive neurons in the NBM. NBM-DBS improves VPA-induced autistic behavior and increases the number of acetylcholinesterase-immunoreactive neurons in the PFC. CONCLUSION: The correlation between ASD-like behavior and cholinergic markers in the mPFC supports our hypothesis that NBM-DBS improves behavioral deficits by modulating cholinergic neurotransmission in the PFC in a rat model of autism.
