title: Paclitaxel-induced disruption of lysosome motility and function in DRG neurons.
abstract: Lysosomal trafficking and homeostasis are biological functions that are pivotal for DRG neurons, given their metabolic demands and extremely long axons. Previous studies indicate that lysosomal signaling is altered in a mouse model of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) and that blocking mitogen activated protein kinase-associated kinase (MNK1/2) signaling can alleviate pain behaviors in CIPN. Here, we investigated lysosome dynamics and lysosome-associated signaling in a mouse model of CIPN induced by paclitaxel (PTX), a chemotherapeutic agent used for various types of cancer. Using spinning disk super-resolution microscope (SPINSR), we demonstrate that PTX treatment in vivo causes reduced lysosome motility observed in vitro. PTX likewise drives the accumulation of Sequestosome 1 (SQSTM1), also known as P62, in cultured mouse DRG neurons, indicating lysosomal dysfunction in DRG neurons. The transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, was also upregulated in the nucleus of cultured mouse DRG neurons treated with PTX. In line with this, increased lysosomal-associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP1) expression was observed in PTX-treated mice. Given that our previous work demonstrated PTX treatment increases MNK1/2-eIF4E signaling in DRG neurons, we examined whether MNK1/2 inhibition could rescue lysosomal dysfunction. Treatment with Tomivosertib (eFT508), a potent MNK1/2 inhibitor, restored P62 levels in DRG neurons of PTX-treated mice and reduced TFEB in DRG treated in vitro. To establish translation relevance, we further show that PTX elevates phosphorylated eiF4E (p-eIF4E) in human DRG neurons, and concurrent eFT508 administration attenuates this effect. Collectively, these findings indicated that PTX disrupts lysosome trafficking and biogenesis, and that MNK inhibition with eFT508 restores lysosomal signaling and can serve as a neuroprotective strategy for CIPN.

title: FTO deficiency mediates ferroptosis to exacerbate cobalt-induced neurotoxicity.
abstract: Cobalt, a toxic environmental contaminant, has been implicated in human neurological damage. However, the detailed molecular basis of cobalt-triggered neurotoxicity remains poorly uncovered. In the present study, we elucidated the N6-methyladenosine (m6A) demethylase fat mass and obesity-associated protein (FTO) downregulation mediates the activation of ferroptosis to drive cobalt-triggered neurodegeneration. We established an in vitro model using H4 cells and an in vivo model using C57BL/6 mice. Animal experiments provided initial evidence underscoring the critical involvement of ferroptosis in cobalt-associated neurotoxicity. Furthermore, in vitro assays revealed that ferroptosis is triggered subsequent to oxidative stress induced by cobalt exposure. Notably, MeRIP-seq profiling of H4 cells and mouse cortex revealed that ferroptosis-associated genes exhibited differential m6A modification, suggesting m6A modification might be involved in modulating ferroptosis. Concurrently, Gene Ontology and KEGG enrichment analyses revealed that genes bearing differential m6A modifications were significantly clustered within pathways linked to ferroptosis as well as neurodegenerative diseases. Moreover, we found that FTO depletion effectively enhanced ferroptosis following cobalt-induced oxidative stress. Mechanistically, FTO depletion enhanced m6A modification of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and transferrin receptor protein 1 (TFRC) mRNAs, leading to reduced GPX4 and elevated TFRC expression, which aggravated cobalt-induced ferroptosis. More importantly, we observed that central nervous system specific knockout of Fto exacerbated cobalt-induced neurobehavioral deficits and neuropathological damage through ferroptosis activation. Collectively, these results provide important insights into cobalt-induced neurotoxicity by targeting FTO deficiency-mediated ferroptosis and offer an innovative strategy for investigating neurodegenerative processes driven by environmental toxicants.

title: Exosomes derived from N2 neutrophils reprogram the immune microenvironment to promote spinal cord injury repair.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Spinal cord injury induces irreversible neurological impairments via secondary pathological cascades dominated by excessive inflammation, oxidative stress, and neuronal apoptosis. As the first-responder immune cells following spinal cord trauma, neutrophils can acquire an N2-like reparative phenotype, yet direct neutrophil transplantation is hampered by poor cellular survival. Exosomes, nanoscale cell-secreted vesicles with low immunogenicity and favourable biostability, constitute promising cell-free candidates for regenerative therapy. Nevertheless, the therapeutic potential of exosomes derived from N2-polarized neutrophils remains poorly defined for spinal cord injury repair. METHODS: Murine bone-marrow-derived neutrophils were polarized toward the N2 phenotype using interleukin-6 (IL-6) and granulocyte-colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), with non-polarized neutrophils set as the control group. Exosomes were purified by ultracentrifugation and comprehensively characterized by transmission electron microscopy, nanoparticle tracking analysis, and western blotting. In vitro functional assays were performed to evaluate macrophage phenotypic reprogramming, neuronal axonal regeneration, and neuronal apoptosis. A modified Allen's weight-drop mouse spinal cord injury model was adopted for in vivo intervention. Motor functional recovery was evaluated using the Basso Mouse Scale and gait analysis, while neural tissue repair was assessed via immunofluorescence staining. RESULTS: Exosomes derived from N2-polarized neutrophils (N2-exos) exhibited canonical exosomal hallmarks. In vitro, these exosomes drove lipopolysaccharide-primed macrophages to switch to an anti-inflammatory reparative phenotype, alleviated oxidative-stress-mediated axonal injury, and suppressed neuronal apoptosis. In vivo administration of N2-exos markedly enhanced hind-limb motor performance and gait coordination, and facilitated axonal regeneration across the injury epicenter. CONCLUSIONS: N2-exos remodel the post-traumatic immune microenvironment and confer combined neuroprotective and axon regenerative effects. This cell-free modality represents a promising therapeutic candidate for regenerative interventions against spinal cord injury.

title: Cellular-resolution three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) of neuronal population activity at 2-mm depth in the mammalian brain.
abstract: Extending the depth reach of multiphoton microscopy for imaging neuronal population activity in the scattering mammalian brain is an 'exponentially hard' problem. Three-photon (3p) microscopy has enabled imaging of neuroactivity at depths up to ~1.2 mm in the mouse brain; however, the fundamental depth limit of 3p imaging, as set by the depth at which out-of-focus background fluorescence exceeds the in-focus fluorescence signal, is well beyond 2 mm. Reaching this fundamental depth limit in 3p imaging has been hampered by insufficient in-focus fluorescence signal. Here we demonstrate a three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) system that approaches this fundamental depth limit via systematic and principled optimization of the in-focus fluorescence signal. TrUDI matches the parameters of the excitation laser, the optical system, and the acquisition to linear and nonlinear limits for safe laser exposure while satisfying the spatiotemporal requirements of single-cell resolution calcium (Ca2+) imaging. TrUDI achieves a ~250-fold increase in detected fluorescence photon yield at the same laser power as in previous approaches thereby enabling in vivo cellular-resolution recordings of neuronal population activity within fields of view of ~230 × 230 µm2 at 8.6 Hz at tissue depths of up to ~2 mm in mouse cortex and hippocampus.

title: DINOSim: Training-Free Semantic Segmentation on Microscopy Images.
abstract: We present DINOSim, a training-free method for segmenting objects in microscopy images without the need for large annotated datasets or additional model training. DINOSim builds on the pretrained DINOv2 image encoder, which captures semantic information from images. By comparing the encoder's features of image patches to those of a user-selected reference, DINOSim generates pseudo-labels that guide semantic segmentation. Subsequently, a k-nearest neighbors framework is used to refine predictions across new images. Our experiments show that DINOSim can effectively segment previously unseen objects in diverse microscopy datasets, offering performance comparable to supervised approaches while avoiding the need for costly manual labeling. We also investigate how different choices of user prompt selection and model size affect accuracy and generalization. To make the method widely accessible, we provide an open-source napari plugin (github.com/AAitorG/napari-DINOSim), enabling researchers to apply DINOSim to their own data easily. Overall, DINOSim offers a fast, flexible and practical solution for bioimage analysis, particularly valuable in resource-constrained settings.

title: The pathological roles of intrinsically disordered proteins in lysosomal acidification dysfunction in neurodegenerative diseases.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and Parkinson's disease (PD) are characterized by the accumulation of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), including amyloid-β (Aβ), tau, and α-synuclein (αSyn). These proteins disrupt neuronal homeostasis through toxic aggregation, impaired proteostasis, and progressive neurodegeneration, in part via dysfunction of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway (ALP). A central feature of this impairment is defective vacuolar-type (H+)-ATPase (V-ATPase) function, leading to lysosomal deacidification and reduced degradative capacity. Pathological IDP species converge on V-ATPase through direct interactions with its subunits or by perturbing its assembly, while also exerting protein-specific effects, including lysosomal membrane destabilization, impaired hydrolase activity, and disrupted endolysosomal trafficking. These combined mechanisms create a reciprocal relationship between lysosomal dysfunction and IDP accumulation, in which impaired lysosomal degradation further promotes the persistence and aggregation of pathological IDP species. This review synthesizes current insights into the molecular interplay between IDPs and lysosomal acidification across AD, FTD, and PD, and highlights how these processes contribute to disease progression. We further discuss emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring lysosomal function. These findings underscore lysosomal dysfunction as a common feature of IDP-driven neurodegeneration and a potential therapeutic target across these disorders.

overview: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and Parkinson's disease (PD) are characterized by the accumulation of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), including amyloid-β (Aβ), tau, and α-synuclein (αSyn).
main: These findings underscore lysosomal dysfunction as a common feature of IDP-driven neurodegeneration and a potential therapeutic target across these disorders.

title: From exercise-associated lactate to the tubulin code: α-tubulin lactylation as a candidate mechanism for poststroke neural remodeling.
abstract: Aerobic exercise promotes functional recovery after ischemic stroke, but the proposed link between an exercise-associated lactate pulse and durable neural remodeling remains unproven. The metabolite relevant to the hypothesis is L-lactate generated by skeletal-muscle glycolysis. In the principal mouse study, moderate treadmill exercise begun on poststroke day 6 (10 m/min, 30 min/day for 14 days) increased circulating and brain lactate together with α-tubulin lysine 40 (K40) lactylation and recovery; this regimen cannot be assumed feasible in patients with acute or severe disability. Electrically evoked skeletal-muscle contraction offers a preclinical exercise-mimetic option for nonambulatory subjects and increased circulating lactate in stroke mice, but it has not established a therapeutic lactate target, brain K40 lactylation, or clinical efficacy. Mechanistically, concurrent changes in L-lactate, K40 lactylation, and recovery show association rather than causal mediation. Exogenous L-lactate and dichloroacetate broadly alter metabolism and signaling, while substrate oxidation, HCAR1/VEGF signaling, BDNF/NMDAR-related plasticity, and lactylation of other proteins remain parallel explanations. The in vivo role of K40 lactylation has not been tested by a selective blockade. Moreover, the LacAVC phase IIa intravenous lactate trial was terminated after 28 enrollments for recruitment and protocol-related reasons. Although no results have been posted in the trial registry, a 2026 conference abstract reported preliminary safety and cerebral-bioavailability findings without establishing clinical efficacy or α-tubulin K40 target engagement.

title: Comprehensive Clinical, Neuroradiologic, and Oral Health of 23 Individuals With MOPDII: Molecular Spectrum and Phenotypic Features.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type II (MOPDII; MIM #210720) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by severe growth failure and microcephaly, frequently complicated by central nervous system (CNS) anomalies and early-onset cerebrovascular disease. This study aimed to define the neurologic, radiologic, molecular, and oral-dental features of a MOPDII cohort, with particular emphasis on cerebrovascular involvement, and to assess genotype-phenotype correlations. METHODS: Molecular diagnosis was established using next-generation sequencing, including targeted gene panel sequencing (n = 11) and exome sequencing (n = 1), or Sanger sequencing (n = 11). Clinical data, neuroimaging and vascular findings, systematic oral-dental examinations, and molecular results were retrospectively reviewed. RESULTS: Twenty-three patients from 18 unrelated consanguineous families were included. Seventeen distinct homozygous PCNT variants were identified, including 5 splice-site, 5 frameshift, and 7 nonsense variants; of these, 12 were novel. Structural CNS anomalies were common, with the thin corpus callosum being the most frequent finding, observed in 14 of 17 patients (82%) who underwent cranial imaging. Moyamoya disease was identified in 12 patients (70.5%), of whom 7 experienced chronic or acute cerebral infarctions and/or intracranial hemorrhage. Three patients with moyamoya disease died of complications related to vascular involvement. The 2 oldest patients developed severe peripheral arterial and coronary artery occlusions, leading to spontaneous limb amputation and acute myocardial infarction. Oral-dental evaluation, performed in 14 patients (61%), revealed microdontia, malformed teeth, and root shortening. No consistent genotype-phenotype correlation was identified for cerebrovascular or orodental manifestations. DISCUSSION: MOPDII is strongly associated with moyamoya disease and represents a major cause of neurologic morbidity and mortality. Early and longitudinal neuroimaging, including brain MRI and angiographic assessment, should be integral to patient management. Oral-dental abnormalities are common and merit routine evaluation.

title: Progranulin haploinsufficiency disrupts cathepsin D function, resulting in lysosomal abnormalities and elevated TDP-43 levels in the mouse brain.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a leading cause of early-onset neurodegeneration, frequently linked to mutations in the GRN gene, which encodes the protein progranulin (PGRN). PGRN is known to play a crucial role in lysosomal function, and its deficiency contributes to FTD pathogenesis. Here, we examined the consequences of PGRN loss on lysosomal homeostasis, focusing on the lysosomal protease cathepsin D (CTSD) and TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) aggregation, hallmarks of FTD and related neurodegenerative diseases. METHODS: Using mouse models with homozygous and heterozygous GRN deletions and double knockouts for GRN and CTSD, we assessed lysosomal function, CTSD expression and activity, lysosomal-associated membrane protein (LAMP) levels and localization, TDP-43 aggregation, and survival. RESULTS: PGRN deficiency resulted in significant alterations in lysosomal function. Despite significantly elevated levels of mature and immature CTSD in PGRN-deficient mice, enzymatic activity was significantly reduced. PGRN deficiency also caused accumulation of lysosomal-associated membrane protein (LAMP) and perinuclear clustering of LAMP1-positive lysosomes, suggestive of disrupted lysosomal trafficking. Correspondingly, insoluble TDP-43 levels significantly increased, implicating lysosomal impairment in defective protein degradation and aggregation. Remarkably, double-knockout mice lacking both PGRN and CTSD exhibited significantly shortened lifespans, highlighting a potential functional interaction between these proteins in maintaining neuronal health and longevity. DISCUSSION: These findings underscore the importance of PGRN as a central regulator of lysosomal function and protein homeostasis. Together, the data provide mechanistic insight into PGRN-dependent lysosomal biology and identify pathways that may contribute to GRN-associated FTD and other neurodegenerative disorders.
authors: Fazal R, Tharkeshwar AK, Beel S, Storm A, Schevenels B, Tomé SO, Thal DR, Van Den Bosch L, Beckers J, Van Damme P

title: Alzheimer's genetic risk factor CASS4 controls microglial focal adhesion biology and amyloidosis.
abstract: Recent genome-wide association studies have identified numerous Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk genes enriched in microglia, including Crk-associated substrate (Cas) scaffold protein family member 4 (CASS4), which encodes the adaptor protein CASS4. Despite its strong genetic association with AD, the role of CASS4 in disease remains poorly understood. Here, we show that full-body Cass4 deletion in 5xFAD mice increases amyloid-β (Aβ) deposition, neuronal dystrophy, and cognitive deficits. Since microglia are the predominant brain-resident cells expressing Cass4, we investigated its role in microglial responses to Aβ pathology. Loss of CASS4 impaired microglial mobilization to Aβ plaques and reduced plaque compaction. Phosphoproteomic analysis of purified microglia revealed marked disruption of focal adhesion signaling following Cass4 deletion. Consistent with this, CASS4 deficiency abrogated in vivo microglial recruitment to injury and in vitro wound healing responses, two processes that are centrally orchestrated by focal adhesion biology. Together, these findings identify CASS4 as a critical regulator of microglial function and focal adhesion biology and suggest that CASS4 may represent a therapeutic target for AD.

title: Non-electrophilic TRPA1 modulator MNP-021 protects neuronal and glial function from diabetes-associated glucotoxicity and neuroinflammation.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Diabetes-associated neurodegeneration is amplified by methylglyoxal (MGO)-driven dicarbonyl stress linking hyperglycemia to neuronal insulin resistance and maladaptive neuroinflammation. We tested the neuroprotective activity of MNP-021, a non-electrophilic transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) modulator, in neurons and glial cells in vitro. METHODS: SH-SY5Y neurons were pretreated with MNP-021 and challenged with MGO, then profiled by high-content imaging, RNA-seq, Seahorse Oxygen Consumption Rate (OCR) and Extracellular Acidification Rate (ECAR), glycolytic stress assays, and immunoblotting for AKT, ERK, and cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB). In an additional sustained glucotoxicity paradigm, differentiated SH-SY5Y cells were exposed to high glucose for 7 days and viability was assessed by LIVE/DEAD™ high-content imaging. HMC3 glial cells were treated with MNP-021, exposed to Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), Tumor Necrosis Factor-α (TNF-α) or Aβ(25-35), and tested for viability and inflammatory markers by Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) and RT-qPCR. RESULTS: MGO increased nucleus-to-cytoplasm area ratio by 49% and dysregulated glucose handling, increasing 2-(N-(7-Nitrobenz-2-oxa-1,3-diazol-4-yl)Amino)-2-Deoxyglucose (2-NBDG) uptake by ~ 25%, with GLUT1/GLUT4 membrane redistribution; MNP-021 normalized morphology, glucose uptake, and transporter localization without cytotoxicity up to 10 µM. RNA-seq identified 754 MGO-deregulated genes, including ISR/metabolic nodes such as glucokinase (GCK), Sestrin-2 (SESN2), phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH), Phosphoserine Aminotransferase 1 (PSAT1), phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 2 (PCK2); MNP-021 buffered stress-induced transcription with limited baseline effects, modulated mitochondrial morphology and redox-associated fluorescence while preserving overall respiratory flux and blunting stress-evoked compensatory glycolysis. MNP-021 restored pro-survival signaling (pAKT/pERK and nuclear pCREB), including insulin responsiveness during MGO exposure. In a sustained high-glucose model, MNP-021 reduced the high-glucose-associated increase in cell death, extending its protective effects beyond the acute MGO paradigm. MNP-021 reduced Interleukine-6 (IL-6)/TNF-α release while increasing Interleukine-10 (IL-10) and Arginase 1 (ARG1) (~ 1.9-fold vs. LPS/TNF-α) in HMC3 glial cells, shifting them toward a pro-resolving IL-10/ARG1 program with reduced amyloid β-peptide 25-35 (Aβ(25-35))-evoked cytokine release and Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 (GLP-1) remaining very low (≤ 10 pg/mL) and not significantly increased in this system. CONCLUSIONS: MNP-021 coordinates transcriptomic restraint, transporter-level glucose handling, mitochondrial resilience, and pro-survival/pro-resolving signaling in neuron-microglia cell models. These findings support further preclinical evaluation of MNP-021 in dicarbonyl-linked neuro-metabolic stress and provide pharmacological evidence consistent with a TRPA1-linked component of its activity.

title: hucMSC-derived exosomes rescue cognitive impairment and Alzheimer-like pathology in APP/PS1 mice via metabolic remodeling.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder driven by β-amyloid (Aβ) deposition, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress and metabolic dysregulation, with the latter as a central pathological hub. hucMSC-derived exosomes (hucMSC-exosomes) show therapeutic potential for AD, but their metabolic remodeling mechanisms remain unclear. We combined behavioral tests, pathological assays and untargeted metabolomics to investigate the neuroprotective effects and mechanisms of hucMSC-exosomes in APP/PS1 AD mice. Seven-month-old male APP/PS1 mice were randomly divided into AD-vehicle and AD-hucMSC-exosome groups, with age-matched C57BL/6 mice as wild-type controls. All mice received tail vein injections for 6 weeks. Morris Water Maze tests revealed that hucMSC-exosomes significantly improved spatial learning and memory in AD mice. Pathological analyses confirmed that hucMSC-exosomes reduced cerebral Aβ deposition, suppressed hippocampal pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and restored antioxidant capacity (SOD, GPx, GSH/GSSG). Untargeted metabolomic analysis of brain tissues revealed that 6 primary carbon, 8 primary nitrogen and 3 secondary metabolites were common differential metabolites across the two comparison cohorts (AD-vehicle vs. WT, AD-hucMSC-exosome vs. AD-vehicle), and their aberrant expression in AD mice was all reversed by hucMSC-exosomes. KEGG enrichment analysis showed that hucMSC-exosomes largely reversed dysregulated metabolic pathways in AD, including lipid, amino acid, nucleotide metabolism and autophagy/mitophagy. Collectively, hucMSC-exosomes ameliorate AD pathological phenotypes and cognitive deficits, an effect accompanied by metabolic homeostasis remodeling through cascades of reduced Aβ deposition, suppressed neuroinflammation and alleviated oxidative stress. Metabolic remodeling represents a prominent correlative feature of the neuroprotective effects of hucMSC-exosomes, providing candidate molecular targets for metabolically targeted AD therapy.

title: Mitochondrial quality-control states in cadmium neurotoxicity: Adaptive clearance, disproportionate elimination and stalled flux.
abstract: Cadmium (Cd) is a persistent environmental toxicant associated with neurological injury, but the role of mitophagy remains unresolved because increased pathway markers may indicate protective clearance, broad mitochondrial selection or incomplete downstream degradation. This review evaluates mitochondrial quality-control checkpoints in Cd-exposed neural systems, focusing on PINK1-Parkin, BNIP3L/NIX and autophagy-lysosome completion, and examines intervention evidence from puerarin, daidzein and ginsenoside Rg1. Three states are proposed as a conceptual synthesis: adaptive clearance, candidate disproportionate mitochondrial elimination and initiated but stalled flux. Protective PINK1- and BNIP3L-dependent activity has loss-of-function support, whereas selection-pathway engagement accompanied by mitochondrial loss is consistent with, but does not establish, disproportionate elimination because degradation and replacement have not been measured together. Cd also disrupts trafficking, autophagosome-lysosome fusion, lysosomal integrity and proteolysis, providing stronger evidence for incomplete bulk autophagic processing than for mitochondria-specific stalled flux. Among the compounds examined, puerarin has the broadest checkpoint coverage, largely from related cortical studies, linking reduced Cd burden and mitochondrial stress with pool preservation and improved bulk autophagic processing. Evidence for daidzein remains marker-limited, whereas Rg1 protects neuronal and glial endpoints without an established Cd-specific mitochondrial quality-control mechanism. This narrative, non-systematic synthesis is limited by potential selection bias, reliance on static markers, dominance of acute or high-dose exposure models, limited measurement of mitochondria-specific degradation and replacement, inadequate cell-type resolution and scarce independent replication. Resolving these states requires mitochondria-specific flux reporters, direct degradation and replacement indices, causal pathway perturbation and matched Cd and compound exposure. Therapeutic benefit is more likely to arise from restoring selective, proportionate and completed mitochondrial turnover balanced by replacement than from uniformly activating or suppressing mitophagy.

title: TREM2/IGF-1 signaling axis-induced microglial senescence underlies benzo[a]pyrene-associated Parkinson's disease-like lesions.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder worldwide. Accumulating evidence has linked environmental polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), with benzo[a]pyrene (B[a]P) as a representative ubiquitous member, to elevated PD risk and disease pathogenesis. The present study aimed to investigate whether B[a]P can trigger typical PD-like lesions in mice, and further dissects the functional role of microglial senescence as well as its underlying regulatory mechanism, using complementary systems in vivo mouse model and in vitro BV2 microglia cell. Behavioral assessments revealed that B[a]P exposure induced significant, dose-dependent impairments in motor coordination and cognitive function compared with the control group. Moreover, the degree of functional impairments measured in the high-dose B[a]P group was comparable to that observed in the MPTP positive-control group. Following B[a]P treatment, brain-resident microglia cells exhibited signs of cell senescence, as evidenced by typical ultrastructural alterations, increased senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity, and elevated expression of the core senescence markers p16, p21, and p53 proteins. Consistent with these in vivo observations, B[a]P was confirmed to also induce cell cycle arrest in cultured BV2 microglia cells. This pro-senescent effect was significnatly attenuated by Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) overexpression, whereas it was markedly exacerbated following TREM2 knockout. Subsequent experiments further validated that insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), as a direct downstream effector regulated by TREM2, is functionally required for B[a]P-triggered microglial senescence. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that B[a]P exposure can induce PD-like lesions and microglial senescence, and which is primarily mediated via the TREM2/IGF-1 signaling axis.

title: Macamide B alleviates neuronal pyroptosis in spinal cord injury by activating acid ceramidase to inhibit lysosome membrane permeabilization.
abstract: Spinal cord injury is a devastating neurological disorder that causes severe and persistent functional deficits, for which effective pharmacological treatments remain limited. Acid ceramidase is a key lysosomal hydrolase involved in sphingolipid metabolism and has been implicated in cellular homeostasis and central nervous system disorders. However, its role in lysosomal membrane permeabilization and autophagic flux following spinal cord injury remains unclear. In this study, virtual screening identified macamide B as a potential activator of acid ceramidase, and its neuroprotective effects and underlying mechanisms were investigated in a mouse model of spinal cord injury. We found that macamide B treatment significantly reduced glial scar formation and motor neuron loss, thereby improving functional recovery after spinal cord injury. Moreover, macamide B suppressed neuronal pyroptosis and restored impaired autophagic flux associated with lysosomal membrane permeabilization. Mechanistically, macamide B activated acid ceramidase through the extracellular signal-regulated kinase/mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling pathway, thereby alleviating lysosomal membrane permeabilization and restoring autophagic flux, ultimately attenuating neuronal pyroptosis and neuronal loss. Collectively, these findings reveal an extracellular signal-regulated kinase/mitogen-activated protein kinase/acid ceramidase-mediated mechanism underlying the neuroprotective effects of macamide B after spinal cord injury and suggest that pharmacological activation of acid ceramidase may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for promoting neurological recovery following spinal cord injury.

title: Postsynaptic remodeling and F-actin dysregulation in the Dctn1Δ2-4 mouse model of motor neuron disease.
abstract: The microtubule motor dynein and its co-adaptor dynactin govern organelle positioning within highly polarized neurons. The dynactin subunit p150Glued, encoded by DCTN1, is associated with motor neuron disease. The p150Glued G59S mutation disrupts the microtubule-binding domain and drives selective motor neuron degeneration in patients and animal models. The p150Glued microtubule-binding domain mediates the initiation of retrograde transport at axonal terminals and stabilizes presynaptic sites at neuromuscular junctions. Nevertheless, the key functions of p150Glued and its microtubule-binding domain within postsynaptic compartments remain poorly defined. Using Dctn1Δ2-4 mice, in which exons 2-4 of Dctn1 encoding the microtubule-binding domain are deleted, we performed morphological, biochemical, and cellular physiological analyses, together with genetic manipulation and pharmacological intervention, to investigate how loss of p150Glued microtubule-binding function affects excitatory postsynaptic organization and neuronal vulnerability. We found that excitatory postsynaptic remodeling occurred before overt dendritic degeneration and motor neuron loss in Dctn1Δ2-4 mice. We further demonstrated that p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction induced early remodeling of excitatory postsynaptic densities, leading to increased postsynaptic accumulation of N-methyl- D-aspartate receptors, dysregulated Ca2+ homeostasis, and heightened susceptibility to glutamate-induced excitotoxicity. Mechanistically, p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction promoted the postsynaptic accumulation of endosomes and the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog complex, resulting in excessive F-actin assembly and pathological enhancement of postsynaptic density architecture. Furthermore, these postsynaptic abnormalities were rescued by re-expression of wild-type p150Glued, but not the disease-associated G59S mutant. Pharmacological inhibition of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors, in turn, attenuated excitotoxic injury and neurodegeneration. Our findings identify a previously unrecognized postsynaptic pathogenic mechanism in DCTN1-associated motor neuron disease. We propose that loss of p150Glued microtubule-binding function disrupts postsynaptic endosome positioning, leading to aberrant Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog-mediated F-actin remodeling, pathological enhancement of excitatory postsynaptic densities, excessive N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor targeting, and increased vulnerability to excitotoxicity.
authors: Zheng J, Yang X, Wang X, Cai H, Yu J
overview: The microtubule motor dynein and its co-adaptor dynactin govern organelle positioning within highly polarized neurons.

title: Digital twin control framework uncovers individualized cross-scale links between functional connectivity deviations, communication impairment, and molecular mechanisms in autism.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is hallmarked by pronounced inter-individual heterogeneity in brain function and clinical manifestations. Conventional neuroimaging studies yield highly inconsistent findings, as extrinsic confounding factors and intrinsic disease heterogeneity mask ASD-specific functional connectivity (FC) signatures, hampering the identification of individualized neural mechanisms linked to symptom severity. METHODS: We developed a digital twin control analytical framework based on deep contrastive learning. By comparing each ASD participant with their matched digital twin control, we quantified individual-specific FC deviations. Principal component analysis was applied to extract the core aberrant pattern, followed by multi-dimensional analyzes and validation including clinical correlation, transcriptomic decoding, neurotransmitter and mitochondrial co-localization, as well as disease and cognitive enrichment. RESULTS: The model effectively disentangled disease‑related from non‑disease‑related variations. The identified dominant aberrant FC pattern was significantly associated with Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) communication scores, suggesting it is associated with to communication impairment. This pattern showed convergent associations with synaptic pathways, excitatory/inhibitory neuronal signatures, critical developmental windows and subcortical structures, and exhibited negative spatial association with multiple neurotransmitter systems and mitochondrial respiratory complexes. Biological validation further supported its ASD specificity and communication‑related cognitive relevance. CONCLUSIONS: Leveraging the twin control analytical framework, this study provides an exploratory cross-scale framework linking individualized FC deviations with clinical, transcriptomic, neurochemical, and mitochondrial maps. The findings indicate that communication difficulties in ASD may partly arise from multi-scale disturbances in neural integration, social-perceptual processing and activity-dependent cellular energy regulation.
authors: Liu G, Qiu J
overview: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is hallmarked by pronounced inter-individual heterogeneity in brain function and clinical manifestations.

title: Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6)-mediated α-tubulin (K40) deacetylation and microtubule destabilization disrupt autophagosome-lysosome fusion in PBDE-47-induced neurotoxicity.
abstract: 2,2',4,4'-tetrabromodiphenyl ether (PBDE-47) is a pervasive environmental brominated flame retardant that accumulates in nervous tissues and induces persistent neurotoxicity. Emerging evidence indicates that PBDE-47 perturbs neuronal autophagy, yet the definitive upstream molecular mechanism remains uncharacterized, hindering the development of effective protective strategies. This study was performed to clarify the toxic regulatory cascade and explore feasible pharmacological interventions using in vivo neonatal rat hippocampal tissue and in vitro PC12 neuronal cell models. Animals were neonatally exposed to PBDE-47 (0.1, 1.0, 10.0 mg/kg·bw), and PC12 cells were treated with PBDE-47 (1, 10, 20 µM) for mechanistic exploration. Results showed that PBDE-47 dose-dependently upregulated histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), decreased α-tubulin (K40) acetylation, and destabilized neuronal microtubules. Such microtubule structural damage impaired autophagosome retrograde trafficking, blocked autophagosome-lysosome fusion, and eventually caused neuronal loss, synaptic protein reduction, and cognitive impairment. For mechanism validation and rescue experiments, 1 mg/kg·bw paclitaxel (PTX) and 1 mg/kg·bw tubastatin A (TBA) were administered to neonatal rats, whereas 12.5 nmol/L PTX and 10 µmol/L TBA were used for PC12 cell treatment to stabilize microtubules and selectively inhibit HDAC6, respectively. Both pharmacological interventions effectively restored tubulin acetylation, rescued defective autophagic flux, and mitigated PBDE-47-induced neuronal injury, with TBA showing better applicability due to its high blood-brain barrier permeability and biosafety. Behavioral tests in vivo verified that PTX and TBA treatment significantly ameliorated PBDE-47-elicited learning and memory deficits. Collectively, these findings define the HDAC6/microtubule acetylation axis as a core upstream pathway responsible for PBDE-47-triggered autophagic transport failure and neurotoxicity, providing robust experimental evidence and a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of PBDEs-mediated neurological disorders.
authors: Tang H, Hou H, Tian Z, Liu W, Chen G, Li D, Wang C, Liu R, Wang D, Xia T

main: Results showed that PBDE-47 dose-dependently upregulated histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), decreased α-tubulin (K40) acetylation, and destabilized neuronal microtubules.

title: Xanthohumol promotes cognitive function-associated neuroprotein changes in two mouse models of Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder that progressively impairs cognitive function for which there is no effective treatment. Natural dietary compounds such as xanthohumol (Xn) potentially offer a new therapeutic approach in AD. We aim to employ quantitative proteomic techniques to investigate the effects of Xn on cognitive impairment in two established murine models of AD. Treatment with 0.5 mg/kg Xn significantly improved the ability of stimulating learning and memory and cognitive function of 3 ×Tg AD mice while 5 mg/kg Xn ameliorated cognitive decline in APP/PS1 mice. We identified two common differential proteins and 12 pathways in the hippocampi of 3 ×Tg AD mice and 70 common differential proteins and 22 pathways in APP/PS1 mice. Moreover, Nine common signaling pathways mainly involved in energy metabolism, neurodegenerative disease, cardiovascular disease and cancer. So multi high-throughput proteomic analyses of hippocampus add to the scientific basis for development of effective drugs for AD, one candidate of which is Xn.

title: 53BP1 as a cofactor in the activation of the p53-family transcriptional program: A correlative multimodal microscopy approach.
abstract: Understanding how molecular mechanisms regulate cell function in tissues requires approaches that link phenotypes to mechanisms across different spatial scales. Here, we present automated multimodal multiplexed microscopy for image cytometry (A.M3.I.CO), a correlative imaging platform that combines multiscale resolution, from millimeters to nanometers, with automated workflows for high-throughput phenotypic profiling and targeted single-molecule analysis in situ. Applying A.M3.I.CO, we observed that 53BP1 is recruited at transcribed p53 target genes independently of the activating stimulus, providing evidence for the formation of a putative complex between 53BP1, p53, and the basal transcription machinery in single cells, as also supported by in vivo observations in tumor models. Extending our measurements to p63 and p73, we found that 53BP1 localized at p63- and p73-targeted transcription sites, suggesting a broader role in participating in p53 family-dependent transcription. These findings indicate an additional genome-surveillance pathway in transcriptional control regulating diverse cellular functions while establishing A.M3.I.CO as a platform for spatially resolved functional analysis.

title: Chronic thoracic aortitis versus primary medial degeneration in ascending aorta: a digital morphometric analysis of aortic layers remodelling.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Chronic aortitis (CA) represents a diverse group of inflammatory conditions often diagnosed incidentally in ascending aorta biopsies. While the 2015 and 2016 Consensus Statements on the surgical pathology of the aorta provide standardised histological classifications, data quantifying structural remodelling within individual aortic layers remain limited. Furthermore, distinguishing CA from primary non-inflammatory medial degeneration (MD) can be challenging, particularly when inflammation is sparse or burnt out, and secondary degenerative changes predominate. We aimed to compare morphological changes in CA and MD aneurysms and apply digital image analysis to quantify aortic wall layers. METHODS: Retrospective histological analysis was performed on 63 ascending aortic specimens: CA (n=21), MD (n=21), and autopsy controls (n=21). Digitised elastic-stained sections were analysed using QuPath software to measure the thickness and cross-sectional area of the intima (I), media (M), and adventitia (A). Overall MD scores (i.e., summaries of each MD grade component) were evaluated. Diagnostic performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis based on binary logistic regression models. RESULTS: CA demonstrated a profound architectural shift, characterised by medial thinning alongside marked intimal and adventitial expansion, resulting in significantly lower M/(I+A) thickness and area ratios compared with MD and controls (p <0.001). CA specimens also exhibited the most severe secondary degenerative changes, with significantly higher overall MD scores (median: 15 vs. 8; p < 0.001). ROC curve analysis revealed diagnostic utility of both the M/(I+A) thickness ratio (AUC = 0.964) and the M/(I+A) area ratio (AUC = 0.955) for identifying CA. A multivariable model combining the overall MD score with the M/(I+A) thickness ratio achieved an AUC of 0.971 (accuracy 88.1%), whereas combining it with the M/(I+A) area ratio yielded an AUC of 0.968 (accuracy 90.5%). CONCLUSION: Digital morphometric analysis provides a reproducible and feasible method for quantifying structural remodelling in chronic aortitis. Changes in the proportions of the aortic layers, specifically intimal and adventitial expansion combined with medial thinning and severe secondary medial degeneration, can facilitate accurate differentiation of aortic wall pathologies, particularly in cases with sparse inflammation.
journal: Cardiovascular pathology : the official journal of the Society for Cardiovascular Pathology
authors: Vasova B, Sokolova T, Hrnciarova L, Karalko M, Stejskal V
overview: INTRODUCTION: Chronic aortitis (CA) represents a diverse group of inflammatory conditions often diagnosed incidentally in ascending aorta biopsies.
main: Diagnostic performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis based on binary logistic regression models.

title: Protective role of Galectin-3 in prion disease through regulation of microglial PrPSc uptake.
abstract: Microglia constitute a major innate defense mechanism against prion infection; however, the molecular pathways regulating microglial responses during disease progression remain incompletely understood. Galectin-3 (Gal3), a β-galactoside-binding lectin associated with reactive microglia in multiple neurodegenerative disorders, has been implicated in phagocytosis, inflammatory signaling, and lysosomal homeostasis. Here, we investigated the role of Gal3 in prion disease pathogenesis using prion-infected mice. Gal3 expression was undetectable in healthy brain but became upregulated beginning at late preclinical stages, increasing with disease progression. Gal3 localized predominantly to a subpopulation of reactive IBA1-positive microglia, particularly within the thalamus, and inversely correlated with expression of the homeostatic microglial markers P2Y12 and TMEM119, consistent with acquisition of a reactive phenotype. Microglia engaged in neuronal envelopment displayed elevated Gal3 expression during terminal disease. Constitutive deletion of Gal3 significantly accelerated clinical disease progression without altering total PrPSc accumulation, reactive gliosis, neuronal envelopment, or overall microglial and astrocytic activation. However, Gal3 deficiency markedly reduced microglial uptake of PrPSc, resulting in a lower intracellular-to-extracellular PrPSc ratio, supporting a role for Gal3 in phagocytic sequestration of prions. In contrast, Gal3 deficiency did not impair lysosomal activity, lysosomal membrane integrity, or expression of genes involved in lysosomal repair pathways. Likewise, selective inhibition of autophagy in myeloid cells exerted only minor effects on disease progression. Collectively, these findings identify Gal3 as a sensitive marker of reactive microglia that contributes to microglial uptake of PrPSc and exerts a protective role during prion disease progression.

title: Pathogenesis and therapeutic targets of neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease mediated by microglia lysosomal dysfunction.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by two core pathological features: senile plaques formed by amyloid-β protein (Aβ) deposits and neurofibrillary tangles formed by hyperphosphorylated tau protein. In recent years, neuroinflammation has been recognized as a key driver in the pathogenesis of AD, and microglia, as innate immune cells of the central nervous system, play a central role in regulating the onset and progression of neuroinflammation. Lysosomes are key organelles within microglia responsible for degrading pathological proteins and regulating inflammatory signaling; dysfunction of lysosomes in microglia severely impairs their ability to clear Aβ, damaged proteins, and cellular debris, thereby promoting inflammatory responses. This manuscript summarizes upstream mechanisms that may influence microglial lysosomal dysfunction from four perspectives: pathological proteins, genetic factors, lipid metabolism disorders, and proinflammatory cytokines. Pathological proteins can impair lysosomal acidification and biogenesis by interfering with key pathways such as the TFEB-v-ATPase axis; various genetic factors exacerbate functional dysregulation by influencing the expression of lysosome-related genes and lipid metabolism; lipid metabolism disorders promote lysosomal membrane permeabilization, block the autophagy cascade and activate the inflammasome; proinflammatory cytokines can exert varying effects on the clearance of pathological substrates and by regulating lysosomal function. The aforementioned factors can influence microglial lysosomal function through various mechanisms, thereby contributing to impaired clearance of pathological substrates and the onset and progression of neuroinflammation. Intervention strategies targeting microglial lysosomal dysfunction, including enhancing lysosomal degradation capacity, regulating autophagy related pathways, correcting cellular metabolic dysregulation and suppressing excessive neuroinflammation, may offer new avenues for AD treatment.

overview: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by two core pathological features: senile plaques formed by amyloid-β protein (Aβ) deposits and neurofibrillary tangles formed by hyperphosphorylated tau protein.

title: The N-Ank protein Ankrd24 shapes neurons and couples to syndapin and the F-actin promoter Cobl-like.
abstract: Proper neuromorphogenesis is pivotal for neuronal network formation and brain function. The underlying cell biological tasks are complex, as they include both remodeling of membrane topologies and of cytoskeletal structures. Yet, mechanisms coordinating these two different cell biological functions are largely unknown. Here, we molecularly and functionally characterize ankyrin repeat domain-containing protein 24 (Ankrd24) and demonstrate that this ankyrin-repeat protein is able to interact with and bend membranes and mechanistically and functionally belongs to the recently proposed N-Ank superfamily. Mutational analyses revealed that the N-Ank functions of Ankrd24 are indispensable for Ankrd24's role in neuromorphogenesis. Ankrd24 furthermore physically cooperated with the F-BAR domain protein syndapin I (PACSIN1) and with Cobl-like (Cobll1), a protein promoting actin filament formation, by ternary complex formation. Both partners were critical for Ankrd24-mediated dendritic arborization. This identified Ankrd24 as critical part of a larger, coordinated effort in inducing new dendritic branches. Our work thereby sheds light on the molecular mechanisms underlying the complex task of proper neuronal arbor development.

title: Cross-species molecular mapping of the photoreceptor sensory cilium and periciliary structures identifies conserved and species-specific architectural features.
abstract: Photoreceptor sensory cilia comprise a microtubule-based structural core and the phototransductive outer segment. The microtubule-based ciliary axoneme extends from the basal body through the connecting cilium into the outer segment, thereby linking the inner and outer segments. Around this central axis, specialized periciliary structures are distributed across the apical inner segment and basal outer segment. Yet how these ciliary and periciliary structures differ between rods and cones and across mammals remains incompletely defined. Using ultrastructure expansion microscopy, we compared their nanoscale molecular organization across canine, non-human primate and human retinas. Key rod-cone differences in ciliary organization were broadly conserved among all three species, whereas the scale and morphology of individual ciliary subcompartments differed between species. Periciliary structures showed even greater species-specific diversification, particularly in rods. Human photoreceptors shared several structural features with non-human primate photoreceptors but also displayed inter-individual variability in accessory inner segment-like structure. These findings refine current understanding of photoreceptor sensory cilia and associated periciliary structures in large mammals, revealing that conserved rod-cone differences co-exist with pronounced species-specific structural and molecular specializations.

title: A fibril-selective single-domain antibody targets pathogenic amyloid-β assemblies and protects human neurons.
abstract: Alzheimer disease is characterized by extracellular amyloid-β deposition that contributes to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration. Although anti-amyloid-β antibodies reduce plaque burden, their use requires monitoring for amyloid-related imaging abnormalities. Here, phage display against immobilized Aβ40 fibrils representing a patient-relevant polymorph identified J8, a fibril-selective, Fc-free single-domain antibody. J8 bound fibrils with high apparent affinity, showed no detectable binding to monomeric Aβ40, decorated fibril surfaces, and recognized plaque-associated amyloid in Alzheimer disease brain tissue. During concurrent fibril exposure, J8 reduced apoptotic signaling in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cortical neurons and forebrain organoids. Single-nucleus profiling of pooled organoids identified fibril-associated stress programs and opposite-direction expression patterns in the FibJ8 condition; fibril-associated changes showed the strongest directional concordance with advanced disease pathology. These findings identify J8 as a fibril-selective candidate and support organoid-based evaluation of anti-amyloid reagents as a fit-for-purpose preclinical tool.
authors: Greenlee MA, Amniouel S, Rivera I, Suh J, Martinez NJ, Simeonov A, Head E, Tycko R, Zheng W, Fleming BD

title: Combined γ-oryzanol and α-lipoic acid treatment suppresses inflammation and apoptosis in hSOD1G93A models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis via the AKT/GSK3β pathway.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease with complex pathogenic mechanisms, and the efficacy of single-target interventions remains limited. γ-Oryzanol (Orz) and α-lipoic acid (ALA) exert neuroprotective effects individually, yet their combined effects and molecular mechanisms in ALS remain unclear. AIM: To investigate the therapeutic effects and mechanisms of combined Orz and ALA treatment in ALS. METHODS: Network pharmacology was used to identify potential targets shared by the compounds and ALS. Core targets and pathways were identified through protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis, molecular docking, and functional enrichment analysis, followed by experimental validation in hSOD1G93A cell and transgenic mouse models. RESULTS: Six core targets (EGFR, AKT1, HSP90AA1, BCL2, SRC, HSP90AB1) were identified. In hSOD1G93A cells, combined treatment modulated mRNA expression and protein phosphorylation of the core targets and attenuated cellular injury. In hSOD1G93A transgenic mice, the combination delayed disease progression, prolonged survival, improved motor function, and reduced motor neuron loss. This combination alleviated inflammation and apoptosis by activating the AKT/GSK3β pathway. CONCLUSION: Combined Orz and ALA treatment modulates core targets, activates the AKT/GSK3β pathway, and suppresses inflammation and apoptosis. This combination represents a promising therapeutic strategy for ALS.
authors: Han L, Hou J, Zhang D, Zhang W, Wang D, Huo D, Su X, Tan X, Wang M, Xu J
overview: BACKGROUND: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease with complex pathogenic mechanisms, and the efficacy of single-target interventions remains limited.
main: RESULTS: Six core targets (EGFR, AKT1, HSP90AA1, BCL2, SRC, HSP90AB1) were identified.

title: Elastin-derived peptide VGVAPG induces redox-associated pro-inflammatory activation and early disease-associated microglia (DAM) molecular profile in a human microglia-neuron in vitro model involving NEU1/TLR4-related signaling.
abstract: The elastin-derived hexapeptide Val-Gly-Val-Ala-Pro-Gly (VGVAPG) exhibits well-documented biological activityHowever, its role in brain inflammation remains insufficiently characterized. This is an important issue, as VGVAPG levels increase with age and have been implicated in processes contributing to neurodegeneration. The present study aimed to evaluate the ability of aging-related VGVAPG to activate human microglial (HMC3) cells in vitro and to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms. Our results demonstrated no cytotoxic effect of VGVAPG. However, further analyses revealed NF-κB nuclear translocation, elevated ROS and •NO production, enhanced iNOS, and accumulation of NLRP3-containing vesicles in the cytoplasm, consistent with the peptide's pro-inflammatory potential. Additionally, activation of stress- and inflammation-related signaling pathways involving p38-MAPK, JNKs, and ERK1/2 was observed, accompanied by upregulation of NFKB1, IL1B, and TNFα mRNA. Using a transwell co-culture model of HMC3 and cholinergic-like neurons (differentiated SH-SY5Y), we observed potential DAMP-associated molecular changes involving HMGB1 and APP. Additionally, NEU1 siRNA-mediated knockdown in HMC3 cells, together with the observed NEU1/TLR4 colocalization, raises the possibility that NEU1 and TLR4 may be involved in the effects induced by VGVAPG. Moreover, VGVAPG induced alterations in early disease-associated microglia (DAM)-related protein profiles, including β2M, ITGAX, and ICAM1. Collectively, these findings identify VGVAPG as a candidate pro-neuroinflammatory matrikine in vitro and provide associative evidence for selected redox, NEU1-, TLR4-related, and early DAM-associated molecular changes. Further investigations employing advanced in vivo and translational models are warranted to validate these observations and to clarify the pathophysiological role of VGVAPG in the progression of neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Protocol for imaging and analyzing the synaptic coverage of astrocytes with super-resolution STED microscopy in mouse brain slices.
abstract: Super-resolution has allowed us to image areas previously inaccessible due to the limits of standard microscopy techniques. Here, we present a protocol to determine the astroglial coverage of synapses. We detail the steps to obtain and label mouse brain slices followed by imaging using 3D stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy and analysis using a custom-made Fiji plug-in, with imaging at a lateral resolution of 80 nm. This technique ascertains the interaction between astrocytes and the glial cell's role in signaling and brain region function.
authors: Waldron L, Garnero M, Mazaud D, Rouach N
overview: Super-resolution has allowed us to image areas previously inaccessible due to the limits of standard microscopy techniques.

title: Research Progress of Low-Intensity Pulsed Ultrasound in Parkinson's Disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder where current pharmacological and surgical interventions, including Deep Brain Stimulation, often fail to reverse neuronal degeneration or halt disease progression. Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) has emerged as a novel, non-invasive neuromodulation technology with significant therapeutic potential. This review synthesizes current research on the key acoustic parameters, biological mechanisms, and clinical applications of LIPUS in PD. Unlike High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU), which relies on thermal ablation to destroy target nuclei (e.g., Vim, STN), LIPUS utilizes low-energy mechanical waves (typically <3 W/cm²) to exert non-thermal regulatory effects without damaging tissue. Mechanisms of action include the modulation of mechanosensitive ion channels (e.g., Piezo1), enhancement of neuroplasticity via brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), promotion of autophagy, and regulation of microglial phenotypes to reduce neuroinflammation. We further compare LIPUS with HIFU, highlighting the superiority of LIPUS regarding safety, reversibility, and the absence of requirement for MRI-based thermal monitoring. While preliminary clinical studies using wearable LIPUS devices indicate improvements in motor and cognitive functions, a unified consensus on optimal stimulation parameters and targeting strategies is lacking. Future research should focus on large-scale, standardized clinical trials to establish precise protocols for LIPUS as a disease-modifying therapy for PD.

title: Preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal cord D2R expression via the PP2A/AKT-dependent NMDA receptor phosphorylation.
abstract: Preoperative sleep deprivation (SD) is known to exacerbate postoperative pain, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Using a male mouse model of 48-h continuous SD followed by incisional surgery, we found that SD alone induced transient mechanical hyperalgesia, and when combined with surgery (SI group) it significantly aggravated and prolonged postoperative pain recovery until day 10. On postoperative day 7, SI mice showed marked downregulation of spinal dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) expression and decreased spinal dopamine concentration. D2R was predominantly expressed on spinal glutamatergic neurons. Overexpression of D2R on these neurons via intrathecal AAV injection effectively alleviated the prolonged hyperalgesia, normalizing pain sensitivity by day 7. Mechanistically, D2R downregulation led to increased phosphorylation of NMDA receptor subunits (p-NR1 and p-NR2B) without altering total NMDA receptor levels. Co-immunoprecipitation revealed an interaction between D2R and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A). SI mice exhibited decreased PP2A expression but increased p-AKT, p-GSK3β, and β-catenin, indicating activation of the PP2A/AKT signaling pathway, which were reversed by D2R overexpression. Furthermore, pharmacological activation of PP2A with DT-061 not only downregulated p-AKT, p-GSK3β, β-catenin, p-NR1 and p-NR2B, but also produced significant analgesia in SI mice. Collectively, these results demonstrate that preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal D2R on glutamatergic neurons, which disinhibits the PP2A/AKT pathway and enhances NMDA receptor phosphorylation. Targeting D2R or its downstream PP2A/AKT signaling may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for managing persistent postoperative pain caused by preoperative sleep deprivation in male mice.

title: Cucurbituril-modulated NIR emission and two-photon mitochondrial imaging of an acridine derivative.
abstract: Host-guest assemblies of an acridine dye with cucurbit[7]uril and cucurbit[8]uril give distinct NIR emissions at 674 and 708 nm, respectively. Both exhibit efficient two-photon absorption near 925 nm and successfully enable single- and two-photon mitochondrial imaging in live A549 cells.
authors: Lin X, Wu J, Shen FF, Duan LT, Wang S, Zhang ZL, Chen KH, Yu HJ, Song R
overview: Host-guest assemblies of an acridine dye with cucurbit[7]uril and cucurbit[8]uril give distinct NIR emissions at 674 and 708 nm, respectively.
main: Both exhibit efficient two-photon absorption near 925 nm and successfully enable single- and two-photon mitochondrial imaging in live A549 cells.

title: QuRad: Radiomics Feature Extraction for QuPath.
abstract: Radiomic features provide a quantitative description of tissue organization in histopathology images. QuPath, a widely used open-source platform for whole-slide image analysis, offers morphology, intensity, and Haralick texture measurements but no standardized radiomic feature set such as that of PyRadiomics. Researchers must therefore export data to external Python pipelines, interrupting their QuPath workflow. QuRad extracts radiomic features from cell detections and annotation regions directly inside QuPath. The extension and equivalent Groovy script implement 119 features: 103 two-dimensional features enabled by default and 16 optional legacy shape descriptors. We compared QuRad 0.4 with PyRadiomics 3.0.1 on identical grayscale images and pixel masks. All 103 default features met a 10-9 absolute-or-relative agreement tolerance on a breast-cancer benchmark tile (410 cells). On 20 melanoma tiles (8,644 nuclei), 97 of 103 features met this tolerance and 6 polygon-derived shape features differed from PyRadiomics' raster-derived mesh (minimum concordance correlation coefficient 0.942). The 22 synthetic regions accepted by PyRadiomics reproduced the expected intensity and texture values. A single-threaded server benchmark reached about 1,900 nuclei per second, and processing the 184,242 cells of a whole-slide image took 2.7 min on a laptop. A random forest distinguished tumor cells from lymphocytes in melanoma (pooled macro-F1 0.853) and classified 197 tissue regions of 6 breast-cancer slides into 3 compartments (0.696). QuRad exports the features with object coordinates and extraction settings for use in QuPath or downstream analyses.

title: TMEM175: lysosomal ion channel physiology, therapeutic potential, and emerging pharmacology.
abstract: Transmembrane protein 175 (TMEM175) is a lysosomal cation channel that has emerged as a promising drug target for Parkinson's disease (PD). Genetic and functional studies linking TMEM175 loss-of-function variants to increased PD risk, lysosomal dysfunction, and α-synuclein accumulation have generated considerable interest in developing pharmacological approaches to enhance channel activity. As a lysosomal cation channel with reported K+ and H+ permeability, TMEM175 regulates lysosomal membrane potential, pH stability, autophagic flux, and degradative capacity, placing it at a critical control point for cellular proteostasis. Recent advances in high-throughput screening, automated and lysosomal patch clamp electrophysiology, cryoelectron microscopy, and structure-guided medicinal chemistry have transformed TMEM175 from a relatively obscure lysosomal ion channel into a tractable drug target. These approaches have enabled the discovery of multiple classes of TMEM175 modulators while providing new insights into channel gating and mechanisms of activation. In this review, we summarize current progress in TMEM175 pharmacology, including advances in functional assay development and the emerging landscape of tool compounds used to study channel function. We discuss TMEM175 physiology and structure-function relationships, the growing evidence supporting therapeutic intervention, and recent discoveries revealing multiple mechanisms of channel activation. Finally, we highlight key challenges that remain for the field, including the development of potent and selective modulators, opportunities afforded by synergistic channel activation, and the potential application of TMEM175-directed therapeutics beyond Parkinson's disease in a broader range of neurodegenerative and lysosome-associated disorders.

title: A seamless workflow for STXM-NEXAFS data analysis using napari: implementation of an ROI spectrum extraction function.
abstract: Scanning transmission soft X-ray microscopy (STXM), combined with near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure (NEXAFS), enables the mapping of elemental distributions and chemical properties at a spatial resolution of tens of nanometers. A common approach for analyzing STXM data is to compare NEXAFS spectra obtained from regions of interest (ROIs). However, ROI-based spectral comparison typically requires frequent switching among multiple software applications. ROI spectrum extraction, spectrum normalization, and figure creation are often performed using separate applications, which increase analytical time and the likelihood of errors.•We developed a Python-based workflow for STXM-NEXAFS data analysis that implements functions for extracting mean ROI spectra in napari, an open-source multidimensional image viewer.•These napari-based functions provide a seamless workflow from ROI selection to figure preparation within Python, without switching between multiple software applications.•The seamless workflow improves analytical efficiency and facilitates broader use of STXM-NEXAFS analysis.

title: Six3 promoting the migration and neural differentiation of BMSCs via Btg2‑mediated Akt signaling pathway activation: A therapeutic strategy for stroke.
abstract: Bone marrow‑derived mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC) transplantation holds therapeutic potential for stroke; however, but its effectiveness requires optimization. The transcription factor Sine Oculis Homeobox Homolog 3 (Six3) regulates processes crucial for BMSC therapy, such as neural cell proliferation and differentiation. However, whether Six3‑modified BMSCs exert enhanced therapeutic effects on stroke remains unknown. In the present study, mouse BMSCs were isolated and identified using surface markers. Six3‑overexpressing BMSCs exhibited enhanced proliferative, migratory and neural differentiation capacities. RNA‑sequencing analysis comparing the gene expression profiles of BMSCs with and without Six3 overexpression identified BTG Anti‑Proliferation Factor 2 (Btg2) as an upregulated gene (log2FC=1.45, P<0.05) in Six3‑overexpressing cells. Further investigations revealed that Six3 directly binds to the TGATACTGTCT sequence within the Btg2 promoter and activates its transcription. Btg2 knockdown abolished the effects of Six3 overexpression. Mechanistically, Six3 promoted Akt phosphorylation via Btg2, enhancing BMSC viability and neural differentiation. A mouse model of stroke was established using transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO, 1.5‑h occlusion and 24‑h reperfusion). BMSCs were administered via tail vein injection at the onset of reperfusion. GFP expression detected in brain tissue at 24 h post‑reperfusion confirmed successful the homing of BMSCs to the brain. The transplantation of Six3‑overexpressing BMSCs ameliorated brain pathology, reducing apoptosis and cerebral infarct volume. Notably, Six3‑modified BMSCs demonstrated a significantly greater therapeutic efficacy than unmodified BMSCs. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that Six3 enhances the therapeutic properties of BMSCs by transcriptionally activating Btg2, which promotes Akt phosphorylation. These findings provide novel mechanistic insight into the optimization of stem cell therapy in stroke.
authors: Fu Z, Li Z, Zhang L, Hu W, Yang H, Wang J
overview: Bone marrow‑derived mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC) transplantation holds therapeutic potential for stroke; however, but its effectiveness requires optimization.
main: The transcription factor Sine Oculis Homeobox Homolog 3 (Six3) regulates processes crucial for BMSC therapy, such as neural cell proliferation and differentiation.

title: Extended field-of-view two-photon imaging in the deep brain of freely behaving mice using lightweight microfabricated corrective optics.
abstract: Investigating neural circuits underlying complex behavior requires high-resolution imaging of large neuronal populations during naturalistic conditions. Miniaturized two-photon microscopes (MINI2Ps) enable deep brain imaging in freely moving animals when coupled with gradient index (GRIN)-based microendoscopes. However, intrinsic optical aberrations in GRIN-based microendoscopes degrade spatial resolution and limit the effective field-of-view (FOV). Here, we address these limitations using lightweight microfabricated optics to correct GRIN aberrations during deep brain MINI2P imaging. The aberration corrected system demonstrated improved and more homogeneous axial resolution across the FOV, resulting in more than fourfold increase in effective FOV. We applied the corrected system to the ventral posteromedial thalamus in freely moving mice and performed optical mapping of head direction (HD) tuned cells. These measurements revealed the absence of spatial clustering of HD preference, suggesting spatially sparse HD coding in sensory thalamus. Combining the MINI2P with aberration corrected GRIN-based microendoscopes is a powerful approach for large-scale and high-resolution functional imaging of deep brain circuits during naturalistic behavior.

overview: Investigating neural circuits underlying complex behavior requires high-resolution imaging of large neuronal populations during naturalistic conditions.
main: These measurements revealed the absence of spatial clustering of HD preference, suggesting spatially sparse HD coding in sensory thalamus.

title: Unraveling the Genotype-Phenotype Landscape of Kleefstra Syndrome Through EHMT1 Variant Analysis.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Kleefstra syndrome type 1 (KLEFS1) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by pathogenic variants in EHMT1, which play a key role in epigenetic regulation. Core features include global developmental delay (GDD), intellectual disability (ID), facial dysmorphism, congenital heart defects (CHDs), and neuropsychiatric manifestations. METHODS: This retrospective study included patients with KLEFS1 evaluated at Seoul National University Hospital between January 2022 and April 2025. Genetic diagnoses were made using chromosomal microarray or whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, and clinical data were extracted from medical records. To enhance statistical power, we conducted a joint analysis with established cohorts of at least 30 clinically characterized patients. RESULTS: Among the 15 patients with KLEFS1, 14 (93.3%) exhibited GDD or ID, with frequent comorbidities such as CHDs (8/12, 66.7%), orthopaedic manifestations (6/12, 50.0%), epilepsy (6/15, 40.0%), and sleep problems (4/11, 36.4%). Brain MRI revealed abnormalities in 10 of the 12 patients (83.3%), including pituitary anomalies in 2 (16.7%). By combining our data with recently published multicenter international cohorts, we assessed genotype-phenotype correlations by comparing the clinical features of 202 patients with different variant subtypes. Patients with multigene deletions had a significantly higher prevalence of CHDs (53.5% vs 25.8%, p value = 2 × 10-4), cortical visual impairment (12.5% vs 1.7%, p value = 0.004), microcephaly (37.1% vs 17.8%, p value = 0.009), corpus callosum abnormalities (17.9% vs 5.9%, p value = 0.02), and hearing impairment (39.7% vs 25.6%, p value = 0.04) than those with single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) or short insertions/deletions (indels), in addition to the previously identified features including epilepsy, constipation, and short stature. We also observed that a recurrent EHMT1 variant (p.Arg948Trp), identified in multiple unrelated patients, was linked to significant phenotypic heterogeneity, including late-onset neurocognitive regression. DISCUSSION: Our study showed that patients with multigene deletions are significantly more likely to exhibit multiorgan involvement, including CHDs, cortical visual impairments, microcephaly, corpus callosum abnormalities, and hearing impairments, compared with those with SNVs or indels, emphasizing the importance of genotype-informed management. We report pituitary gland abnormalities in KLEFS1, expanding the phenotypic and neuroimaging spectrum of KLEFS1. The patient showing regression in their 30s necessitates long-term, comprehensive studies to support care.

title: Female iPSC X chromosome inactivation erosion and its transcriptomic effects during CRISPR gene editing and neural differentiation.
abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), together with CRISPR editing, are commonly used for studying neurodevelopmental disorders. Female iPSCs gradually lose the expression of the noncoding X chromosome inactive-specific transcript (XIST), leading to random X chromosome inactivation (XCI) erosion that affects both X-linked and autosomal gene expression. However, the effects of CRISPR editing and neural differentiation on XCI erosion and how this may confound a real-world analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) are poorly understood. Here, we analyzed hundreds of RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) samples of CRISPR-edited iPSC lines for 66 genes and the matched single-neuron RNA-seq data. We found variable XCI in CRISPR-edited female iPSCs, which was largely preserved in iPSC-derived neurons and predominantly influenced X-linked genes. Mechanistically, XIST mediates allele-specific epigenetic regulation of both X-linked and autosomal genes, with the former showing stronger allele-specific expression (ASE) bias that affects neurodevelopmental genes. These results have significant implications in hiPSC-based modeling of neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Multi-region transcriptomics and unsupervised clustering reveal recurrent and region-specific gene signatures in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits anatomically heterogeneous transcriptomic alterations, complicating the identification of disease-associated genes with consistent external support. We compared four gene-prioritization strategies, absolute log₂ fold change, false discovery rate (FDR), CombinedScore, and RankSum, using laser-capture-microdissected neuronal expression profiles from six brain regions in GSE5281. Differential expression was assessed separately within each region using limma, followed by within-region gene prioritization and cross-region comparison to identify recurrent and anatomically specific candidates. Robustness was evaluated through resampling stability, sensitivity to candidate-list size and scoring formulation, and external benchmarking in three anatomically matched regions of GSE48350. STAT4, SST, and NVL emerged as recurrent candidates, whereas ZNRD2, ANKRD12, and NME7 were prominent regionally prioritized signals. External directional agreement across Top-100 lists ranged from 68.3% to 72.0%; RankSum achieved 71.7% agreement and the highest or joint-highest directional agreement at Top-50 and Top-200. A fixed expression score comprising the three recurrent genes showed higher values in AD in the external cohort. Exploratory six-gene clustering revealed diagnosis-associated structure with modest separation. 14 of 18 gene-region comparisons showed concordant AD-control directions, although cross-dataset effect-size correlations were weak. This study establishes a comparative framework linking regional gene prioritization with stability assessment and independent-cohort benchmarking, identifying recurrent AD-associated candidates and quantifying their external support.

title: Mitochondrial apoptosis imaged by high-throughput confocal microscopy.
abstract: Mitochondrial programmed cell death (i.e. intrinsic apoptosis) is regulated through the formation of pro-apoptotic protein complexes at the mitochondrial outer membrane (MOM), which permeabilize the MOM and commit the cell to die. This step is modulated by mitochondrial dynamics. To capture this, we treated cells with the mitochondrial dynamics inhibitor M1 before inducing apoptosis with actinomycin D (ActD), and imaged them by high-throughput spinning-disk confocal microscopy. In mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) we followed apoptosis by long-term live-cell imaging, and in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) we stained fixed cells for the pro-apoptotc protein BAX at mitochondria. Here, we provide a description of these two large-scale microscopy datasets. Dataset 1 contains 637,632 images of MEFs imaged as time series after labelling of mitochondrial morphology and integrity with the mitochondrial membrane potential-sensitive dye tetramethylrhodamine-ethylester (TMRE) and apoptosis with Annexin V-FITC. The dataset also contains a digital phase contrast channel which can be useful to track cells. Dataset 2 contains 9,504 images of hiPSCs with immunofluorescence labelling of BAX and COX IV. The datasets are made available through the BioImage Archive repository.
